skills.name: Art History
skills.description: From handprints on cave walls to street art, and how to look closely at any work of art.

skills.name: World Geography
skills.description: From reading a map to the mountains, rivers, climates and peoples of every continent.

skills.name: Ancient Rome
skills.description: From a village on the Tiber to an empire around the Mediterranean, and why it still shapes our laws, words and cities.

skills.name: How Money Works
skills.description: From barter and coins to banks, markets, inflation and trade: the ideas behind every price you pay.

skills.name: Astronomy
skills.description: From your cosmic address to the edge of the observable universe: the flagship 1–100 tree.

skills.name: Everyday Technology
skills.description: How the things around you actually work, from light bulbs and engines to phones, the internet and AI.

skills.name: The Middle Ages
skills.description: From Rome's fall in the West to the printing press: castles, crusades, plague and the wider medieval world.

skills.name: The Human Body
skills.description: From a single cell to bones, blood, brain and senses: how your body works and how to keep it working.

skills.name: Ancient Egypt
skills.description: Three thousand years on the Nile: pharaohs, pyramids, gods, hieroglyphs and how we rediscovered it all.

skills.name: The Animal Kingdom
skills.description: Mammals, birds, reptiles, sea life and insects: how animals live, survive, behave and evolve.

concepts.title: Abu Simbel
concepts.description: Ramesses II’s two cliff temples at Abu Simbel, and their 1960s rescue from the Aswan High Dam’s lake.

concepts.title: Amulets: scarab and wedjat eye
concepts.description: The scarab stood for the reborn sun and rebirth; heart scarabs and the wedjat eye protected the living and the dead.

concepts.title: Preparing for eternity
concepts.description: Egyptians prepared for life after death step by step: mummy, Opening of the Mouth, spells, amulets and shabtis, then judgment.

concepts.title: Alexander in Egypt
concepts.description: Alexander the Great took Egypt from Persia without a fight in 332 BCE, was crowned and hailed as son of Amun, founded Alexandria, and was buried there after his death.

concepts.title: Alexandria’s lighthouse and library
concepts.description: Alexandria, Egypt’s capital for nearly a thousand years, had the Pharos lighthouse and a library that tried to collect every book; the library declined gradually, for debated reasons.

concepts.title: Animal mummies
concepts.description: Egyptians mummified pets, food, sacred animals and, by the million, animals bought as offerings to gods.

concepts.title: Egypt before the pharaohs
concepts.description: Farming villages appeared in Egypt by about 5000 BCE; Badarian potters and later towns followed, and Upper Egyptian culture spread north.

concepts.title: Black land, red land
concepts.description: Kemet, the narrow black land of the Nile valley, fed Egypt; Deshret, the red desert around it, was used for burials and guarded the borders.

concepts.title: The Book of the Dead
concepts.description: A papyrus roll of spells for the afterlife, grown from the royal Pyramid Texts and the Coffin Texts, bought and personalized by those who could afford it.

concepts.title: Egypt’s 365-day calendar
concepts.description: The civil calendar had 12 months of 30 days plus 5 extra days; the rising of Sirius marked New Year, and without leap years the calendar drifted through the seasons.

concepts.title: Champollion cracks hieroglyphs
concepts.description: Building on Thomas Young’s work on the name Ptolemy, Champollion showed in 1822 that hieroglyphs mix sound signs with signs for ideas, using Coptic and names like Ramesses.

concepts.title: Cleopatra VII
concepts.description: The last Ptolemaic ruler: Macedonian Greek by family, the first of her line to learn Egyptian, and Rome’s rival.

concepts.title: Bread and beer
concepts.description: Bread and beer, both made from grain, were the staples of the Egyptian diet; beer was thick and nourishing, and food rations served as pay.

concepts.title: Cats in Egypt
concepts.description: Cats protected Egypt's grain, were loved as pets and were linked to the goddess Bastet.

concepts.title: Growing up in Egypt
concepts.description: Egyptian children wore the sidelock of youth; only elite children had a chance at schooling, and most learned by working from a young age.

concepts.title: Games and music
concepts.description: Egyptians played board games such as senet and mehen and made music with harps, flutes, singers and the sistrum.

concepts.title: How we know daily life
concepts.description: Ordinary Egyptian life is known from clues such as teeth, fingerprints, lost towns and the everyday writing of Deir el-Medina.

concepts.title: Linen and eye paint
concepts.description: Egyptians dressed mainly in linen, and both men and women wore eye paint, which may also have had practical uses.

concepts.title: Homes of mud brick
concepts.description: Egyptians built houses and even palaces of sun-dried Nile mud brick, kept them cool with high windows and roof vents, and saved stone for tombs and temples.

concepts.title: Women's legal rights
concepts.description: Egyptian women could own property, make contracts and go to court in their own name, but society was not equal.

concepts.title: Work and trades
concepts.description: Nearly all Egyptians farmed; craftsmen worked beside them, pay came as rations, and the Satire of the Trades mocked every job but the scribe's.

concepts.title: From pharaohs to foreign rulers
concepts.description: After the New Kingdom, Egypt passed from native pharaohs through Libyan, Kushite, Persian, Macedonian Greek, Roman and Arab rulers, most of whom presented themselves as pharaohs.

concepts.title: Deir el-Medina
concepts.description: The New Kingdom village of the royal tomb builders, whose ostraca and papyri record daily life and the first recorded strike.

concepts.title: Dynasties and dates
concepts.description: Egyptians counted years by reigns; Manetho grouped kings into 30 dynasties, which historians group into kingdoms. Dates before 664 BCE are approximate.

concepts.title: Old, Middle and New Kingdoms
concepts.description: Egyptian history peaks in three kingdoms (Old, Middle, New), separated by Intermediate Periods when the country split.

concepts.title: Egypt’s legacy
concepts.description: Our calendar descends from Egypt’s solar calendar via Julius Caesar, the letter A from an ox-head sign, and the word paper from papyrus.

concepts.title: Egyptian numbers and fractions
concepts.description: Egyptians wrote numbers by repeating signs for 1, 10, 100 and 1,000, used unit fractions, and applied math to practical problems like measuring fields.

concepts.title: Myths about Egypt
concepts.description: Evidence answers popular myths: paid workers, not slaves, built the Giza pyramids; builders’ records like Merer’s logbook leave no room for aliens; the curse and Cleopatra’s looks are shakier than their fame.

concepts.title: Three thousand years
concepts.description: Ancient Egypt lasted about 3,000 years, from unification around 3100 to 3000 BCE to Roman rule in 30 BCE.

concepts.title: Egyptomania
concepts.description: Napoleon’s scholars and their Description de l’Egypte, then Champollion’s decipherment, set off a Western craze for Egyptian style, from buildings to obelisks shipped to London and New York.

concepts.title: Jewelry, faience and glass
concepts.description: Egyptian jewelry paired gold with carnelian, turquoise and lapis lazuli, or with faience and glass made to imitate them; faience came first, glass much later.

concepts.title: Famous pharaohs compared
concepts.description: Egypt’s famous rulers owe their fame to different things: a pyramid, a tomb, building and spin, or Rome.

concepts.title: Farming by the flood
concepts.description: The Egyptian year ran in three seasons set by the Nile: flood, then plowing and sowing in the wet silt, then harvest and low water.

concepts.title: Egypt’s many gods
concepts.description: Egyptians worshipped hundreds of gods, pictured as humans, animals or animal-headed humans, whose animal forms expressed their natures.

concepts.title: Taxes without coins
concepts.description: Egypt taxed in goods and labor, stored grain in state granaries, set taxes by the flood height, and had no coins until the mid-first millennium BCE.

concepts.title: The Great Pyramid of Giza
concepts.description: Khufu’s Great Pyramid, about 146 m tall and built of some 2.3 million blocks, was the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years.

concepts.title: The Great Sphinx
concepts.description: The Great Sphinx was carved from a block left in a quarry at Giza, most likely for Khafre in the 4th dynasty; it has a lion’s body and a king’s head.

concepts.title: Hatshepsut
concepts.description: Hatshepsut went from great royal wife to regent to king (about 1473 to 1458 BCE), was shown with the king’s regalia, and was later partly erased for reasons still debated.

concepts.title: How hieroglyphs work
concepts.description: Hieroglyphs look like pictures, but most signs stood for sounds (consonants only); meaning signs such as determinatives showed what kind of word was meant.

concepts.title: How hieroglyphs were forgotten
concepts.description: The last known hieroglyphs were carved in 394 CE; Egyptians switched to a Greek-based alphabet (Coptic), and later scholars like Horapollo misread the signs as symbols.

concepts.title: Kadesh and the first peace treaty
concepts.description: The Battle of Kadesh ended in a draw that Ramesses sold as victory, and led to the oldest surviving peace treaty.

concepts.title: Khufu
concepts.description: The builder of the Great Pyramid is known from few records and one tiny ivory statuette.

concepts.title: The Nubian pharaohs of Kush
concepts.description: Kush, a major Nubian civilization south of Egypt, conquered Egypt and ruled it as the 25th Dynasty, then carried on for about a thousand years more, building many pyramids.

concepts.title: Ma’at: order and justice
concepts.description: Ma’at meant truth, justice and cosmic order, opposed to isfet (chaos). Keeping it was the king’s central duty, and the Tale of the Eloquent Peasant shows it applied to everyone.

concepts.title: Mastaba tombs
concepts.description: Before pyramids, Egyptians built mastabas: flat-topped, bench-shaped tombs over a shaft to a buried chamber, with a chapel above for offerings.

concepts.title: The medical papyri
concepts.description: Two medical papyri show Egyptian medicine: the Edwin Smith Papyrus, a chiefly practical casebook of injuries, and the Ebers Papyrus, full of remedies and spells.

concepts.title: Studying Egypt today
concepts.description: Muon scans find hidden spaces in the Great Pyramid, CT scans unwrap mummies digitally, and infrared satellite images reveal buried buildings.

concepts.title: Mummification: why and how
concepts.description: Egyptians preserved the body for the ka and ba; over about 70 days embalmers removed organs, dried the body in natron and wrapped it in linen.

concepts.title: The mummy’s curse
concepts.description: The curse of Tutankhamun’s tomb is a myth born of a mosquito bite, newspapers and older fiction.

concepts.title: Narmer and unification
concepts.description: Upper and Lower Egypt became one kingdom around 3100 to 3000 BCE. Tradition credits Menes; the Narmer Palette shows both crowns, but its meaning is debated.

concepts.title: Akhenaten and the Aten
concepts.description: Akhenaten raised the sun disc Aten above Amun, built Akhetaten (Amarna) and attacked Amun's name; whether it was monotheism is debated, and it did not outlast him.

concepts.title: The Amarna Letters
concepts.description: Clay tablets in Akkadian cuneiform show great kings writing to the pharaoh as brothers and vassals begging for his attention.

concepts.title: An Egyptian empire
concepts.description: After the Hyksos, New Kingdom kings built buffer zones that grew into an empire, from Nubia's gold to the Euphrates.

concepts.title: The Hyksos
concepts.description: Rulers of foreign lands from Southwest Asia held northern Egypt from Avaris, brought the horse and chariot, and were driven out by Ahmose, who began the New Kingdom.

concepts.title: Karnak
concepts.description: Karnak at Thebes, Egypt's largest temple complex, was the house of Amun-Re and grew rich on the New Kingdom's victories.

concepts.title: Nefertiti
concepts.description: Akhenaten's queen had an unusually royal role in art; her bust was found at Amarna in 1912, and whether she later ruled is debated.

concepts.title: The voyage to Punt
concepts.description: Egypt sailed the Red Sea to Punt for incense, gold and baboons, carrying ships across the desert; Punt's location is still debated.

concepts.title: The New Kingdom story
concepts.description: From Hyksos rule to empire, Amun's wealth, hidden royal tombs and Akhenaten's short-lived revolution.

concepts.title: Thutmose III
concepts.description: Thutmose III won at Megiddo by a bold route, fought 17 campaigns, raised conquered princes at court and turned buffer zones into an empire.

concepts.title: The Valley of the Kings
concepts.description: New Kingdom kings hid rock-cut tombs in a desert valley at Thebes, with temples built apart; almost all were robbed anyway.

concepts.title: How the Nile made Egypt
concepts.description: River, flood, black land, guarding desert and the joining of two lands add up to one story of how Egypt began and why it lasted.

concepts.title: The Nile’s yearly flood
concepts.description: Summer rains in Ethiopia made the Nile flood Egypt each year, leaving fertile silt on fields in an almost rainless land.

concepts.title: The Nile as Egypt’s road
concepts.description: The north-flowing Nile and the north wind made a two-way road: drift north on the current, sail south with the wind, as far as the First Cataract.

concepts.title: The end of the old gods
concepts.description: Christianity spread through Egypt and the temples closed, the last at Philae in the 6th century; after the Arab conquest of 640 to 642 CE, Egypt became Muslim only gradually.

concepts.title: The myth of Osiris and Isis
concepts.description: Seth killed Osiris; Isis gathered him, Anubis made him the first mummy, Horus avenged him, and Osiris ruled the dead, a promise every Egyptian shared.

concepts.title: Papyrus: paper from a reed
concepts.description: Papyrus sheets were made from crossed strips of a marsh plant pressed so its own sap glued them, then pasted into rolls.

concepts.title: Persian rule
concepts.description: Persia conquered Egypt in 525 BCE; its kings ruled as pharaohs until a revolt restored native kings from 404 to 343 BCE, and Persian rule ended with Alexander in 332 BCE.

concepts.title: Egypt’s army
concepts.description: Early Egypt relied on local militias; horse, chariot and composite bow arrived in the Second Intermediate Period; New Kingdom chariots carried a driver and an archer.

concepts.title: Royal names and the cartouche
concepts.description: A pharaoh had five names; the throne and birth names were written in a protective oval called a cartouche.

concepts.title: Viziers and scribes
concepts.description: The vizier was the chief administrator and judge under the king; the New Kingdom had two, for Upper and Lower Egypt. Provinces had their own officials, and government ran on writing that few could read.

concepts.title: How pharaohs held Egypt together
concepts.description: Ma’at gave the king his job; regalia announced it, officials and scribes ran it, grain taxes paid for it and the army defended it.

concepts.title: What a pharaoh was
concepts.description: The Egyptian king judged, kept the gods content and set order in place of disorder; his divinity came from his office. The word pharaoh (per-aa, great house) meant the palace and was used for the king only from the New Kingdom.

concepts.title: Priests and kings
concepts.description: After the New Kingdom, Egypt split: 21st Dynasty kings ruled the north from Tanis while the High Priests of Amun ruled the south from Thebes, rescuing robbed royal mummies.

concepts.title: The Ptolemies
concepts.description: Ptolemy, Alexander’s Macedonian general, founded a dynasty that ruled Egypt for almost 300 years, presenting itself to Egyptians as pharaohs while keeping its own Greek ways.

concepts.title: Why pyramids stopped
concepts.description: Pyramids advertised treasure. Later pyramids were smaller, robbers beat even Amenemhat III’s maze, and New Kingdom kings chose hidden tombs instead.

concepts.title: The pyramid age
concepts.description: From mastaba to Step Pyramid to true pyramid, then to hidden tombs: how and why Egyptians built pyramids.

concepts.title: Who built the pyramids
concepts.description: The builders’ cemetery, their skeletons and Merer’s logbook show the pyramids were built by Egyptian workers, called up in rotating crews and fed by the state, not by slaves.

concepts.title: Moving the stones
concepts.description: Blocks came by boat on the Nile, slid over wetted sand on sledges and went up ramps; exactly how the ramps worked is still debated.

concepts.title: The Pyramid Texts
concepts.description: The Pyramid Texts, first carved inside the pyramid of Unas in the 24th century BCE, are Egypt’s oldest surviving religious writings: spells and prayers for a dead king’s afterlife.

concepts.title: The Lost City of the pyramid builders
concepts.description: South of the Sphinx lay the builders’ town: galleries for crews, bakeries, silos and meat enough to feed thousands.

concepts.title: Ra’s daily journey
concepts.description: Egyptians believed the sun god Ra sailed the sky by day and the underworld by night, defeating the serpent Apophis to be reborn each dawn.

concepts.title: Ramesses the Great
concepts.description: Ramesses II reigned 66 years and put up more monuments and statues than any other pharaoh, borrowing older ones too.

concepts.title: Who owns the past?
concepts.description: Egyptian voices such as Zahi Hawass call for the return of the Rosetta Stone and the Nefertiti bust; the British Museum and Berlin’s museum argue they were acquired lawfully; Egypt opened the Grand Egyptian Museum in 2025.

concepts.title: Rome’s breadbasket
concepts.description: From 30 BCE Egypt was the Roman emperor’s own closely guarded province, and its Nile-fed grain helped feed the city of Rome.

concepts.title: The Rosetta Stone
concepts.description: Found by French soldiers in 1799, the Rosetta Stone carries one decree in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek, giving scholars a readable translation; it has been in the British Museum since 1802.

concepts.title: The royal court
concepts.description: Palaces were mud brick while temples were stone, so few survive; Malqata shows their painted splendor, and the harem could breed deadly plots.

concepts.title: Crook, flail and regalia
concepts.description: Royal regalia marked the office: the crook (the king as herdsman), the flail (meaning unclear, already on the Narmer Palette), the nemes headcloth, the uraeus cobra and the royal beard.

concepts.title: Royal women
concepts.description: Queenly roles were shared: the Great King’s Wife, other wives and the king’s mother. Tiye rose without royal blood; Sobekneferu ruled as monarch.

concepts.title: Training a scribe
concepts.description: In a land where very few could read, scribes trained in school, above all in hieratic, and wrote with reed brushes and black and red ink.

concepts.title: The Sea Peoples
concepts.description: Around 1177 BCE Ramesses III beat off the Sea Peoples, raiders of debated identity, but Egypt emerged diminished from the wider Late Bronze Age collapse.

concepts.title: Seti I
concepts.description: Seti I, father of Ramesses II, left the finest reliefs at Abydos, a selective king list and a fully decorated tomb.

concepts.title: Sneferu’s pyramids
concepts.description: Sneferu’s builders turned steps into smooth sides: Meidum was reworked, the Bent Pyramid changed angle when cracks appeared, and the Red Pyramid got it right.

concepts.title: Lining up buildings by the stars
concepts.description: Egyptians aligned buildings to the directions with star-sighting tools; one leading idea is that pyramid builders found north from two stars and a plumb line.

concepts.title: Djoser’s Step Pyramid
concepts.description: Imhotep turned Djoser’s mastaba into six stone steps at Saqqara: Egypt’s first pyramid and the world’s oldest known monumental stone building.

concepts.title: Temples as gods’ houses
concepts.description: Egyptian temples were homes for gods living in their statues, served daily by priests and seen by ordinary people mainly at festivals.

concepts.title: Stories on tomb walls
concepts.description: Tomb paintings such as Nebamun’s show daily life as the owner wished to be remembered and hoped to live after death: vivid, but idealised and made for the wealthy.

concepts.title: Tutankhamun, the boy king
concepts.description: A minor New Kingdom king who died young, famous because his small tomb survived nearly intact with its gold.

concepts.title: Finding Tutankhamun’s tomb
concepts.description: Funded by Lord Carnarvon, Howard Carter found Tutankhamun’s largely intact tomb in November 1922 and spent about ten years recording its 5,398 objects.

concepts.title: The Two Lands
concepts.description: Egypt was two lands, Upper Egypt (the southern valley) and Lower Egypt (the Delta), each with its own crown, joined in the double crown.

concepts.title: The weighing of the heart
concepts.description: Egyptians believed the dead were judged by weighing the heart against the feather of Maat; Ammit ate a failed heart, the worthy reached the Field of Reeds.

concepts.title: The Battle of Actium
concepts.description: Octavian’s fleet under Agrippa defeated Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BCE, leaving Octavian sole master of Rome.

concepts.title: The Battle of Adrianople
concepts.description: In 378 CE Goths who had crossed the Danube destroyed a Roman army and killed the emperor Valens.

concepts.title: Virgil and the Aeneid
concepts.description: Virgil’s epic of the Trojan Aeneas gave Rome a founding poem and Augustus a heroic ancestor.

concepts.title: Antony and Cleopatra
concepts.description: Mark Antony ruled the East in alliance with Cleopatra, giving Octavian a foreign enemy to fight.

concepts.title: Aqueducts
concepts.description: Gravity carried water along gentle slopes, mostly underground, to supply Roman cities.

concepts.title: Attila and the Huns
concepts.description: Attila extorted gold from the East, was stopped in Gaul in 451 and turned back from Italy in 452.

concepts.title: Augustus and the Principate
concepts.description: Augustus ruled as princeps, keeping the Republic’s forms while holding the real power.

concepts.title: The Roman baths
concepts.description: Heated public baths with hot, warm and cold rooms were cheap social centers for all classes.

concepts.title: Bread and circuses
concepts.description: Free grain and public games kept Rome’s crowds fed, entertained and loyal to the rulers who paid.

concepts.title: Caesar in Gaul
concepts.description: Caesar conquered Gaul in 58–50 BCE, beat Vercingetorix at Alesia and gained a loyal veteran army.

concepts.title: Caligula
concepts.description: A young emperor who began popular and became autocratic; much of his legend comes from hostile writers.

concepts.title: Cannae
concepts.description: In 216 BCE Hannibal encircled and destroyed a larger Roman army, yet Rome refused to make peace.

concepts.title: The destruction of Carthage
concepts.description: Urged on by Cato, Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE and made its land the province of Africa.

concepts.title: Carthage
concepts.description: A Phoenician trading city in North Africa that ruled the western Mediterranean’s seas and clashed with Rome over Sicily.

concepts.title: The empire of 395
concepts.description: By 395 the empire was Christian, ruled by distant monarchs, split in two and defended partly by Germanic allies.

concepts.title: Chariot racing
concepts.description: Rome’s most popular spectacle, raced by four color factions at the vast Circus Maximus.

concepts.title: A Christian empire
concepts.description: Under Theodosius, Christianity became the official religion and the old cults were shut down.

concepts.title: Cicero and Catiline
concepts.description: The great orator, consul in 63 BCE, exposed Catiline’s plot and executed conspirators without trial.

concepts.title: Roman citizenship
concepts.description: Citizenship spread from Rome to Italy and the provinces until Caracalla extended it to almost all free people in 212.

concepts.title: Life in the city of Rome
concepts.description: A city of perhaps a million, where most lived in crowded insulae and public life centered on the Forum.

concepts.title: Augustus rebuilds Rome
concepts.description: Augustus and Agrippa filled Rome with temples and public works that advertised his piety and his peace.

concepts.title: Cincinnatus and civic virtue
concepts.description: The Roman ideal of the citizen who serves in a crisis and then gives power back.

concepts.title: Claudius and Britain
concepts.description: An emperor few took seriously, Claudius launched the conquest of Britain in 43 CE.

concepts.title: The Conflict of the Orders
concepts.description: Plebeians won political rights from the patricians over about two centuries, using walkouts as leverage.

concepts.title: Conquering Italy
concepts.description: Through the Samnite Wars, roads like the Via Appia and a network of allies, Rome came to control Italy by about 264 BCE.

concepts.title: Constantine
concepts.description: Constantine won at the Milvian Bridge, granted Christians tolerance and called the Council of Nicaea.

concepts.title: Constantinople
concepts.description: Constantine’s new Rome on the Bosporus, closer to the frontiers, lasted as a capital for over a thousand years.

concepts.title: Consuls
concepts.description: Two consuls, elected each year, led Rome and its armies; each could block the other.

concepts.title: Diocletian and the Tetrarchy
concepts.description: Diocletian ended the crisis with rule by four emperors, smaller provinces and a split between East and West.

concepts.title: How Rome began
concepts.description: A strategic river site, merging Latin villages, Etruscan influence and founding legends together explain early Rome.

concepts.title: Rome’s first villages
concepts.description: Archaeology shows Latin hilltop villages from about the 8th century BCE that merged into a town around a drained valley, the Forum.

concepts.title: The Eastern Roman Empire
concepts.description: The Greek-speaking “Byzantine” empire called itself Roman and lasted until 1453.

concepts.title: The Etruscans
concepts.description: Rome’s powerful northern neighbors, whose kings, symbols and rituals shaped early Rome.

concepts.title: Everyday Rome
concepts.description: Cramped homes pushed life into public spaces, bound together by patrons, gods, bread and games.

concepts.title: Fabius the Delayer
concepts.description: Fabius wore Hannibal down by avoiding battle; Rome’s loyal allies starved him of reinforcements.

concepts.title: 476: the last western emperor
concepts.description: Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 CE; historians debate how much actually changed.

concepts.title: The end of the kings
concepts.description: Tarquin the Proud was expelled in 509 BCE after the Lucretia scandal, and Romans swore never to have a king again.

concepts.title: The first Christians
concepts.description: A Jewish movement from Judaea spread through the empire’s cities, carried by its roads, peace and Greek.

concepts.title: The First Punic War
concepts.description: Rome built a navy, used the corvus boarding bridge, and won Sicily, its first province, in 241 BCE.

concepts.title: The First Triumvirate
concepts.description: The 60 BCE alliance of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus, which broke apart after Julia’s and Crassus’s deaths.

concepts.title: The Five Good Emperors
concepts.description: From 96 to 180 CE, emperors chosen by adoption gave Rome its most stable era; Commodus ended it.

concepts.title: The Flavians and the Colosseum
concepts.description: Vespasian and his sons ruled from 69 to 96 CE and built the Colosseum on Nero’s palace grounds.

concepts.title: Romulus and Remus
concepts.description: Rome’s founding legend: twins raised by a she-wolf, a fratricide, and a city named for Romulus.

concepts.title: The Year of the Four Emperors
concepts.description: In 69 CE four men held power in turn, each backed by an army; Vespasian won and founded the Flavian dynasty.

concepts.title: Life on the frontier
concepts.description: Forts, auxiliaries and the towns beside them held the limes, as the Vindolanda letters reveal.

concepts.title: The Gallic sack of Rome
concepts.description: Around 390 BCE Gauls under Brennus sacked Rome; afterwards the city built a great stone wall.

concepts.title: Gladiators
concepts.description: Mostly enslaved or condemned fighters in set types; many bouts ended without a death, and the thumb signal is uncertain.

concepts.title: The Gracchi
concepts.description: Two tribunes who tried to give land to poor citizens and were killed, bringing violence into Roman politics.

concepts.title: Hadrian and his wall
concepts.description: Hadrian stopped expanding, toured the frontiers and fortified them, most famously in northern Britain.

concepts.title: Hannibal crosses the Alps
concepts.description: In 218 BCE Hannibal marched from Spain over the Alps with elephants to invade Italy, starting the Second Punic War.

concepts.title: How Rome held an empire
concepts.description: Roads, citizenship, law, trade and a shared army bound the empire together, not force alone.

concepts.title: The Ides of March
concepts.description: Made dictator for life, Caesar was assassinated on 15 March 44 BCE, but his death did not save the Republic.

concepts.title: Julian the Apostate
concepts.description: Constantine’s nephew tried to restore the old gods, but died in Persia after less than two years.

concepts.title: The Julian calendar
concepts.description: Caesar’s 365-day calendar with a leap year; July and August were renamed for Caesar and Augustus.

concepts.title: Latin and its descendants
concepts.description: Rome’s language spread west, became the Romance languages and still fills English.

concepts.title: Rome in our words, calendars and cities
concepts.description: Roman towns, grids, columns, mottoes and months still shape the world.

concepts.title: Rome in our laws and governments
concepts.description: Senates, vetoes, capitols, balanced constitutions and civil law all come from Rome.

concepts.title: The legion
concepts.description: Citizen soldiers in flexible maniples and three lines, armed with the gladius and pilum.

concepts.title: Marius and the army
concepts.description: Marius opened the legions to the landless poor, who then looked to their generals rather than the Senate.

concepts.title: Master of the Mediterranean
concepts.description: By 146 BCE the Punic and Macedonian wars had made Rome the Mediterranean’s dominant power, ruling provinces through governors.

concepts.title: How the Republic worked
concepts.description: Consuls, Senate and assemblies each checked the others, a “mixed constitution” admired by Polybius.

concepts.title: Money and trade
concepts.description: Silver coins carried the emperor’s face; amphorae carried wine, oil and garum across a connected Mediterranean.

concepts.title: Nero and the Great Fire
concepts.description: Nero, emperor from 54 CE, blamed the Christians for the fire of 64 CE; his death in 68 CE ended Augustus’ line.

concepts.title: Octavian, Caesar’s heir
concepts.description: Caesar’s adopted heir used his name, the Second Triumvirate and victory at Philippi to build his power.

concepts.title: The Pantheon
concepts.description: Hadrian’s temple has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, lit by a single open oculus.

concepts.title: The Pax Romana
concepts.description: About 200 years of relative peace, from Augustus to Marcus Aurelius, in which trade and cities flourished.

concepts.title: Persecution
concepts.description: Local and sporadic at first, persecution became empire-wide under Decius and harshest under Diocletian.

concepts.title: Pompeii and Vesuvius
concepts.description: The eruption of 79 CE buried Pompeii and preserved an ordinary Roman town for historians.

concepts.title: Pompey the Great
concepts.description: A general of extraordinary commands who swept the pirates from the sea and reorganized the East.

concepts.title: Running the provinces
concepts.description: Governors, taxes and local elites ran a vast empire with very few Roman officials.

concepts.title: The Roman Republic
concepts.description: A state run by elected officials with limited terms, the “Senate and People of Rome.”

concepts.title: From Republic to Empire
concepts.description: Violence and loyal armies turned the Republic into one-man rule that kept republican forms.

concepts.title: The arc of Roman history
concepts.description: From 753 BCE to 1453 CE, one thread runs through it: whoever held the army held the state.

concepts.title: Roman concrete
concepts.description: Lime and volcanic ash made a concrete that set underwater, shaped domes and has lasted two thousand years.

concepts.title: How we know about Rome
concepts.description: Historians weigh biased texts against inscriptions, coins and archaeology.

concepts.title: The Roman family
concepts.description: The paterfamilias held legal power over his descendants; the familia included the whole household.

concepts.title: What Romans ate
concepts.description: Grain, oil and wine for most; reclining banquets for the rich; garum fish sauce for everyone.

concepts.title: The seven kings
concepts.description: Tradition counts seven kings from 753 to 509 BCE, chosen with the approval of the Senate and people.

concepts.title: Roman law
concepts.description: From the Twelve Tables to Justinian’s code, Roman law became the base of the world’s civil law systems.

concepts.title: Roman religion
concepts.description: Correct ritual kept the peace of the gods, from household spirits to Jupiter’s temple, Vesta’s fire and augury.

concepts.title: Roman roads
concepts.description: A vast network of layered, drained, straight roads built for the army and used by everyone.

concepts.title: Roman women
concepts.description: Women could own property and wield influence, but could not vote or hold office.

concepts.title: Rome turns east
concepts.description: Rome defeated Macedon and came to dominate Greece, while Greek culture transformed Rome.

concepts.title: Rome’s three eras
concepts.description: Roman history runs from the Kingdom to the Republic (509 BCE) to the Empire (27 BCE); the West fell in 476 CE and the East in 1453.

concepts.title: An empire around a sea
concepts.description: At its height Rome ruled every coast of the Mediterranean, which Romans called “our sea.”

concepts.title: Seven hills and a river
concepts.description: Rome grew at a crossing of the Tiber on a trade route, on defensible hills, with Ostia as its port.

concepts.title: Crossing the Rubicon
concepts.description: In 49 BCE Caesar led his army across the Rubicon into Italy, starting a civil war he won at Pharsalus.

concepts.title: The sack of Rome, 410
concepts.description: Alaric’s Visigoths sacked Rome in 410 CE, a shock that led Augustine to write The City of God.

concepts.title: Scipio and Zama
concepts.description: Scipio took Spain, invaded Africa and beat Hannibal at Zama in 202 BCE, ending the Second Punic War.

concepts.title: The Senate
concepts.description: Former magistrates, usually for life, whose advice on war, diplomacy and money was almost always followed.

concepts.title: Slavery in Rome
concepts.description: Enslaved people did every kind of work; many were freed, and freed slaves of citizens became citizens.

concepts.title: Spartacus
concepts.description: A gladiator who led a huge slave revolt from 73 BCE until Crassus crushed it in 71 BCE.

concepts.title: Sulla
concepts.description: The first general to march on Rome; as dictator without a time limit he killed enemies by proscription.

concepts.title: The Teutoburg Forest
concepts.description: In 9 CE Arminius destroyed three legions under Varus, and Rome settled on the Rhine as its frontier.

concepts.title: The Crisis of the Third Century
concepts.description: From 235 to 284 CE, rapid-fire emperors, invasions, plague and inflation nearly broke the empire apart.

concepts.title: Tiberius and succession
concepts.description: Augustus’ adopted stepson ruled from 14 to 37 CE; with no law of succession, every heir was a gamble.

concepts.title: Trajan
concepts.description: The first emperor from outside Italy conquered Dacia and brought the empire to its greatest extent in 117 CE.

concepts.title: Tribunes of the plebs
concepts.description: Plebeian officials who could veto any magistrate and who were sacrosanct.

concepts.title: The Twelve Tables
concepts.description: Rome’s first written laws, displayed in the Forum around 450 BCE so everyone could know them.

concepts.title: Why did Rome fall?
concepts.description: Invasions, civil wars and lost revenue broke the West; some historians prefer to speak of transformation.

concepts.title: Two foxes fitted to heat and cold
concepts.description: The desert fennec fox has the largest ears for its size in the dog family, which shed heat, plus furry paws and a daytime burrow; the Arctic fox's small ears reduce heat loss.

concepts.title: What an adaptation is
concepts.description: An adaptation fits living things to their environment and improves their chances of survival there; it can be a body feature or a behavior. Individuals don't adapt: populations do, over generations.

concepts.title: Chytrid and the amphibian crisis
concepts.description: The chytrid fungus attacks amphibian skin and upsets the body's salt balance until the heart stops; it has driven declines in at least 501 species, and IUCN's 2023 assessment found 41% of amphibian species threatened.

concepts.title: Amphibians: a double life
concepts.description: 'Amphibian' loosely means 'dual life'; many start life in water and change shape as they grow; most lay soft, shell-less eggs in water or damp places; the class has three branches: frogs, salamanders and caecilians.

concepts.title: Amphibian skin drinks and breathes
concepts.description: Amphibians have moist, permeable skin kept wet by mucus glands; they take in most of their water through it and use it as one of their breathing surfaces.

concepts.title: The main groups of animals
concepts.description: The animal kingdom includes five familiar groups (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish) and a huge crowd of animals without backbones, from insects and crabs to snails, worms, jellyfish, sea stars and sponges.

concepts.title: What makes an animal an animal
concepts.description: Animals are many-celled organisms whose cells lack cell walls; they eat other living or dead things, and most can move at some stage of life. Sponges pass the test.

concepts.title: How an ant colony works
concepts.description: An ant colony’s queen lays the eggs; the workers are sterile females who build, defend and feed; males only mate and then die. Some ants lay pheromone scent trails for nestmates to follow.

concepts.title: Leafcutter ants farm fungus
concepts.description: Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they cut: they feed them to a fungus they grow, and the fungus feeds the colony. Ants farmed fungus tens of millions of years before people farmed.

concepts.title: How antivenom is made
concepts.description: Since Albert Calmette's cobra antivenom in the 1890s, antivenom has been made by giving horses (or sheep) small doses of venom and collecting the antibodies their immune systems make.

concepts.title: Apes and monkeys
concepts.description: Apes are tailless primates, unlike most monkeys. The great apes are gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans, and humans are in the same family.

concepts.title: Archaeopteryx, part bird and part dinosaur
concepts.description: Archaeopteryx, about 150 million years old and found in Germany from 1861, had feathers like a bird but teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail like small theropod dinosaurs.

concepts.title: Arthropods: jointed feet
concepts.description: Insects, spiders and crustaceans are arthropods: jointed outer skeletons of chitin and protein, segmented bodies and jointed legs. About 84 percent of described animal species are arthropods; mollusks like snails are not.

concepts.title: How the bald eagle recovered
concepts.description: DDT passed from water to fish to bald eagles and thinned their eggshells; by 1963 only 417 nesting pairs were known in the lower 48 states. After the 1972 DDT ban, eagles recovered and left the endangered list in 2007; USFWS estimates about 316,700 today.

concepts.title: Bats: one mammal species in five
concepts.description: There are more than 1,300 bat species, about one in five of all mammal species.

concepts.title: Echolocation
concepts.description: Many bats find their way and their food by echolocation: they call, mostly in ultrasound, and listen for the echoes, calling faster as they close in on an insect.

concepts.title: The only flying mammals
concepts.description: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight; the wing is a modified hand with skin stretched between long fingers.

concepts.title: How honeybees make honey and wax
concepts.description: Honeybee workers (all females) turn nectar into honey with enzymes, fan it with their wings to evaporate water, and seal it in comb built from wax made by their own glands. Honey is about 18 percent water.

concepts.title: How bees pollinate flowers
concepts.description: Pollination moves pollen from a flower’s anther to a stigma. Pollen catches in a bee’s branched hairs as she feeds and rubs off on the next flower; honeybees also carry pollen home in leg baskets.

concepts.title: Decoding the bee dance
concepts.description: Karl von Frisch decoded the bee dance and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize with Lorenz and Tinbergen. The 1973 view was that the dance is inborn; a 2023 study showed young bees also learn it from experienced dancers.

concepts.title: Courtship signals
concepts.description: Courtship runs on signals: songs that name the species and draw mates, displays performed step by step, and the satin bowerbird's decorated stage of sticks.

concepts.title: Why animals live in groups
concepts.description: Groups dilute each member's risk, confuse predators and help hunters corner prey. They also cost something: competition for food, and a crowd can draw predators.

concepts.title: Imprinting
concepts.description: Imprinting is fast learning in an early critical period: a hatchling learns to follow the first moving thing it sees. Lorenz's ducklings followed him; Tex the whooping crane imprinted on people, so crane chicks are now raised by keepers in crane costumes.

concepts.title: Instinct and learning
concepts.description: Instincts are innate behaviors performed without practice, like a gull chick pecking at the red spot on its parent's bill. Learned behaviors are shaped by experience, like prairie dogs tuning out harmless footsteps. Most behavior mixes both.

concepts.title: Mate choice
concepts.description: In many species one sex chooses and the other competes to be chosen. Peahens favor the most showy peacocks, so traits that win mates spread even when they make survival harder.

concepts.title: The mirror mark test
concepts.description: Gordon Gallup Jr.'s 1970 test puts a mark where an animal can see it only in a mirror. Great apes, dolphins, elephants and magpies have passed, but often only some individuals.

concepts.title: Limits of the mirror test
concepts.description: The mirror test is a sight test. Dogs, who live by smell, fail it but react to changes in their own scent; a fish that passed was doubted even by the test's inventor.

concepts.title: The price of parental care
concepts.description: Care costs future offspring, so animals trade many young with little care against few young with a lot. Mammal mothers carry and nurse their young; orangutans sit at the extreme.

concepts.title: Why young animals play
concepts.description: Play looks useless and costs energy. It may not be simple practice: young elk never head-butt in play. Rats deprived of play grow up anxious and socially clumsy, so play seems to train social judgment.

concepts.title: Play signals and fair play
concepts.description: Canids ask to play with a bow, a signal used almost only in play. Players keep it fair by holding back and letting the other win sometimes.

concepts.title: Seahorse fathers
concepts.description: Male-only care is rare. In seahorses and pipefishes the male carries the eggs: the female places them in his brood pouch, and he gives birth to young that get no further care.

concepts.title: How animals send signals
concepts.description: A signal is information one animal gives off that another can use to decide what to do. Signals travel by smell (pheromones), sound, sight and touch; displays can even replace a fight.

concepts.title: Key stimuli and supernormal stimuli
concepts.description: Instincts are triggered by a few key features. Tinbergen tested gull chicks with dummy bills and found that exaggerating those features makes a supernormal stimulus that beats the real thing.

concepts.title: What counts as a tool
concepts.description: In 1960 Jane Goodall saw chimpanzees use and make tools to fish for termites, overturning the idea that only humans do. A tool pays off only when it is used for a job, which is why a hermit crab's shell doesn't count.

concepts.title: Tool users beyond chimps
concepts.description: Sea otters crack prey with rocks, which spares their teeth; veined octopuses carry coconut shells to build shelters later, the first known tool use by an invertebrate.

concepts.title: Vervet monkey alarm calls
concepts.description: Vervet monkeys give different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes. Played back with no predator present, each call still triggers the right escape.

concepts.title: The honeybee waggle dance
concepts.description: A forager does a round dance for food near the hive and a waggle dance for food farther away. The waggle run's angle from straight up on the comb gives the direction relative to the sun; its duration gives the distance.

concepts.title: Wolf packs are families
concepts.description: The "alpha wolf" came from captive packs of unrelated wolves. In the wild, L. David Mech found, a pack is a family: a breeding pair and their young, led by the parents.

concepts.title: The Big Five mass extinctions
concepts.description: Most species that ever lived are extinct, and five times the fossil record shows mass extinctions: the Ordovician-Silurian, Late Devonian, end-Permian (the worst, about 90 percent of species), end-Triassic and end-Cretaceous.

concepts.title: Lions in prides, tigers alone
concepts.description: Lions are the most social cats, living in prides of related females with their cubs and resident males, and the lionesses do most of the hunting. Tigers, the largest cats, live alone.

concepts.title: Why big cats roar
concepts.description: Lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars (genus Panthera) often roar; smaller cats have a fully hardened hyoid bone that prevents roaring. A lion's roar marks territory and carries up to five miles.

concepts.title: Two-part scientific names
concepts.description: Carl Linnaeus gave each species a two-part scientific name, genus then species, replacing long descriptive phrases; the system is used internationally, so one name points to one species. Zoological names start from 1758.

concepts.title: Biomimicry and Velcro
concepts.description: Biomimicry imitates natural designs in engineering. Velcro came from burdock burrs (a plant) that stuck to George de Mestral and his dog: tiny hooks, paired with loops, patented in 1955.

concepts.title: Kingfisher trains and gecko grippers
concepts.description: The 500 Series Shinkansen's nose copies the kingfisher's beak to end tunnel booms. Gecko toe hairs stick by van der Waals forces, and NASA JPL's gecko-inspired grippers work even in a vacuum.

concepts.title: Small brains, packed with neurons
concepts.description: A 2016 study found parrot and songbird brains hold about twice as many neurons as primate brains of the same mass; large-brained parrots and corvids match or beat primates with bigger brains in forebrain neurons.

concepts.title: What makes a bird a bird
concepts.description: Feathers set birds apart from all other animals; not every bird flies. Birds have toothless beaks (jaws in a horny sheath) and lay hard-shelled eggs.

concepts.title: Flight muscles and the keel
concepts.description: Flying birds anchor their flight muscles on the keel, a ridge on the breastbone. The large pectoralis pulls the wing down; the smaller supracoracoideus lifts it.

concepts.title: The ostrich: a bird that gave up flying
concepts.description: The ostrich, the largest living bird, cannot fly: like other ratites it has no keel on its breastbone to anchor flight muscles. It runs instead, on two-toed feet, and lays the world's largest egg.

concepts.title: Incubation and hatching
concepts.description: A sitting bird warms its eggs through a bare, blood-rich brood patch, near 38 °C, and turns them. The chick breaks out with an egg tooth that it soon loses.

concepts.title: A light skeleton for flight
concepts.description: In the largest flying birds part of the bone is replaced by air; hollow wing bones are braced by internal struts. A frigatebird's skeleton weighs less than its feathers.

concepts.title: Bird nests, from nothing to woven
concepts.description: Nests range from no real structure (falcons, owls, many seabirds and shorebirds) to woven weaver nests, built of twigs, leaves, mud, feathers or spiderwebs, from about 2 cm to more than 2 m across.

concepts.title: How a bird's wing lifts and pulls
concepts.description: A wing makes lift by turning the airflow, which pushes back the opposite way (Newton's third law). A bird's wing is also its propeller: the inner wing mostly lifts, the wing tip mostly pulls it forward.

concepts.title: Birds descend from theropod dinosaurs
concepts.description: Birds evolved from small meat-eating theropod dinosaurs, the group that includes T. rex. Feathered non-bird dinosaurs like Sinosauropteryx show feathers came before birds, and when the other dinosaurs died out, birds survived: they are living dinosaurs.

concepts.title: The food cost of making your own heat
concepts.description: Keeping a steady inside temperature costs energy: reptiles, with a low metabolic rate, need less food than endotherms of the same size and can go long periods without eating.

concepts.title: Endotherms and ectotherms
concepts.description: Endotherms (mainly mammals and birds) make most of their body heat inside and hold a steady temperature; ectotherms (fish, amphibians, reptiles, invertebrates) absorb it from their surroundings. "Cold-blooded" is misleading: a lizard can be warmer than some mammals.

concepts.title: Complete metamorphosis
concepts.description: A butterfly passes through four stages, egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis) and adult, a process called complete metamorphosis.

concepts.title: Rebuilding a caterpillar into a butterfly
concepts.description: Inside the chrysalis, a caterpillar dissolves most of its tissues into caterpillar soup, while imaginal discs, grown before it hatched, survive and build the adult’s wings, legs and eyes.

concepts.title: Camouflage: background matching, countershading and seasonal coats
concepts.description: Animals hide by matching their background in color, shape or movement, by countershading (dark back, pale belly) that flattens their look, and by changing coats with the seasons.

concepts.title: Toothed whales and baleen whales
concepts.description: Cetaceans split into toothed whales, which include dolphins and porpoises, and baleen whales, which strain small prey through keratin plates instead of teeth.

concepts.title: Whales and dolphins are mammals
concepts.description: Whales, dolphins and porpoises breathe air through blowholes, are warm-blooded, have hair at some stage and nurse their young. Dolphins rest half the brain at a time, and bottlenose calves nurse for about 20 months.

concepts.title: How chameleons change colour
concepts.description: A 2015 University of Geneva study showed panther chameleons shift colour by tuning a lattice of guanine nanocrystals in skin cells called iridophores: packed close they reflect blue, loosened they reflect yellows and reds.

concepts.title: Why chameleons change colour
concepts.description: Chameleons' dramatic colour changes are mainly signals to other chameleons and responses to temperature and light, not attempts to match the background; darkening helps an ectotherm warm up.

concepts.title: The asteroid that ended the non-bird dinosaurs
concepts.description: In 1980 the Alvarezes linked a worldwide iridium-rich clay layer to an asteroid impact. The Chicxulub crater on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula matches the extinction's age, 66 million years ago, and the impact is the most widely accepted cause.

concepts.title: The California condor and the humpback whale
concepts.description: By 1987 every wild California condor was in captive breeding; releases began in 1992 and there are now more than 500, though lead remains the top known killer. Humpbacks recovered after the 1985 whaling moratorium; in 2016 NOAA found 9 of 14 populations no longer needed listing.

concepts.title: Coral bleaching
concepts.description: Most corals house algae (zooxanthellae) that are their main food and color. Stressed corals, above all by warmer water, expel the algae and turn white; they can recover if the stress eases, or die if it lasts.

concepts.title: Coral is a colony of animals
concepts.description: A coral is hundreds to thousands of tiny animals called polyps, each building a limestone skeleton. Corals are animals because they catch food instead of making it, using stinging nematocysts like their jellyfish relatives.

concepts.title: Salt glands and saltwater crocodiles
concepts.description: Alligators lack salt glands and stay mostly in fresh water; crocodiles have salt glands in their tongues, which lets the saltwater crocodile, the largest living crocodilian, travel far out to sea.

concepts.title: Telling crocodiles from alligators
concepts.description: Crocodiles have narrow, V-shaped snouts and show some lower teeth with the mouth closed; alligators have broad, U-shaped snouts with lower teeth tucked inside, the big fourth tooth hidden in a socket.

concepts.title: Crocodilians, built to lurk
concepts.description: Crocodiles, alligators, caimans and gharials form the crocodilians; eyes, ears and nostrils on top of the head let them watch and breathe while hidden underwater.

concepts.title: New Caledonian crows make tools
concepts.description: Wild New Caledonian crows make standardized hook tools from twigs and pandanus leaves (Hunt, 1996). In a 2002 Oxford study, Betty bent a straight wire into a hook to lift food from a tube.

concepts.title: Crustaceans and their armor
concepts.description: Crabs, lobsters, shrimps and wood lice are crustaceans, with two pairs of antenna-like feelers and an outer skeleton stiffened with calcium carbonate.

concepts.title: Molting to grow
concepts.description: A rigid outer skeleton cannot grow, so crabs and lobsters molt: they climb out, stretch a soft new skeleton with water or air, and hide while it hardens. Lobsters often eat the old shell to regain calcium.

concepts.title: Darwin's voyage on the Beagle
concepts.description: From 1831 to 1836, the young Charles Darwin sailed around the world on HMS Beagle, collecting animals, plants and fossils. In South America he dug up giant ground sloths like Megatherium, extinct giants related to living sloths.

concepts.title: Island-to-island differences in the Galápagos
concepts.description: In the Galápagos, Darwin noticed mockingbirds differed from island to island. John Gould later showed they were separate species, and that Darwin's mixed bag of birds were all ground finches, which set Darwin wondering how they diverged. He published his theory in 1859.

concepts.title: Deep-sea animals that make light
concepts.description: Most deep-sea animals can glow: a 2017 MBARI study found three quarters of animals from the surface to 4,000 meters in Monterey Bay make light. Female anglerfish use a glowing lure lit by bacteria.

concepts.title: The dark, hungry deep sea
concepts.description: Below about 1,000 meters no sunlight reaches the ocean. Darkness, cold, pressure and distance from the sunlit plankton at the base of the food chain limit deep-sea life.

concepts.title: Armor, spines and spray
concepts.description: Some animals defend themselves with armor (the three-banded armadillo rolls into a ball), spines (porcupine quills that detach in an attacker) or chemicals (the skunk's aimed spray, announced by a warning).

concepts.title: Surviving with little water
concepts.description: A camel's hump is fat, not water; it drinks huge amounts at once and can then go nearly a week without. A kangaroo rat makes water from dry seeds and wastes almost none.

concepts.title: Sorting animals, and diets that change with age
concepts.description: Backbone, heat source and diet sort most animals, but some answers change with age: gray tree frog tadpoles eat algae and debris, while adults eat insects.

concepts.title: Herbivores, carnivores and omnivores
concepts.description: Herbivores eat mainly plants, carnivores mostly meat, and omnivores regularly eat both; teeth often reveal which.

concepts.title: A diet label is not a family name
concepts.description: The giant panda belongs to the order Carnivora and kept a carnivore-like gut, yet it eats mostly bamboo: diet and classification answer different questions.

concepts.title: Why dinosaurs became so varied
concepts.description: Dinosaurs began on one supercontinent, Pangaea. As it split apart, dinosaurs on separate continents evolved independently and became more diverse, from Jurassic sauropods to Cretaceous titanosaurs.

concepts.title: Dinosaur eggs and nests
concepts.description: In 1978 a Maiasaura nesting site near Choteau, Montana, turned up nests of eggs, eggshells and babies; the babies could not yet walk but had worn teeth, so parents likely fed them. Dinosaurs laid eggs like the reptiles they were.

concepts.title: Naming the dinosaurs
concepts.description: After William Buckland described Megalosaurus in 1824, Richard Owen proposed the group Dinosauria in 1842, from Greek deinos ('terrible' or 'fearfully great') and sauros ('reptile' or 'lizard'); dinosaurs were a diverse group of reptiles.

concepts.title: What made a dinosaur a dinosaur
concepts.description: Dinosaurs held their legs straight under the body like pillars instead of sprawling like lizards, and had a hole through the hip socket; pterosaurs and sea reptiles such as plesiosaurs were reptiles on separate branches.

concepts.title: The Oberkassel puppy
concepts.description: About 14,000 years ago a sick puppy buried with two people at Oberkassel, Germany, survived for weeks only with human care: the earliest known evidence of dogs treated as pets.

concepts.title: Dogs came from ancient wolves
concepts.description: Dogs came from an ancient gray wolf population not well represented by wolves alive today, at least 15,000 years ago; where and how many times is still debated.

concepts.title: How cattle and horses were domesticated
concepts.description: All domestic cattle trace back to about 80 aurochs domesticated about 10,500 years ago in the Near East; the wild aurochs died out in 1627. Modern domestic horses come from the lower Volga-Don steppe around 2200 BCE and carry changes linked to docility and a stronger backbone.

concepts.title: Domestication versus taming
concepts.description: Domestication changes a line of animals by selective breeding over generations, often choosing calmer animals; taming changes only one animal's behavior. Dogs were the first animals domesticated, by hunter-gatherers.

concepts.title: Earthworm bodies breathe through skin
concepts.description: Earthworms have no lungs and breathe through moist skin; their bodies are chains of ringlike segments.

concepts.title: How earthworms help the soil
concepts.description: Earthworms eat decaying plants and soil, open burrows for air, water and roots, and leave casts richer than the surrounding soil. Darwin’s 1881 book estimated they move more than ten tons of earth per acre each year.

concepts.title: What an ecosystem is
concepts.description: An ecosystem is a place where living things and nonliving parts such as rocks, temperature and humidity work together; it can be as small as a tide pool, and every part depends on the others.

concepts.title: Elephant families and the matriarch's memory
concepts.description: African elephants live in female-led herds under a matriarch, usually the oldest female. Families led by older matriarchs are better at telling strangers' calls from familiar ones.

concepts.title: The elephant and its trunk
concepts.description: Elephants, in three living species, are the largest land animals. The trunk is a boneless fusion of nose and upper lip with about 150,000 muscle bundles, used to smell, breathe, trumpet, drink and grab.

concepts.title: Why species become endangered
concepts.description: Habitat loss is the most pervasive threat to species, alongside introduced species, climate change, pollution, overhunting and disease. The giant panda's biggest threat is habitat destruction; in 2016 IUCN moved it from Endangered to Vulnerable.

concepts.title: The 10 percent rule
concepts.description: On average only about 10 percent of the energy at one food-chain level passes to the next; the rest is lost as waste, heat and uneaten dead, which is why most ecosystems have at most five levels.

concepts.title: What "theory" means in science
concepts.description: In everyday talk a theory is a hunch; in science it is a comprehensive explanation of part of nature backed by a vast body of evidence. The National Academy of Sciences says there is no scientific controversy about the basic facts of evolution.

concepts.title: The dodo and the passenger pigeon
concepts.description: The dodo, a flightless relative of pigeons found only on Mauritius, was hunted and preyed on by animals sailors brought, and was gone by the late 1600s. Passenger pigeons numbered 3 to 5 billion but were slaughtered for markets; the last, Martha, died in 1914.

concepts.title: The thylacine
concepts.description: The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, was the largest meat-eating marsupial of recent times. Hunted as a threat to sheep, with a bounty from 1888 to 1909, it was protected in July 1936; the last known one died at Hobart Zoo on 7 September 1936.

concepts.title: Where farm animals came from and what they give
concepts.description: Chickens come from the red junglefowl and may first have been kept for fighting or religion. Cattle give meat, milk, hides and pulling power; high milk yields came from later breeding. Cattle, sheep and goats are ruminants that chew cud because they cannot digest cellulose directly.

concepts.title: Farm animals outweigh wild ones
concepts.description: By carbon mass, livestock make up about 60% of Earth's mammals, people about 36% and wild mammals about 4%; domestic poultry has almost three times the mass of all wild birds (2018 estimate).

concepts.title: Fins and scales
concepts.description: Paired pectoral fins steady and steer a fish, working with its back and tail fins; the scales of bony fishes are thin overlapping plates of bone that keep growing all its life.

concepts.title: How fish breathe with gills
concepts.description: Fish breathe through gills: water flows over blood-rich gill filaments, oxygen dissolved in the water passes into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes out.

concepts.title: The warm-blooded opah
concepts.description: Most fish species are cold-blooded, but the opah is warm-blooded, keeping warm with a heat-exchange system in its gills.

concepts.title: Fish: nearly half of all vertebrates
concepts.description: Of about 76,000 described vertebrate species in IUCN's 2025 table, about 37,000 are fish: nearly half of the backbone family.

concepts.title: Food chains and webs
concepts.description: A food chain runs from producers, which make their own food, through primary, secondary and tertiary consumers to apex predators, with decomposers recycling the dead; overlapping chains form a food web.

concepts.title: How fossils form
concepts.description: Fossils are rare: most dead things rot away. Quick burial in sediment is key, which is why around 99% of fossils are sea animals. In petrification, minerals left by water turn buried bones to stone. Body fossils are remains; trace fossils are signs like footprints.

concepts.title: Reading the age of fossils from rock layers
concepts.description: In undisturbed rock, lower layers were laid down first, so their fossils are older (superposition). Radiometric dating of volcanic ash above and below a fossil brackets its age, and comparing layers worldwide built the geologic timescale.

concepts.title: From tadpole to frog
concepts.description: A tadpole has gills and a finned tail and no legs; during metamorphosis hind legs sprout first, then lungs and front legs, the tail is absorbed, the mouth turns froglike and the gills disappear.

concepts.title: Thyroid hormone drives metamorphosis
concepts.description: In 1912 Friedrich Gudernatsch found that feeding tadpoles horse thyroid, and no other organ, sped up metamorphosis; removing a tadpole's thyroid stops it. Thyroid hormone directs the change.

concepts.title: The Grants' finches: selection seen in two years
concepts.description: On Daphne Major, Peter and Rosemary Grant saw a 1977 drought kill most medium ground finches; birds with larger beaks, able to crack big seeds, survived, and their offspring inherited larger beaks. Later rains reversed the trend.

concepts.title: Do bears truly hibernate?
concepts.description: Bears cool only a few degrees and wake fairly easily, so Britannica does not count them as true hibernators; a 2011 study found black bears cut metabolism to about 25 percent and called it hibernation.

concepts.title: Hibernation and torpor
concepts.description: Hibernation is a long, deep drop in metabolism and body temperature, with brief wake-ups every few weeks; torpor is the same slowdown on a shorter scale, sometimes just a few hours.

concepts.title: The hummingbird's engine
concepts.description: A ruby-throated hummingbird's heart runs from about 225 beats a minute at rest to more than 1,200 in flight. Hummingbirds are the only vertebrates that can hover for long, beating their wings about 70 times a second.

concepts.title: Hummingbird energy and torpor
concepts.description: Weighing 2 to 20 grams, with poor insulation and huge metabolic demands, hummingbirds can drop into torpor on cold nights; a black metaltail cooled to 3.3 °C in a 2020 study.

concepts.title: How many insects there are
concepts.description: About 1 million insect species have been described, and the Smithsonian estimates some 10 quintillion individual insects are alive at any one time. Both are estimates.

concepts.title: The insect body plan
concepts.description: An insect’s body has three parts: a head with a pair of antennae, a thorax carrying six legs and usually wings in adults, and an abdomen; its skeleton is on the outside.

concepts.title: What makes a species invasive
concepts.description: An invasive species causes ecological or economic harm in a place where it is not native. Most are moved by people. Invasives can compete with natives, change habitats and drive native species extinct.

concepts.title: Cane toads and brown treesnakes
concepts.description: Cane toads released in Queensland in 1935 to eat cane beetles barely affected the beetles but spread in the millions and poison native predators. Brown treesnakes that reached Guam in cargo helped wipe out 9 of its 11 native forest bird species.

concepts.title: Most animals are invertebrates
concepts.description: Invertebrates, animals without a backbone, are about 95 percent of described animal species; many wear a hard outer skeleton instead.

concepts.title: A body with no brain or heart
concepts.description: A jellyfish is about 95 percent water, with no brain, blood or heart; a nerve net senses its world, and one opening serves as mouth and anus.

concepts.title: How jellyfish sting
concepts.description: Jellyfish sting with nematocysts: capsules holding coiled harpoons that fire in about 700 nanoseconds, hard enough to pierce a crustacean shell.

concepts.title: Keystone species
concepts.description: A keystone species holds its ecosystem together, like the wedge stone at the top of an arch. Robert Paine showed it by removing sea stars from a Washington shore: mussels took over and variety collapsed.

concepts.title: The largest animal ever
concepts.description: The blue whale, a living mammal, is the largest animal known to have lived: up to about 33 meters and more than 150 metric tons, feeding almost only on tiny krill.

concepts.title: Egg, pouch or placenta
concepts.description: Mammals start life three ways: monotremes lay eggs, marsupials finish growing in a pouch, and placental mammals, everyone else, grow in the womb fed by a placenta. Elephants carry their young up to about 22 months.

concepts.title: How many mammal species there are
concepts.description: The Mammal Diversity Database (July 2026) lists about 6,800 living mammal species, a tiny share of all described animal species.

concepts.title: What makes a mammal
concepts.description: Mammals breathe air, make their own heat, have hair at some point in life and feed their young milk from mammary glands; they also share three middle ear bones. Linnaeus named the class after the milk.

concepts.title: Marsupials: born early, raised in a pouch
concepts.description: Marsupial young are born tiny and embryo-like and finish developing outside the womb, usually in a pouch. A red kangaroo is born after about 33 days at the size of a jellybean.

concepts.title: Where marsupials live
concepts.description: Most marsupials live in Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands; the rest live in the Americas, and the Virginia opossum is the only one north of Mexico.

concepts.title: When dinosaurs lived
concepts.description: Non-bird dinosaurs lived from about 245 to 66 million years ago, in the Mesozoic Era: the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods. The span was so long that Stegosaurus was long extinct before Tyrannosaurus appeared.

concepts.title: Fuel and navigation for migration
concepts.description: Migrants fuel long flights with stored fat (some double their weight; B6 fattened up in Alaska) and find their way using the sun, the stars and Earth's magnetic field.

concepts.title: Record-breaking bird migrations
concepts.description: In 2022 a juvenile bar-tailed godwit flew about 13,560 km nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania in 11 days. Tracked Arctic terns fly about 70,900 km a year (2010 study), with one Farne Islands tern estimated at 96,000 km (2016).

concepts.title: Batesian and Müllerian mimicry
concepts.description: In Batesian mimicry a harmless species copies a dangerous one (Bates, 1862); in Müllerian mimicry harmful species share one pattern (Muller, 1878). The viceroy turned out to be Müllerian.

concepts.title: Monotremes: mammals that lay eggs
concepts.description: The platypus and the echidnas are monotremes, the only mammals that lay eggs. The first platypus skin in Europe was suspected to be a hoax.

concepts.title: How egg-laying mammals raise their young
concepts.description: Platypus eggs hatch in about ten days and the young lick milk from fur-covered patches, since monotremes have no nipples. A young echidna suckles in the pouch until its spines grow.

concepts.title: Only female mosquitoes bite
concepts.description: Only female mosquitoes bite, because they need a blood meal to produce eggs; both sexes drink nectar and fruit juices. Anopheles mosquitoes develop in water from egg to larva to pupa to adult.

concepts.title: Mosquitoes carry deadly germs
concepts.description: Mosquitoes pick up germs from infected people and animals and spread them by biting; malaria parasites travel this way. WHO estimated 610,000 malaria deaths in 2024, and the CDC calls the mosquito the world’s deadliest animal.

concepts.title: How natural selection works
concepts.description: Natural selection needs three things: variation among individuals, differences in how many offspring they leave, and heredity. Given those, advantageous traits become more common over generations.

concepts.title: Seeing in the dark
concepts.description: Nocturnal animals are active after dark to hunt, mate or avoid daytime heat and predators. Many have enlarged eyes, and many have a tapetum lucidum, a mirror behind the retina that causes eyeshine; tarsiers lack one and have huge eyes instead.

concepts.title: An octopus thinks with its arms
concepts.description: The common octopus has about 500 million neurons, as many as a dog, and about two thirds are in its arms, so arms can work on problems while the brain does other things. Octopuses open wired-shut clams, run mazes and remember solutions.

concepts.title: Three hearts and blue blood
concepts.description: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood past the gills and one pumps it to the body (and stops when the octopus swims). Its blood is blue because its oxygen carrier, hemocyanin, uses copper instead of iron.

concepts.title: Owls' silent flight
concepts.description: Serrated leading edges, a velvety surface and soft trailing fringes on owl feathers muffle flight, so prey can't hear the owl and the owl can keep hearing its prey.

concepts.title: Owls hunt by ear
concepts.description: Barn owls can strike prey in total darkness by sound alone (Payne and Drury, 1958). Lopsided ears let them find a sound's height as well as direction, and the facial disc funnels sound to the ears.

concepts.title: Alex the African grey parrot
concepts.description: Irene Pepperberg's African grey parrot Alex learned to identify 50 objects, 7 colors, 5 shapes and quantities up to 6.

concepts.title: How penguins stay warm
concepts.description: Dense waterproof feathers, a thick fat layer and a countercurrent heat exchanger in the legs and feet keep penguins warm; emperor males fast for 9 weeks through the Antarctic winter on their fat.

concepts.title: Penguins are built to swim
concepts.description: Penguins' wings became flippers, and their limb bones are dense with almost no air spaces, cutting buoyancy for diving. Emperor penguins dive to about 550 m, deeper than any other bird.

concepts.title: Majerus's experiment confirms bird predation
concepts.description: After critics questioned earlier experiments, Michael Majerus released 4,864 moths near Cambridge over six years. Birds ate dark moths more often, enough to explain their decline. Colleagues published his results in 2012, the most direct evidence yet for camouflage and bird predation.

concepts.title: The peppered moth and industrial soot
concepts.description: Dark peppered moths, first noticed in Manchester in 1848, took over as soot blackened trees and killed pale lichens, because birds found light moths more easily. After the air was cleaned up, the dark form declined.

concepts.title: The peregrine falcon's dive
concepts.description: In 1999 a trained peregrine named Frightful was clocked at 242 mph diving from nearly three miles up; Audubon says wild peregrines may possibly reach 200 mph.

concepts.title: Phytoplankton make oxygen
concepts.description: Phytoplankton photosynthesize like plants, so they live near the sunlit surface. Roughly half of Earth's oxygen production comes from the ocean, mostly from plankton.

concepts.title: Plankton: the ocean's drifters
concepts.description: Plankton are living things carried by tides and currents because they cannot swim against them. Phytoplankton are plant drifters; zooplankton are animal drifters such as krill, young fish and jellyfish, which rise to the surface at night to feed.

concepts.title: Surviving polar cold
concepts.description: Polar bears keep warm with thick fur over black skin, a fat layer and furred soles; penguins trap air in tight feathers over fat, and swap heat between leg arteries and veins so little is lost through the feet.

concepts.title: Our closest living relatives
concepts.description: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives, with about 1.2 percent DNA difference. Humans did not evolve from any living primate: we share ancestors.

concepts.title: What makes a primate
concepts.description: Primates have forward-facing eyes with overlapping views, flat nails instead of claws, and large brains for their body size.

concepts.title: Birds of prey and how they kill
concepts.description: All birds of prey have hook-tipped beaks and talons. Eagles and hawks kill mainly with their feet, squeezing prey; falcons kill with a bite, using the tomial tooth on the beak.

concepts.title: The IUCN Red List
concepts.description: The IUCN Red List sorts assessed species from Least Concern to Extinct; Vulnerable, Endangered and Critically Endangered count as threatened. In version 2025-1, 47,187 of 169,420 evaluated species were threatened, including about 41% of amphibians; only about 1% of insects had been evaluated.

concepts.title: The amniotic egg
concepts.description: A reptile embryo grows inside the amnion, a fluid-filled sac, within a leathery or hard shell that holds water in, so reptiles can lay eggs on dry land; most amphibians still lay soft, jelly-like eggs in water.

concepts.title: The living reptile groups
concepts.description: Today's reptiles are turtles, the tuatara, lizards and snakes, and crocodilians: more than 12,500 species, most of them ectotherms.

concepts.title: Reptile scales keep water in
concepts.description: Most reptiles wear a continuous coat of scales made mostly of keratin; with waxy lipids, this skin cuts water loss and helped reptiles live on land.

concepts.title: Salamander or lizard?
concepts.description: Salamanders look like lizards but are amphibians: smooth, moist skin, no claws, no ear openings and eggs in jelly, versus a lizard's dry scales, claws and leathery-shelled eggs. Many salamanders even breathe without lungs.

concepts.title: How salmon find their home stream
concepts.description: Before heading to sea, young salmon imprint on the smell of their home stream, and adults follow those odor memories back; they also imprint on Earth's magnetic field where they enter the sea.

concepts.title: A salmon's round trip
concepts.description: Sockeye salmon hatch in fresh water, go to sea to grow, then swim upstream to spawn where they were born, turning red. All die within weeks, and their bodies feed the river and the next generation.

concepts.title: Senses we lack
