concepts.description: A cellular network splits land into cells, each with a base station that talks to phones by radio; low-power signals let frequencies be reused.

concepts.title: Handoff between cells
concepts.description: As a phone moves from one cell to another during a call, the network automatically passes the call to the new cell.

concepts.title: Confidently wrong
concepts.description: Because a language model predicts likely-sounding text rather than checking facts, it can state false things confidently: a hallucination.

concepts.title: How language models write
concepts.description: A large language model splits text into tokens and writes by predicting a likely next token, adding it and repeating; it learned this from huge amounts of text.

concepts.title: Circuits and switches
concepts.description: Current flows only around a closed loop of conductors; a switch opens or closes a gap in that loop.

concepts.title: Series and parallel circuits
concepts.description: In series, devices share one path and fail together; homes are wired in parallel so each device has its own branch.

concepts.title: How CO2 warms the planet
concepts.description: CO2 traps heat; burning coal, oil and gas has raised it more than 50%, and the IPCC finds humans have unequivocally warmed the planet.

concepts.title: Emissions by power source
concepts.description: Coal emits the most CO2 per kilowatt-hour, gas about half as much, and wind, solar, nuclear and hydro far less over their whole lives.

concepts.title: Debating the energy path
concepts.description: Countries set the Paris goal; named groups such as OPEC and Greenpeace disagree sharply on how fast to move away from fossil fuels.

concepts.title: What the cloud is
concepts.description: The cloud is on-demand access over the network to shared computers and storage in data centers.

concepts.title: Data centers and energy
concepts.description: Data centers used about 415 TWh (around 1.5% of world electricity) in 2024; most of it ends up as heat, and cooling can take up to 40%.

concepts.title: Signals: electricity as a messenger
concepts.description: In communication technology, electricity carries information in the pattern of a current or wave: on-off pulses, or a continuous copy of a sound wave.

concepts.title: Algorithms
concepts.description: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that solves a problem in a finite number of steps; a program is an algorithm written in code.

concepts.title: Letters and pictures as numbers
concepts.description: Computers store text, pictures and sound as binary: each letter gets a number (lowercase a is 01100001 in ASCII), and each pixel's color is stored as numbers.

concepts.title: Counting in binary
concepts.description: Binary uses only 0 and 1 because a transistor switch is either on or off; each place is worth double the one before, and 8 bits make a byte.

concepts.title: What a computer is
concepts.description: A computer is a programmable machine for processing, storing and displaying information; the word once meant a person who calculated.

concepts.title: The first computers
concepts.description: There is no single first computer: Babbage's mechanical designs, the ABC, Zuse's Z3, Colossus and ENIAC were each first by a different measure.

concepts.title: The instruction cycle and clock speed
concepts.description: A CPU runs one loop, fetch, decode, execute, from start-up to shutdown, paced by a clock that ticks billions of times a second.

concepts.title: Input, processing, memory, output
concepts.description: Every computer takes input, processes it in the CPU, holds data and instructions in memory, and sends out output.

concepts.title: Memory and storage
concepts.description: RAM is fast working memory that forgets without power; storage (hard drives and SSDs) keeps files for the long term with the power off.

concepts.title: From rooms to pockets
concepts.description: Transistors and then microprocessors shrank computers from 30-ton room-fillers to desktop personal computers to handheld smartphones.

concepts.title: Moore's law
concepts.description: Moore's law is Gordon Moore's observation (1965, revised 1975) that chip transistor counts double about every two years; it is a trend the industry chased, not a law of nature.

concepts.title: Operating systems
concepts.description: An operating system manages a computer's resources, shares processor time among programs in tiny slices, and is loaded into memory at start-up.

concepts.title: Software and code
concepts.description: Software is the instructions that tell hardware what to do; programmers write code in high-level languages that a compiler or interpreter translates into binary machine code.

concepts.title: Sorting algorithms
concepts.description: Different algorithms can solve the same problem with very different effort: selection sort work quadruples when the list doubles, merge sort work only slightly more than doubles.

concepts.title: Transistors and the microchip
concepts.description: A transistor is a tiny semiconductor switch flipped by a small electrical signal; an integrated circuit puts many of them, and their wiring, on one piece of silicon.

concepts.title: Casgevy, the first CRISPR medicine
concepts.description: Casgevy, approved in the UK in November 2023 and the US in December 2023, edits a sickle cell patient's own blood stem cells to make fetal hemoglobin.

concepts.title: The gene-editing line
concepts.description: Editing body cells affects one patient; editing eggs, sperm or embryos could pass changes to future generations, which the 2023 genome editing summit called unacceptable at this time.

concepts.title: How CRISPR edits genes
concepts.description: CRISPR-Cas9, borrowed from a bacterial defense against viruses, uses a guide RNA to lead the Cas9 enzyme to a matching DNA sequence and cut it; the cell's repair machinery then makes the edit.

concepts.title: Encryption basics
concepts.description: Encryption uses an algorithm and a key to turn plaintext into ciphertext; Caesar's shift cipher is a simple, easily broken example.

concepts.title: Public-key encryption
concepts.description: Diffie and Hellman (1976) showed how to keep messages secret with no prearranged key; public-key cryptography uses one key to lock and another to unlock.

concepts.title: How a quadcopter flies
concepts.description: A quadcopter's four propellers push air down for lift; two spin each way so their twisting forces cancel, and it steers only by changing propeller speeds under a flight computer's control.

concepts.title: What drones are used for
concepts.description: Drones carry out jobs such as delivering blood to hospitals in Rwanda (from 2016) and counting birds and watching volcanoes for the USGS.

concepts.title: Radar
concepts.description: Radar sends out radio pulses and times their echoes; half the round trip at the speed of light gives the distance, and the Doppler shift gives speed.

concepts.title: Sonar
concepts.description: Sonar times echoes of sound pulses in water, where sound travels far and fast, to find the seafloor or objects.

concepts.title: Electric current
concepts.description: Current is moving charge, counted in amperes. Electrons already in the wire drift slowly, but the push travels almost at light speed.

concepts.title: The electric motor
concepts.description: A motor spins a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field, reversing the current each half turn to keep it going; Faraday built the first in 1821.

concepts.title: Watts and kilowatt-hours
concepts.description: Power is how fast energy flows: a watt is a joule per second, volts times amps; bills charge for energy in kilowatt-hours.

concepts.title: Electromagnetic induction
concepts.description: A changing magnetic field through a coil induces a current, as Faraday found in 1831.

concepts.title: Electricity makes magnetism
concepts.description: An electric current makes a magnetic field, as Ørsted saw in 1820; a coil of wire becomes a switchable electromagnet.

concepts.title: What energy is
concepts.description: Energy is the ability to do work. It is stored (potential) or working (kinetic) and is measured in joules.

concepts.title: Energy changes form
concepts.description: Energy is never created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another; in most conversions a lot of it ends up as heat.

concepts.title: The four forces of flight
concepts.description: Weight, lift, drag and thrust act on every plane; in steady flight lift balances weight and thrust balances drag.

concepts.title: How a wing makes lift
concepts.description: A wing turns the passing air downward, so the air pushes it up; seen as pressure, faster air above the wing means lower pressure there. The equal-transit story is a myth.

concepts.title: A fridge moves heat
concepts.description: A refrigerator does not make cold: it forces heat out of its cold inside and releases it into the room, which is why an open fridge door warms a kitchen.

concepts.title: The refrigerant loop
concepts.description: A fridge's refrigerant evaporates inside, soaking up heat, then is compressed so it condenses in outside coils and gives that heat up; the loop repeats.

concepts.title: Why fusion is hard
concepts.description: Positively charged nuclei repel, so fusion fuel must be heated to about 150 million degrees C, becoming a plasma that has to be held by magnetic fields or squeezed by lasers.

concepts.title: NIF's 2022 ignition
concepts.description: On December 5, 2022, NIF's lasers delivered 2.05 MJ to a fusion target and got 3.15 MJ back: gain on the target, while the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid.

concepts.title: Fusion versus fission
concepts.description: Fusion joins very light nuclei, such as the hydrogen isotopes deuterium and tritium, into helium; fission splits heavy nuclei such as uranium.

concepts.title: Gas turbines and combined cycle
concepts.description: Gas turbines spin directly on hot gases; combined-cycle plants reuse the exhaust heat to make steam for a second turbine, getting more electricity from the same fuel.

concepts.title: The generator
concepts.description: A generator is a motor run in reverse: turbines spin a rotor inside coils to turn motion into electricity.

concepts.title: GPS clocks and relativity
concepts.description: GPS works only because its satellites carry very precise atomic clocks, corrected for relativity: a millionth of a second means about 300 meters.

concepts.title: How GPS finds you
concepts.description: GPS receivers only listen: they time one-way signals from at least four satellites, turn the delays into distances, and solve for position and time.

concepts.title: Balancing the grid
concepts.description: Grid operators must match electricity supply to demand at every moment, or blackouts can happen.

concepts.title: How power reaches your socket
concepts.description: Electricity is stepped up to high voltage for long transmission lines, then stepped down at substations and near homes; the lower 48 US states run on three main grids.

concepts.title: Germ theory
concepts.description: Germ theory says microorganisms that invade and multiply in the body cause infectious disease; Pasteur and Koch established it, and it underpins disinfection, vaccines and antibiotics.

concepts.title: Air conditioning
concepts.description: Air conditioners work like a fridge for a whole house, moving heat from indoors to outdoors; Carrier's 1902 system was built to control humidity at a printer.

concepts.title: Heat pumps
concepts.description: A heat pump moves heat either way: out of the house in summer and in from the cool outdoors in winter, delivering about 3 kWh of heat per 1 kWh of electricity.

concepts.title: Head and flow
concepts.description: A hydro plant's output depends on how much water flows and how far it falls; hydropower is a much bigger share of the world's electricity than of US electricity.

concepts.title: How a dam makes electricity
concepts.description: Water falling from a reservoir through a penstock turns a turbine and generator, turning gravitational energy into electricity.

concepts.title: MRI scans
concepts.description: MRI lines up protons in the body's water with a powerful magnet, knocks them with radio pulses and reads the energy they release; no ionizing radiation.

concepts.title: X-rays and CT scans
concepts.description: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by calcium-rich bone, which shows white; CT spins an X-ray beam around the body to build slices and 3D images.

concepts.title: The incandescent bulb
concepts.description: An incandescent bulb makes light by heating a tungsten filament until it glows, wasting most of its energy as heat.

concepts.title: How the internet began
concepts.description: ARPANET, funded by the US Defense Department, sent its first message ("lo") in 1969 and grew into an internet now used by about 6 billion people.

concepts.title: Light in glass fibers
concepts.description: Undersea cables carry data as laser light in hair-thin glass fibers inside a cable about as wide as a garden hose.

concepts.title: How long the internet takes
concepts.description: Light in optical fiber covers about a kilometer every 5 millionths of a second, so 1,000 km takes about 5 thousandths of a second.

concepts.title: Where packets came from
concepts.description: Paul Baran (RAND) and Donald Davies (NPL) independently invented packet switching; Baran wanted a network that survived damage, and Davies named the packets.

concepts.title: Packet switching
concepts.description: Data is chopped into small addressed packets that travel independently by any available route and are reassembled at the destination.

concepts.title: TCP/IP: the network of networks
concepts.description: Cerf and Kahn's TCP (1974) let separate networks join into one; ARPANET switched to TCP/IP in 1983, and TCP resends lost packets.

concepts.title: Undersea internet cables
concepts.description: Over 99% of intercontinental data crosses the oceans in cables; anchors and fishing, not sharks, cause most faults, so traffic is spread across many cables.

concepts.title: The jet engine
concepts.description: A jet engine squeezes air in a compressor, burns fuel in it, spins a turbine that drives the compressor, and blasts the gas out of a nozzle. Airliners use turbofans.

concepts.title: The LED
concepts.description: An LED makes light directly from a semiconductor junction, with no hot filament, using far less energy.

concepts.title: How a microwave oven heats food
concepts.description: A magnetron fills a metal box with microwaves whose field tugs food's water molecules back and forth about 2.45 billion times a second; their jostling is heat.

concepts.title: Microwaves are non-ionizing
concepts.description: Microwaves, like visible light and radio waves, are non-ionizing: too weak to knock electrons out of atoms. Their energy becomes heat and doesn't make food radioactive.

concepts.title: The world's electricity mix
concepts.description: In 2025 coal and renewables each made about a third of the world's electricity, gas about a fifth, and low-emissions sources more than 40%.

concepts.title: Why some bikes balance themselves
concepts.description: A moving riderless bike can steer itself into a lean and recover; in 2011 a bike with neither gyroscopic effect nor trail still did, so the full reason is a subtle mix of effects.

concepts.title: Balancing a bike by steering
concepts.description: A rider stays up by steering the wheels back under the falling bike, the way a hand moves under a balanced broom; a stopped bike cannot do this.

concepts.title: How an electric car works
concepts.description: An all-electric car drives its wheels with an electric motor powered by a battery pack; counting from the plug, over 77% of the energy reaches the wheels.

concepts.title: Factories and the Industrial Revolution
concepts.description: The Industrial Revolution moved work from homes into powered factories with divided labor; steam freed mills from riversides so they could grow in towns.

concepts.title: The four-stroke cycle
concepts.description: Intake, compression, power and exhaust: only the power stroke pushes, and a crankshaft turns the piston's up-and-down motion into rotation.

concepts.title: Friction
concepts.description: Friction resists surfaces sliding over each other; rough surfaces catch, starting to slide takes more force than keeping going, and friction lets you grip the ground.

concepts.title: How brakes stop a car
concepts.description: Friction brakes press pads on a spinning disc and turn the energy of motion into heat; energy of motion grows with the square of speed, so doubling speed quadruples braking distance.

concepts.title: Gear ratios
concepts.description: Meshing gears cannot slip, so their tooth counts set the speed ratio: a driven gear with twice the teeth turns at half the speed.

concepts.title: Gears trade speed for force
concepts.description: A small gear driving a big one gives more turning force at lower speed; a big gear driving a small one gives speed instead, like a bike's low and high gears.

concepts.title: Horsepower
concepts.description: James Watt set one horsepower at 33,000 foot-pounds per minute, about 746 watts, more than an average horse can keep up over a working day.

concepts.title: Hydraulic force multiplication
concepts.description: Equal pressure on a piston with 10 times the area gives 10 times the force, but the small piston moves 10 times as far; car brakes work this way.

concepts.title: Factory work and the first factory laws
concepts.description: Factory work meant long, clock-driven shifts, often for children; Britain's 1833 Factory Act banned under-9s from textile mills and sent inspectors to enforce it.

concepts.title: The internal combustion engine
concepts.description: A car engine burns fuel inside its cylinders, where a spark ignites fuel and air; only about 12%-30% of the fuel energy moves the car, and most of the rest is lost as heat.

concepts.title: Trading force for distance
concepts.description: A pulley system shares a load among its rope strands, cutting the force needed, but you pull proportionally more rope: no machine puts out more work than goes in.

concepts.title: Newcomen's steam engine
concepts.description: Newcomen's 1712 engine pumped water from mines: it condensed steam under a piston to make a partial vacuum, and air pressure pushed the piston down.

concepts.title: Pascal's principle
concepts.description: Press on a liquid at rest in a closed container and the pressure rises equally everywhere in it; liquids barely compress, so they pass a push along.

concepts.title: Regenerative braking
concepts.description: When an electric car slows, the turning wheels drive its motor as a generator, recharging the battery instead of wasting all the energy of motion.

concepts.title: Simple machines
concepts.description: Levers, wheels and axles and pulleys are simple machines: a lever multiplies a push by the ratio of its arm lengths, a wheel and axle by the ratio of its radii.

concepts.title: Watt's steam engine
concepts.description: James Watt's separate condenser (1765, patented 1769) kept the cylinder hot and cut fuel costs; from 1781 his engines turned a shaft, and the watt is named for him.

concepts.title: How nuclear power works
concepts.description: Neutrons split uranium-235 atoms in a controlled chain reaction; the heat makes steam to spin a turbine, with no CO2 released while running.

concepts.title: The nuclear debate
concepts.description: Spent fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years; groups such as the IEA and Greenpeace weigh nuclear power's role very differently.

concepts.title: How oil forms and is found
concepts.description: Crude oil formed from ancient marine life under heat and pressure, sits in tiny spaces in rock, and is reached by drilling wells.

concepts.title: Refining and using oil
concepts.description: Refineries separate crude by boiling point and crack heavy molecules into fuels like gasoline; oil mostly powers transport, not the grid.

concepts.title: Why plastic lasts
concepts.description: Microbes' enzymes don't recognize plastic's bonds, so plastic doesn't rot: it breaks into smaller pieces, down to microplastics under five millimeters.

concepts.title: What plastic is
concepts.description: Plastics are polymers, long chains of repeating units, mostly built from fossil-fuel carbon; Baekeland's 1907 Bakelite was the first fully synthetic plastic.

concepts.title: Gutenberg's printing system
concepts.description: Gutenberg combined reusable metal type, oil-based ink and a press into a system that printed pages again and again; movable type itself came first in China and Korea.

concepts.title: Printing spreads ideas
concepts.description: Cheap printed copies multiplied Europe's books into the millions by 1500 and let ideas such as Luther's theses spread in weeks.

concepts.title: Pumped-storage hydropower
concepts.description: Pumped storage pumps water uphill with spare electricity and lets it run back through turbines when power is needed.

concepts.title: Qubits
concepts.description: A qubit can be 0, 1 or a mix of both (superposition), but measuring it always gives a plain 0 or 1.

concepts.title: What quantum computers are (and aren't) for
concepts.description: Quantum computers are expected to help with specific jobs such as simulating molecules and factoring huge numbers, not to replace ordinary computers; qubits are fragile and error-prone.

concepts.title: Who invented radio
concepts.description: Hertz made radio waves; Marconi, Popov and Tesla all have claims on radio, and even a 1943 US Supreme Court case weighed priority.

concepts.title: How radio sends sound
concepts.description: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves made by changing currents in antennas; stations carry sound by varying a carrier wave (AM or FM).

concepts.title: Electric trains
concepts.description: Most modern trains are driven by electric motors: electric trains take current from an overhead wire or third rail, and diesel-electrics make it on board.

concepts.title: Maglev trains
concepts.description: A maglev train is lifted by magnets so no wheels touch its guideway, and guideway coils that keep changing polarity pull it along.

concepts.title: Goddard's rockets
concepts.description: Robert Goddard flew the first liquid-fueled rocket in 1926, after a 1920 newspaper editorial claimed rockets could not work in a vacuum.

concepts.title: How rockets work in space
concepts.description: A rocket pushes on its own exhaust, not on air, and carries its own oxidizer, so it works in a vacuum where jet engines cannot.

concepts.title: Pixels and LCD screens
concepts.description: A screen image is a grid of pixels, millions on an HD or 4K screen; an LCD makes no light and uses liquid crystals to let a backlight through or block it.

concepts.title: Mixing red, green and blue light
concepts.description: The eye has three kinds of cones, so screens can make a broad range of colors by mixing red, green and blue light.

concepts.title: Crawling and indexing
concepts.description: Search engines send crawlers along links and build an index, like a book's, that searches look through instead of the live web.

concepts.title: Ranking search results
concepts.description: BackRub, which became Google, treated links as votes; ranking today weighs many signals such as meaning, relevance, quality and location.

concepts.title: SAE levels of driving automation
concepts.description: SAE J3016 sorts driving automation into Levels 0 to 5, by who is driving: you at Levels 0-2, the system at Levels 3-5 when engaged.

concepts.title: How self-driving cars sense the road
concepts.description: Self-driving cars combine cameras, radar, lidar, GPS and detailed maps into a 3-D picture, and computers steer, brake and accelerate from it.

concepts.title: London's sewers and the Great Stink
concepts.description: The Great Stink of 1858 pushed Parliament to fund Bazalgette's sewers, built to remove 'bad air'; the 1866 cholera outbreak hit only unconnected areas, proving Snow right.

concepts.title: How a sewage plant cleans wastewater
concepts.description: Gravity carries sewage to a plant; screens and settling tanks remove solids, microbes eat the organic material, and the water is disinfected and released.

concepts.title: Archimedes' principle
concepts.description: Water pushes up on a ship with a force equal to the weight of the water it pushes aside; a ship settles until that water weighs as much as the ship.

concepts.title: The Plimsoll line
concepts.description: A mark on a ship's hull shows the deepest it may safely sit; separate marks allow for fresh water, which is less dense than seawater.

concepts.title: Inside a smartphone
concepts.description: A smartphone packs a phone, radio, camera and screen together with a speaker, a vibration motor and a rechargeable lithium-ion battery.

concepts.title: Capacitive touchscreens
concepts.description: A capacitive touchscreen senses where a conducting finger disturbs its electric field; insulators like plastic have no effect.

concepts.title: Solar DC and inverters
concepts.description: Solar cells make direct current, so inverters convert it to the grid's alternating current.

concepts.title: How solar cells work
concepts.description: Sunlight knocks electrons loose in a semiconductor cell, making current with nothing spinning; panels have grown far more efficient since 1954.

concepts.title: Space spinoffs
concepts.description: NASA research gave everyday life technologies such as the CMOS image sensor in phone cameras and memory foam, recorded in NASA's yearly Spinoff report since 1976.

concepts.title: Spinoff myths
concepts.description: Tang, Teflon and Velcro are not NASA inventions; astronauts used them, which made people link them with space.

concepts.title: Why storing electricity is hard
concepts.description: Storage must convert electricity to another form and back, losing some on the way; big batteries now shift midday solar to the evening.

concepts.title: Rules matched to risk
concepts.description: The EU's AI Act, in force since August 2024, bans a few AI uses, strictly regulates high-risk ones like hiring and leaves most everyday AI, such as spam filters, free of new obligations.

concepts.title: The Collingridge dilemma
concepts.description: David Collingridge's 1980 dilemma: early on, a technology is easy to change but its effects are hard to foresee; once the effects are clear, it is entrenched and hard to change.

concepts.title: Weighing a new technology
concepts.description: Every technology trades benefits against costs; asking who benefits, who bears the risk and who supplies the evidence helps judge it, as leaded petrol and the War of the Currents show.

concepts.title: What technology is
concepts.description: Technology is knowledge put to work on the practical jobs of daily life, from stone tools to light switches.

concepts.title: Inventions that changed daily life
concepts.description: A few big inventions, from stone tools and the wheel to printing and the electric light, reshaped everyday life; nearly all of them are very recent.

concepts.title: Morse code
concepts.description: Morse code spells letters with dots and dashes, giving the commonest letters the shortest codes; Morse and his partner Vail share the credit.

concepts.title: The electric telegraph
concepts.description: A telegraph key opens and closes a circuit, sending pulses of current that switch an electromagnet at the far end; Morse in the US and Cooke and Wheatstone in Britain built working systems.

concepts.title: Who invented the telephone
concepts.description: Bell received the patent, but Gray filed on a similar idea the same day and Meucci had filed a caveat earlier, so the credit is still argued.

concepts.title: How a telephone carries a voice
concepts.description: A telephone turns sound into a current that rises and falls like the sound wave, then turns it back into sound with an electromagnet and a diaphragm.

concepts.title: Steam power plants
concepts.description: Coal and many gas plants burn fuel to boil water; the steam spins a turbine and generator, and most of the fuel's energy is lost as heat.

concepts.title: Roundabouts
concepts.description: Roundabouts cut the points where drivers' paths cross from 32 to 8, remove right-angle and head-on crashes, and slow traffic, so far fewer crashes injure anyone.

concepts.title: Traffic signals
concepts.description: Traffic lights take turns so conflicting movements never both get green, and wire loops in the road tell a signal when a car is waiting.

concepts.title: Action and reaction push vehicles
concepts.description: Every engine that moves a vehicle accelerates a working fluid backward, and the reaction pushes the vehicle forward: Newton's third law.

concepts.title: The propeller
concepts.description: A propeller is a spinning wing: its blades make lift pointed forward, throwing air or water backward, so it needs a fluid to push and cannot work in space.

concepts.title: Television's pioneers
concepts.description: Baird's mechanical system, Farnsworth's electronic camera tube and Zworykin's work at RCA all shaped television; no one person invented it.

concepts.title: Scanning a picture
concepts.description: Television sends a picture as a signal by scanning it spot by spot and line by line, then rebuilding it in the same order fast enough to look whole.

concepts.title: Vaccines: history and safety record
concepts.description: Jenner's 1796 smallpox vaccine led to smallpox's eradication in 1980; vaccines pass clinical trials before use and are monitored after, and WHO calls them very safe.

concepts.title: How vaccines train the immune system
concepts.description: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless form, piece or blueprint of a germ; it makes antibodies and remembers, so a later infection is stopped fast.

concepts.title: Voltage
concepts.description: Voltage is the energy given to each coulomb of charge: one volt is one joule per coulomb.

concepts.title: Volta's first battery
concepts.description: Galvani's twitching frog legs led Volta to build the voltaic pile in 1800, the first reliable battery.

concepts.title: How a VR headset works
concepts.description: A VR headset shows each eye a slightly different image for depth and uses motion sensors to redraw the view as your head moves; mismatched signals can cause motion sickness.

concepts.title: Why AC won
concepts.description: AC beat Edison's DC because transformers can raise its voltage for efficient long-distance transmission and lower it for homes.

concepts.title: Germs in water, and killing them
concepts.description: Snow showed in 1854 that cholera spread through contaminated water; today plants disinfect with chlorine or chloramine, a practice US cities began in 1908.

concepts.title: How tap water is treated
concepts.description: Treatment plants clump dirt with coagulation and flocculation, let the clumps settle, filter the water through sand, gravel or charcoal, and then disinfect it.

concepts.title: Inventing the World Wide Web
concepts.description: Tim Berners-Lee invented the web at CERN in 1989 using HTML, URLs and HTTP; CERN gave the software away in 1993.

concepts.title: The web versus the internet
concepts.description: The internet is the infrastructure; the web is one service that runs on it, like email.

concepts.title: Wi-Fi bands
concepts.description: Routers use a 2.4 GHz band (longer reach, better through walls) and a 5 GHz band (faster, shorter range); 2.4 GHz is 2.4 billion cycles a second.

concepts.title: What Wi-Fi is
concepts.description: Wi-Fi carries data by radio over the short hop between your devices and the router; the modem links the home network to the provider.

concepts.title: Where wind works best
concepts.description: Wind power rises with the cube of wind speed, so turbines go on windy plains, hilltops, water and tall towers.

concepts.title: How a wind turbine works
concepts.description: Wind turns wing-shaped blades and a rotor that drives a generator in the nacelle atop a tall tower.

concepts.title: Advertising that informs
concepts.description: Advertising can tell buyers what exists and what it costs. Lee Benham found eyeglasses cost more in US states that banned advertising.

concepts.title: Advertising that persuades
concepts.description: Advertising also shapes preferences: people with strong ketchup favorites often cannot tell brands apart blindfolded, and De Beers's "A Diamond Is Forever" helped make the diamond solitaire the standard engagement ring.

concepts.title: Rival advertising can cancel out
concepts.description: A. C. Pigou argued in 1920 that when competing firms advertise against each other, the spending may simply cancel out.

concepts.title: Commodities, futures and gold
concepts.description: Commodities such as metals, grains and oil trade mostly through futures contracts, a practice pioneered at Osaka's Dojima rice market (1730). Gold pays no income, and precious metals are highly volatile.

concepts.title: Property as an investment
concepts.description: Real estate can pay through rent and through changes in its value. REITs own income-producing property and let investors share its income; non-traded REITs are hard to sell.

concepts.title: Income and price: where returns come from
concepts.description: An investment can pay through income, such as dividends, interest or rent, and through a change in its price. Total return is the income plus the price gain or minus the price loss.

concepts.title: How automation reshapes jobs
concepts.description: Machines take over tasks, but work often shifts rather than vanishing: US farm jobs fell from 41% of the workforce to 1.9%, and ATMs changed tellers' work instead of ending it.

concepts.title: The Luddites
concepts.description: From 1811, English textile workers known as Luddites smashed machines. They objected less to machines than to how owners used them to undercut skilled, fairly paid work.

concepts.title: Money as bank deposits
concepts.description: Most money today is bank deposits: records of what banks owe their customers, not physical cash.

concepts.title: Bank runs
concepts.description: Banks cannot pay all depositors at once, so a rush to withdraw can sink a bank, and fear of a run makes joining it rational.

concepts.title: Limits on bank money creation
concepts.description: Banks cannot create money without limit: they must lend profitably and manage risk, regulation constrains them, and central bank interest rates are the ultimate limit.

concepts.title: Banks as intermediaries
concepts.description: A bank accepts deposits and makes loans, standing between savers and borrowers.

concepts.title: Bank lending creates money
concepts.description: When a bank makes a loan it creates a matching new deposit; most money today is created this way, and repaying loans destroys it.

concepts.title: Money changers and the first banks
concepts.description: The word bank comes from the Italian banco, the bench of medieval money changers, who began taking deposits and lending them out.

concepts.title: How banks earn: the spread
concepts.description: A bank charges borrowers a higher interest rate than it pays depositors; the difference covers costs and profit.

concepts.title: Barter and the double coincidence of wants
concepts.description: Barter is trading goods or services directly; it only works when each side wants what the other offers.

concepts.title: Barter in history
concepts.description: No society that ran purely on barter has ever been described; barter tends to appear between acquaintances and when money runs short.

concepts.title: Barter has no common measure
concepts.description: Barter has no single unit for measuring value and makes saving for later hard.

concepts.title: The blockchain ledger
concepts.description: A blockchain is a shared, tamper-evident ledger in which each block of transactions is linked to the one before.

concepts.title: How a bond works
concepts.description: A bond is an IOU: you lend to a government, city or company, which pays interest on a schedule and repays the face value at maturity.

concepts.title: Bond risks and who gets paid first
concepts.description: Bonds can default, and a bond sold early may fetch less if interest rates have risen. If a company goes bankrupt, bondholders are paid before shareholders.

concepts.title: Britain's War Loan
concepts.description: Britain's 3.5% War Loan traced back to borrowing in 1917 for World War I. It had no fixed maturity, so the government chose when to repay: in 2015, when rates were low.

concepts.title: What a speculative bubble is
concepts.description: A bubble is a price far above what fundamentals justify for a long time, sustained by buyers expecting to sell higher; bubbles are hard to spot until they burst, and economists disagree about them.

concepts.title: The 50/30/20 rule
concepts.description: A common guideline: 50% of after-tax income to needs, 30% to wants, 20% to saving or paying down debt.

concepts.title: What a budget is
concepts.description: A budget is a written monthly plan: list expenses, note income, subtract, then track what you actually spend.

concepts.title: Booms, recessions and how they are dated
concepts.description: Economies swing irregularly between expansions and recessions, marked by peaks and troughs; the NBER dates US recessions after the fact.

concepts.title: Europe's butter mountains
concepts.description: The EU's Common Agricultural Policy held farm prices artificially high, farmers produced more, and by the 1980s huge surpluses of butter and wine piled up.

concepts.title: Who pays card fees
concepts.description: Merchants pay a fee on card sales, mostly interchange to the card issuer, set by the networks; the cost is passed on in prices, including to cash users.

concepts.title: How a card payment travels
concepts.description: A card payment links the cardholder, the merchant, the merchant's bank (acquirer) and the card issuer through a card network: authorize, then settle.

concepts.title: Paying by changing records
concepts.description: A card payment changes banks' records: the payer's balance goes down and the seller's goes up.

concepts.title: Paper money in China
concepts.description: Paper money began in China, from Tang-era flying money to Song-era notes in Sichuan, where heavy iron coins made paper convenient.

concepts.title: Why firms exist (Coase)
concepts.description: Ronald Coase argued in 1937 that firms exist because using markets has costs, now called transaction costs, such as finding prices and negotiating a contract for each deal. Inside a firm, managers direct the work.

concepts.title: What a coin's stamp did
concepts.description: A coin's stamp showed that an authority stood behind a standard weight of metal, so it no longer had to be weighed in every deal.

concepts.title: Ways to own a business
concepts.description: A sole proprietorship has one owner and a partnership two or more; in both, owners are personally liable for the business's debts. A corporation is a separate legal entity whose owners have limited liability.

concepts.title: Who runs a corporation
concepts.description: Shareholders own a corporation and elect a board of directors, which sets goals and policies and hires officers such as the CEO to run the firm.

concepts.title: Salomon and the company as a separate person
concepts.description: In the Salomon case, Britain's House of Lords ruled that a properly formed company is a separate person in law, so its owner was not personally liable for its debts.

concepts.title: What competition does for buyers
concepts.description: Competition pushes businesses to operate efficiently, keep prices down and keep quality up, and brings more choice and innovation.

concepts.title: Profits attract rivals
concepts.description: Profits draw new firms into a market; their extra supply pushes the price down until profits are squeezed away.

concepts.title: Price takers
concepts.description: In perfect competition, many firms sell identical products, so each must accept the market price.

concepts.title: Cowrie shell money
concepts.description: Cowrie shells served as money in parts of Africa and Asia because they were small, durable and hard to fake.

concepts.title: The consumer price index basket
concepts.description: The CPI tracks the cost of a representative, spending-weighted basket of goods and services, which is updated as habits change.

concepts.title: Why a fixed basket overstates living costs
concepts.description: Substitution bias and quality/new goods bias make a fixed-basket index overstate the rise in the cost of living.

concepts.title: What a credit score is
concepts.description: A credit score predicts how likely you are to repay on time, based on your credit reports; higher scores usually mean easier approval and better rates.

concepts.title: What goes into a credit score
concepts.description: A FICO score weighs payment history, amounts owed, length of history, new credit and credit mix; income isn't in it, and nobody has just one score.

concepts.title: Credit means trust
concepts.description: The word credit comes from Latin credere, 'to trust, entrust, believe': lending and borrowing run on trust.

concepts.title: What a cryptocurrency is
concepts.description: Cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin are digital tokens created and tracked by a network of computers, with no central issuer.

concepts.title: Why crypto prices swing
concepts.description: Bitcoin's price is set by supply and demand; with a nearly fixed supply and no issuer steadying it, the price swings sharply.

concepts.title: What drives the business cycle
concepts.description: Economists disagree about what drives booms and recessions: swings in spending, interest-rate moves, or shocks to productivity and tastes.

concepts.title: What deflation is
concepts.description: Deflation is a general fall in prices, usually a side effect of collapsing spending; falling prices in one sector are not deflation.

concepts.title: Why deflation hurts
concepts.description: Falling prices lead people to delay purchases and raise the real burden of debts, which can slow an economy for years.

concepts.title: Why buyers want less at higher prices
concepts.description: The substitution effect (switching to relatively cheaper goods) and the income effect (a higher price shrinks buying power) both cut the quantity demanded.

concepts.title: The law of demand
concepts.description: When a price rises, buyers want less; when it falls, they want more. The demand curve slopes downward.

concepts.title: What shifts demand
concepts.description: Income, tastes, prices of related goods, population and expectations shift the whole demand curve.

concepts.title: Deposit insurance
concepts.description: US deposit insurance (the FDIC, since 1933) guarantees deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, to keep public confidence.

concepts.title: What caused the Great Depression
concepts.description: Economists still disagree: the 1929 crash and falling spending, a shrinking money supply as banks failed (Friedman and Schwartz), and the gold standard all have advocates.

concepts.title: Enron's one-basket 401(k)
concepts.description: At the end of 2000, most of Enron's 401(k) plan assets were in Enron stock. When Enron went bankrupt in December 2001, many employees lost their jobs and much of their retirement savings.

concepts.title: Diversification
concepts.description: Diversification means spreading money among different investments, across and within asset classes, to reduce risk. Funds make it easy, but it can't prevent losses in a market-wide drop.

concepts.title: The dot-com bubble
concepts.description: In the late 1990s, money poured into internet start-ups; the Nasdaq peaked in March 2000 and fell more than 78% by October 2002.

concepts.title: Engel's law
concepts.description: The lower a household's income, the bigger the share of it spent on food; richer households spend more dollars but a smaller share.

concepts.title: Paper money reaches Europe
concepts.description: Marco Polo described Chinese paper money in the 13th century; Europe's first banknotes came from Sweden's Stockholms Banco in 1661.

concepts.title: Stock exchanges as meeting places
concepts.description: The NYSE traces its origins to the Buttonwood Agreement of 1792. An exchange gathers buyers and sellers so investors can nearly always buy or sell.

concepts.title: Bids, asks and orders
concepts.description: The bid is the highest price a buyer will pay, the ask the lowest a seller will take, and the gap is the spread. Orders are matched automatically; a market order trades now, a limit order only at your price or better.

concepts.title: Fiat money
concepts.description: Fiat money has no value of its own and no commodity backing; a government declares it legal tender.

concepts.title: Franklin's compound-interest bequest
concepts.description: Benjamin Franklin left £1,000 each to Boston and Philadelphia to be lent at 5% for 200 years, calculating that compounding would make it £131,000 in a century.

concepts.title: Exchange rates
concepts.description: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, set in the foreign exchange market; a stronger currency makes imports cheaper and exports dearer.

concepts.title: Why exchange rates move
concepts.description: Floating exchange rates move with supply and demand for a currency, driven by interest rates, inflation and expectations; some countries fix their rates instead.

concepts.title: What GDP measures
concepts.description: GDP is the market value of the final goods and services a country produces in a period; real GDP adjusts it for price changes.

concepts.title: What GDP misses
concepts.description: GDP leaves out unpaid work and ignores pollution, leisure and how income is shared; its pioneer Kuznets warned it is not a measure of welfare.

concepts.title: The 2008 financial crisis
concepts.description: A US housing bubble fed by risky mortgage lending burst, Lehman Brothers failed in 2008, and the Great Recession followed; economists still debate the causes.

concepts.title: The IMF and the World Bank
concepts.description: The 1944 Bretton Woods conference created the IMF, which lends to countries in crisis with conditions, and the World Bank, which funds development.

concepts.title: The World Trade Organization
concepts.description: The WTO, founded in 1995 from the 1947 GATT, sets trade rules, hosts negotiations and settles disputes between its members.

concepts.title: The gold standard
concepts.description: Under a gold standard, a currency's unit is fixed to a set amount of gold and paper money can be exchanged for it.

concepts.title: Leaving the gold standard
concepts.description: Countries left gold because its supply limited their money; the US ended its last gold link, for foreign governments, in 1971.

concepts.title: Rules for when sellers know more
concepts.description: When one side of a deal knows more about quality (asymmetric information), rules like food-safety and truth-in-advertising laws help buyers; The Jungle led to two such laws in 1906.

concepts.title: Capital rules for banks
concepts.description: Regulators make banks fund part of their lending with owners' money (capital), a cushion that absorbs losses before depositors are hurt; higher requirements make banks safer but may slow lending.

concepts.title: Central bank independence
concepts.description: Central banks are kept at arm's length from elected politicians so short-term election pressures do not push up inflation; critics question how much power unelected officials should hold.

concepts.title: What a central bank does
concepts.description: A central bank runs monetary policy, watches over banks and keeps payments safe. Sweden's Riksbank (1668) is the oldest; the US Federal Reserve dates from 1913 and aims for maximum employment and stable prices.

concepts.title: Budget deficits and surpluses
concepts.description: A government runs a deficit in a year when it spends more than it collects, a surplus when it collects more than it spends, and a balanced budget when the two are equal.

concepts.title: Fiscal policy and monetary policy
concepts.description: Fiscal policy is government spending and taxing, set in the US by Congress and the administration; monetary policy is what the central bank does with interest rates and money.

concepts.title: The free rider problem
concepts.description: When non-payers cannot be excluded, each person has an incentive to let others pay and enjoy the good for free, so a good everyone values may never be produced.

concepts.title: The lighthouse debate
concepts.description: Economists long used the lighthouse as a public good; Ronald Coase showed in 1974 that English lighthouses were privately run and paid for by light dues collected at ports, though critics note the dues were backed by the Crown.

concepts.title: Tax brackets and marginal rates
concepts.description: In a bracketed income tax, only the income inside a higher bracket is taxed at that bracket's rate, so a raise never lowers take-home pay.

concepts.title: Money growth and prices
concepts.description: If the amount of money grows faster than the goods and services it buys, prices rise; the link is real over long periods but not mechanical, because how fast money changes hands can shift.

concepts.title: The national debt
concepts.description: The national debt is the sum of past deficits and surpluses: governments cover deficits by selling bonds, and the debt is that borrowing plus interest. Economists weigh its costs and uses differently.

concepts.title: Pay-as-you-go pensions
concepts.description: US Social Security is pay-as-you-go: today's workers' taxes fund today's beneficiaries, so fewer workers per retiree (about four in 1965, 2.7 in 2023) strains the system.

concepts.title: How a central bank's rate moves the economy
concepts.description: A central bank sets a core short-term rate that feeds into loan and savings rates; raising it cools spending and price rises, cutting it encourages borrowing, spending and hiring, with long and variable lags.

concepts.title: The price revolution
concepts.description: In the 16th century, silver from American mines like Potosí flowed into Spain and across Europe while prices rose about sixfold; historians also point to population growth.

concepts.title: Public goods
concepts.description: A public good is nonexcludable and nonrival, like national defense; because non-payers cannot be kept out, governments usually fund such goods through taxes.

concepts.title: The first social insurance
concepts.description: Germany under Otto von Bismarck created the first old-age social insurance in 1889, paid for by workers, employers and the government, with benefits from age 70.

concepts.title: The main kinds of tax
concepts.description: Taxes fall on what people earn (income, payroll and corporate taxes), what they buy (sales taxes, VATs and excise taxes) and what they own (property and estate taxes).

concepts.title: Progressive, proportional and regressive taxes
concepts.description: A progressive tax takes a higher share of higher incomes, a proportional (flat) tax the same share from everyone, a regressive tax a smaller share of higher incomes. Flat taxes have supporters and critics.

concepts.title: What taxes pay for
concepts.description: Governments collect taxes to pay for what they provide: in the US, federal money goes mostly to defense, Social Security, healthcare and interest; states and cities spend most on education.

concepts.title: Unemployment insurance
concepts.description: Unemployment insurance gives temporary, partial wage replacement to workers who lose jobs through no fault of their own; economists weigh its support for families against effects on job search.

concepts.title: The Volcker rate hikes
concepts.description: Under Paul Volcker, the Federal Reserve let its key rate approach 20% in 1980 and 1981 to fight high inflation; inflation fell to 5% by late 1982, but a deep recession pushed unemployment near 11%.

concepts.title: The Great Depression and its legacy
concepts.description: The Great Depression (1929 to about 1941) was the deepest US downturn: output fell by a third, unemployment reached 25% and prices fell; it reshaped economic policy.

concepts.title: Hanoi's rat bounty
concepts.description: In colonial Hanoi, a bounty paid per rat tail led people to cut off tails, release rats to breed, and farm rats.

concepts.title: Hyperinflation and its causes
concepts.description: Hyperinflation is inflation above 50% a month, usually begun by governments creating money to pay for spending and fed by collapsing trust.

concepts.title: Loss aversion and the endowment effect
concepts.description: People tend to feel losses more strongly than equal gains, so owners value things more than non-owners: the endowment effect, shown in the 1990 mug experiment.

concepts.title: Mental accounting
concepts.description: Thaler's idea that people sort money into separate accounts in their heads and judge each decision on its own.

concepts.title: Coase and bargaining over externalities
concepts.description: Ronald Coase argued in 1960 that when deals cost little to make, affected parties can bargain to an efficient fix without government.

concepts.title: Market, command and mixed economies
concepts.description: In a market economy decisions are spread among buyers and sellers; in a command economy goals come from rulers; most real economies mix the two.

concepts.title: Externalities
concepts.description: An externality is the effect of a deal on a third party outside it; when costs like pollution are ignored, markets make too much of the product.

concepts.title: The Gini coefficient
concepts.description: A single number from 0 (everyone has the same) to 1 (one person has everything) that measures how unequally income is shared.

concepts.title: Hayek and prices as signals
concepts.description: Hayek argued that the knowledge an economy needs is scattered among many people, and that prices pass it along in a way no central planner could.

concepts.title: Keynes and spending in a slump
concepts.description: Keynes argued that unemployment comes from too little total spending, and that government should spend, even by borrowing, to fill the gap.

concepts.title: Keynes's 15-hour week
concepts.description: In 1930, Keynes predicted much higher living standards and a 15-hour work week a century later; longer lives and retirements delivered extra leisure instead.

concepts.title: Keynes's legacy and critics
concepts.description: Keynes helped design Bretton Woods and dominated Western policy until the 1970s, when monetarists led by Milton Friedman gained ground; Hayek never accepted his case.

concepts.title: Marx's critique of capitalism
concepts.description: Marx argued that labor creates value, that owners keep the surplus as profit, and that class struggle would end in the overthrow of capitalism.

concepts.title: Marx's reach and his critics
concepts.description: Marx's ideas inspired communist governments ruling about a third of the world, while critics such as the Austrian school rejected the labor theory of value.

concepts.title: Nudges and defaults
concepts.description: Behavioral economics shows that details like the default option steer decisions; Thaler and Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow lets people commit now to save more later.

concepts.title: Pigou's tax on externalities
concepts.description: In 1920, Arthur Pigou proposed taxing activities that impose costs on others and subsidizing those that spread benefits; a carbon tax is a modern example.

concepts.title: The prisoner's dilemma
concepts.description: A game in which each player does better by betraying whatever the other does, yet both end up worse off than if both had cooperated.

concepts.title: Cooperation in repeated games
concepts.description: When a game repeats with no known last round, cooperation can pay; tit for tat, which cooperates first and then copies, did well in Axelrod's tournaments.

concepts.title: Adam Smith's invisible hand
concepts.description: Smith's idea that many people pursuing their own interest through trade can produce outcomes that benefit society, though no one intends them.

concepts.title: Smith's limits and critics
concepts.description: Smith gave government real duties and distrusted collusion among traders; modern critics such as Joseph Stiglitz argue the invisible hand often fails.

concepts.title: The sunk cost effect
concepts.description: The tendency to keep going with something because of money, effort or time already spent; Arkes and Blumer showed it with theater season tickets.

concepts.title: Wealth versus income inequality
concepts.description: Income is a flow of money coming in; wealth is a stock of what you own. Wealth is far more unequally shared than income.

concepts.title: Incentives
concepts.description: Incentives are rewards (positive) and penalties (negative) that encourage or discourage choices; people respond to them in predictable ways. Prices are incentives too.

concepts.title: Four kinds of income
concepts.description: Land earns rent, labor earns wages, capital earns interest and entrepreneurship earns profit; wages are most people's main income.

concepts.title: The factors of production
concepts.description: Economists group the resources that make goods and services into land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship.

concepts.title: Index funds: from 'Bogle's Folly' to the majority
concepts.description: John Bogle's First Index Investment Trust (1976) raised about $11 million and was mocked as 'Bogle's Folly'. Most active large-cap funds have trailed the S&P 500 over 15 years, and US index-style funds overtook active funds in assets at the end of 2023.

concepts.title: How index funds work
concepts.description: An index fund tracks a market index such as the S&P 500 by holding all or a sample of its securities. It trades rarely, can cost less to run, and carries the same risks as its index.

concepts.title: Why prices rise, and the debate
concepts.description: Demand-pull, cost-push and expectations drive inflation; economists disagree about how much the money supply matters.

concepts.title: What inflation is
concepts.description: Inflation is the rate at which prices rise across an economy over time; it lowers the purchasing power of money.

concepts.title: Interest in ancient Mesopotamia
concepts.description: Mesopotamian laws, including Hammurabi's code in the 18th century BCE, set interest rates: 20% on silver and more on riskier barley loans.

concepts.title: Compound interest
concepts.description: Compound interest is paid on the original amount plus the interest already earned, so growth speeds up over time.

concepts.title: Interest: the price of borrowing
concepts.description: Interest is the price a borrower pays a lender for the use of money, usually stated as a rate; lenders charge it for giving up money now and for taking risk.

concepts.title: The Rule of 72
concepts.description: Dividing 72 by an annual interest rate estimates how many years compounding takes to double money.

concepts.title: Comparing homes for money: safety, growth and access
concepts.description: Every saving and investment product differs in how safe the money is, how fast it can grow and how readily you can get it back. A liquid asset can be turned into cash quickly.

concepts.title: Secured and unsecured loans
concepts.description: Secured loans are backed by collateral and usually cost less; unsecured loans have none, so lenders see more risk and may charge more.

concepts.title: The first coins
concepts.description: The first coins were probably made in Lydia, in modern Turkey, around 650 BCE; coinage also arose separately in China.

concepts.title: What a market is
concepts.description: A market is any way buyers and sellers get in contact to exchange goods and services, directly or through go-betweens. It need not be a place.

concepts.title: eBay's first sale
concepts.description: In 1995, the first item sold on AuctionWeb, the site that became eBay, was a broken laser pointer, for $14.83.

concepts.title: Markets for work and savings
concepts.description: Supply and demand apply to any market: goods and services, labor and financial capital.

concepts.title: Marshall's scissors
concepts.description: Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: price comes from both together.

concepts.title: Why metal made good money
concepts.description: Metal suits money because it is portable, does not perish and is hard to counterfeit.

concepts.title: Microcredit and Grameen Bank
concepts.description: Muhammad Yunus showed that small loans without collateral could work for the poor, founding Grameen Bank and sharing the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize.

concepts.title: Six traits of useful money
concepts.description: Useful money is durable, portable, divisible, uniform, limited in supply and acceptable.

concepts.title: The three jobs of money
concepts.description: Money is whatever works as a medium of exchange (a way to pay), a unit of account (a measure of value) and a store of value (a way to save).

concepts.title: Money runs on trust
concepts.description: Money is valuable because people trust that others will accept it; when that trust goes, its value goes too.

concepts.title: What a monopoly is
concepts.description: A monopoly is a single supplier of something with no substitute, protected by barriers to entry.

concepts.title: Why monopolies hurt buyers
concepts.description: A monopoly sells less at a higher price than a competitive market, and faces less pressure to improve.

concepts.title: Standard Oil and antitrust
concepts.description: Standard Oil dominated US refining until the Supreme Court broke it up in 1911 under the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890.

concepts.title: A mortgage: a loan pledged on a home
concepts.description: A mortgage lets the lender take the property if the loan isn't repaid; the word means 'dead pledge' because the pledge ends either way.

concepts.title: Why mortgages last decades
concepts.description: Longer mortgages mean lower monthly payments but more total cost; early payments are mostly interest (amortization).

concepts.title: Needs set by custom
concepts.description: Adam Smith counted as necessaries whatever local custom made shameful to go without, so the line between needs and wants moves with time and place.

concepts.title: Needs and wants
concepts.description: Needs are essential to survival and basic living; wants are for enjoyment. A need can come in a want-sized version.

concepts.title: Opportunity cost
concepts.description: Every choice costs the value of the next best alternative you give up, including time and lost earnings.

concepts.title: No such thing as a free lunch
concepts.description: Saloons once gave free lunch to drink buyers; the saying that no lunch is free became an economic maxim.

concepts.title: Paycheck deductions
concepts.description: Employers withhold payroll taxes and income tax, and may deduct retirement or health contributions, before pay arrives.

concepts.title: Gross and net pay
concepts.description: Gross pay is what you earn before deductions; net (take-home) pay is what you receive after them.

concepts.title: The division of labor and the pin factory
concepts.description: In The Wealth of Nations (1776), Adam Smith showed that splitting pin-making into about 18 operations let ten workers make upwards of 48,000 pins a day, and explained why specializing raises output.

concepts.title: Smith's warning about repetitive work
concepts.description: Smith also warned that a lifetime of a few simple, repeated operations could dull a worker's mind.

concepts.title: Cigarettes as money in a POW camp
concepts.description: In a WWII prisoner-of-war camp described by R. A. Radford in 1945, cigarettes became the currency and did all three jobs of money.

concepts.title: Price ceilings cause shortages
concepts.description: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price. Set below equilibrium, it creates a shortage, as with rent control.

concepts.title: Equilibrium price
concepts.description: The price where supply and demand cross: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

concepts.title: Price floors cause surpluses
concepts.description: A price floor is a legal minimum price. Set above equilibrium, it creates a surplus.

concepts.title: How surpluses and shortages move prices
concepts.description: Above equilibrium there is a surplus and sellers cut prices; below it there is a shortage and sellers raise prices.

concepts.title: Prices carry information
concepts.description: Hayek (1945): the price system communicates information. When something becomes scarcer, its price tells users to economize without their needing to know why.

concepts.title: Pricing cues
concepts.description: Shoppers rarely know what a price should be, so cues like prices ending in 9 and sale signs sway them.

concepts.title: The decoy effect
concepts.description: Adding a third, worse option can steer people toward one of the original two.

concepts.title: Fixed and variable costs
concepts.description: Fixed costs, such as rent, machinery and advertising, stay the same however much a firm produces; variable costs, such as labor and raw materials, rise and fall with output.

concepts.title: Revenue, costs and profit
concepts.description: Revenue is what a business takes in from sales (price times quantity); profit is revenue minus total cost, and a loss when costs are bigger. Amazon sold billions and still lost money in 2002.

concepts.title: Pensions and 401(k)-style plans
concepts.description: A traditional pension pays a set benefit the employer funds and invests. In a 401(k)-style plan the worker chooses how much to save and how to invest it, sometimes with an employer match, and carries the investment risk.

concepts.title: Starting early: time does the work
concepts.description: The earlier you start saving, the more time money has to grow. In the SEC's example, $365 saved once at 5% a year becomes $465.84 after five years and $1,577.50 after 30.

concepts.title: How a credit card borrows
concepts.description: A credit card is revolving credit: you borrow up to a limit, and a balance paid in full by the due date may avoid interest on purchases.

concepts.title: Credit card interest and minimum payments
concepts.description: Card interest rates are high and compounding makes unpaid balances grow; US statements must warn about paying only the minimum.

concepts.title: The risk-return tradeoff
concepts.description: In finance, risk is uncertainty about what an investment will return. As risk rises, investors seek higher returns to compensate, and people with longer time horizons can more easily ride out risky investments.

concepts.title: Stocks and Treasury bills since 1928
concepts.description: From 1928 to 2025, US stocks grew far more than Treasury bills but had big losing years, while bills never lost money in a year.

concepts.title: Salt money
concepts.description: In Ethiopia, bars of salt served as money for centuries; salt was useful as well as accepted.

concepts.title: Emergency funds
concepts.description: An emergency fund is cash set aside for unplanned costs, kept somewhere safe and easy to reach. In 2024, 63% of US adults said they could cover a $400 surprise with cash or its equivalent.

concepts.title: Saving for goals, and the price of safety
concepts.description: Saving toward a specific goal helps people stay motivated. Savings kept safe and reachable usually earn a low interest rate: the tradeoff between security and availability.

concepts.title: Diseconomies of scale
concepts.description: A firm can grow so large that it becomes hard to manage, and then its cost per unit rises again.

concepts.title: Economies of scale
concepts.description: Making more of something can lower the cost of each unit, mainly because fixed costs are spread over more units. Ford's mass-produced Model T fell from $850 to as little as $260.

concepts.title: How much scams cost
concepts.description: In 2024 people reported losing more than $12.5 billion to fraud to the FTC, most of it through bank transfers and crypto.

concepts.title: Four signs of a scam
concepts.description: Scammers pretend to be someone you know, claim a problem or prize, pressure you to act now, and demand a specific way to pay.

concepts.title: Scarcity, the basic problem of economics
concepts.description: Scarcity means people's wants exceed what's available, for everyone; time is the ultimate scarce resource. Economics studies how people choose under scarcity.

concepts.title: Forgotten subscriptions
concepts.description: People underestimate recurring subscription spending and often forget charges they no longer use.

concepts.title: Small costs over a year
concepts.description: A small recurring cost looks small month by month; added up over a year it becomes a big number, and a big opportunity cost.

concepts.title: Start-up costs and funding
concepts.description: Starting a business involves one-time costs (equipment, permits, licenses) and ongoing ones (rent, salaries, utilities), usually funded by savings, loans or investors who take a share of ownership.

concepts.title: Entrepreneurs and the risk of starting up
concepts.description: An entrepreneur organizes, runs and carries the risk of a business. HP began in a garage with $538; about half of new US businesses close within five years.

concepts.title: What a share of stock is
concepts.description: A stock is a share of ownership in a company. Companies sell shares to raise money; shareholders can gain from dividends and rising prices, and common shareholders usually vote, but prices can fall.

concepts.title: The VOC and the first public shares
concepts.description: In 1602 the Dutch East India Company (VOC) let the public buy its shares, making it the first publicly traded company. Shares changed hands in a register, and the first dividend (1610) was paid in mace.

concepts.title: The law of supply
concepts.description: When a price rises, sellers offer more; when it falls, they offer less, because higher prices mean more profit.

concepts.title: What shifts supply
concepts.description: Supply and demand curves assume other things stay equal (ceteris paribus). Costs, weather, technology and government policy shift the whole supply curve; a price change only moves along it.

concepts.title: The tariff debate
concepts.description: Supporters say tariffs protect industries, jobs and national security; critics say they raise costs, distort markets and invite retaliation.

concepts.title: Tariffs and who pays them
concepts.description: A tariff is a tax on imports paid by the importing company; the cost can pass to consumers, be absorbed, or squeeze foreign exporters.

concepts.title: The balance of trade
concepts.description: The trade balance is exports minus imports: a surplus if exports are bigger, a deficit if imports are; whether deficits matter is debated.

concepts.title: The Big Mac index and purchasing power parity
concepts.description: The Economist's Big Mac index compares burger prices to test purchasing power parity, the idea that exchange rates drift toward equalizing prices.

concepts.title: Comparative advantage
concepts.description: A country has a comparative advantage in a good it makes at a lower cost in terms of the other goods it gives up; specializing by comparative advantage lets both sides gain.

concepts.title: Container shipping
concepts.description: Malcolm McLean's 1956 container voyage showed that loading whole boxes, rather than loose cargo, made shipping far cheaper.

concepts.title: Gains from trade
concepts.description: Voluntary trade happens only when both sides expect to gain, but a country's gains are spread widely while some workers and firms lose.

concepts.title: Global supply chains
concepts.description: Many products are made from parts and services sourced in many countries, so trade statistics and single disruptions can mislead or ripple worldwide.

concepts.title: The globalization debate
concepts.description: Globalization has lowered prices and helped poor countries grow, while job losses from import competition have been concentrated in particular places.

concepts.title: Imports and exports
concepts.description: Exports are goods and services sold abroad and imports are those bought from abroad; services, including travel spending, count too.

concepts.title: Why countries make different things
concepts.description: Countries differ in resources, climate and skills, so each can make some things far more cheaply than others and trade for the rest.

concepts.title: Ricardo's wine and cloth
concepts.description: In 1817, David Ricardo showed that Portugal and England both gain by specializing and trading, even though Portugal made both wine and cloth with fewer workers.

concepts.title: The Silk Road
concepts.description: The Silk Road linked China with the West by caravan, with goods passing in stages through middlemen.

concepts.title: Dutch tulip mania
concepts.description: The 1630s Dutch tulip craze, long called the first speculative bubble, crashed in February 1637; historian Anne Goldgar found it far smaller than legend says.

concepts.title: How unemployment is measured
concepts.description: The US counts unemployment with a monthly household survey; the unemployed must lack a job, have looked for work and be available, and people outside the labor force are not counted.

concepts.title: Frictional, structural and cyclical unemployment
concepts.description: Unemployment is frictional (between jobs), structural (skills mismatch) or cyclical (caused by recession); the first two make up the natural rate.

concepts.title: Unions and collective bargaining
concepts.description: A union is an association of workers acting together to improve their conditions. It negotiates with employers through collective bargaining and can strike. About 1 in 10 US workers is a member.

concepts.title: The Flint sit-down strike
concepts.description: In 1936 and 1937, autoworkers occupied General Motors plants in Flint, Michigan, for 44 days until GM recognized their union, the United Auto Workers.

concepts.title: Compensating differentials
concepts.description: Dirty, dangerous or unpleasant jobs tend to pay more than pleasant jobs needing similar skill. Adam Smith noticed it; economists call it a compensating differential.

concepts.title: Wages as the price of labor
concepts.description: A wage is the price of labor, set in a labor market where employers demand and workers supply labor. More productive workers are in more demand, and jobs needing long training have fewer candidates.

concepts.title: The water and diamond puzzle
concepts.description: Water is vital but cheap, diamonds are nearly useless but dear. The standard explanation is scarcity: water is plentiful, diamonds are not.

concepts.title: Institutions and the wealth of nations
concepts.description: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson link prosperity to institutions: inclusive rules support growth, extractive ones enrich an elite.

concepts.title: Other explanations for rich and poor countries
concepts.description: Other economists stress geography, disease and isolation, and all explanations meet at productivity: output per worker.

concepts.title: Weimar Germany's hyperinflation
concepts.description: In 1923, Germany printed money to pay its bills until a dollar cost trillions of marks; historians debate how much reparations were to blame.

concepts.title: Yap's stone money
concepts.description: On Yap, large stone discs quarried on Palau served as money, changing owners by shared agreement without moving.

concepts.title: Zimbabwe's hyperinflation
concepts.description: In 2008, after land reforms crippled farming and the government printed money, Zimbabwe's prices doubled roughly daily until it abandoned its currency in 2009.

concepts.title: Adrenaline and fight or flight
concepts.description: In danger, nerves from the hypothalamus trigger the adrenal glands to release adrenaline within seconds, raising heart rate and blood sugar and preparing the body to fight or flee.

concepts.title: The Hayflick limit and telomeres
concepts.description: Normal human cells divide only about 40 to 60 times (Hayflick, 1961), partly because telomeres at chromosome ends shorten at each division.

concepts.title: Senescent cells and accumulated damage
concepts.description: Cells that stop dividing without dying (senescent cells) build up with age and release inflammatory molecules; the WHO describes ageing as accumulated molecular and cellular damage.

concepts.title: Coughs and sneezes clear the airways
concepts.description: Airway sensors detect irritants and trigger coughs and sneezes. A cough takes a deep breath, holds the glottis shut while muscles build pressure, then blasts air out; a sneeze bursts air through the nose and mouth.

concepts.title: What a hiccup is
concepts.description: A hiccup is a spasm of the diaphragm that pulls in a sudden breath, cut off by the vocal cords snapping shut, which makes the 'hic'. Most bouts pass in minutes.

concepts.title: How bodies adapt to altitude
concepts.description: Given time, the body acclimatizes: deeper, faster breathing, a faster heart and more red blood cells. Altitude sickness, usually above about 2,400 m, is more likely with a fast climb and usually fades in 2 to 5 days.

concepts.title: Why air is thinner up high
concepts.description: Air is about 21 percent oxygen at every altitude, but pressure falls with height, so each breath brings in less oxygen; at Everest's summit pressure is about 30 percent of sea level. Messner and Habeler first climbed it without bottled oxygen in 1978.

concepts.title: A big brain and a young species
concepts.description: Brain size tripled over human evolution; Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago and is one of more than 200 primate species.

concepts.title: Neanderthal DNA in living people
concepts.description: Our species interbred with Neanderthals; about 1 to 4 percent of the DNA of people of European or Asian descent is Neanderthal (Pääbo, Nobel 2022).

concepts.title: Walking upright, an inheritance millions of years old
concepts.description: Walking on two legs goes back to the earliest known humans about 6 million years ago; the shock-absorbing lower-back curve is uniquely human.

concepts.title: What happens in the airways in asthma
concepts.description: Asthma is a long-term airway condition, the most common chronic disease in children. In an attack the airways swell, narrow, make extra mucus and may tighten, set off by triggers like pollen, smoke, cold air, infections or exercise.

concepts.title: How asthma is managed with medical care
concepts.description: Asthma is managed with a healthcare provider and a written action plan; inhalers deliver medicine straight to the lungs, with quick-relief medicines opening airways in an attack and daily controllers reducing inflammation.

concepts.title: What blood is made of
concepts.description: Blood is over half plasma, which is about 92 percent water, plus red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets; an adult has about 4 to 6 liters.
