concepts.title: Red blood cells carry oxygen
concepts.description: Red blood cells, about 45 percent of blood's volume, carry oxygen on hemoglobin, the iron-containing protein that makes blood red; oxygen-rich blood is bright red, oxygen-poor blood dusky red.

concepts.title: Blood pressure categories and why it is checked
concepts.description: The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline keeps four categories (normal, elevated, stage 1, stage 2); high blood pressure usually has no symptoms, so measuring is the only way to know.

concepts.title: What blood pressure measures
concepts.description: Blood pressure is the force of blood on artery walls, read as systolic (as the heart pumps) over diastolic (between beats), in mm Hg.

concepts.title: ABO blood types
concepts.description: Landsteiner published the ABO groups in 1901 after seeing red cells clump when blood was mixed; your type depends on A and B antigens on red cell membranes.

concepts.title: Why transfusions must match
concepts.description: Antibodies attack donated red cells carrying a marker the recipient lacks; Rh is a second label; O negative can go to anyone in an emergency and AB positive can receive any type.

concepts.title: Circadian rhythms and the master clock
concepts.description: Body rhythms follow a roughly 24-hour cycle set mainly by light and run by the SCN master clock, which controls melatonin; in teens melatonin timing runs later.

concepts.title: Why jet lag happens
concepts.description: Crossing time zones leaves the body clock on home time; it adapts about 1 hour a day eastward and 1.5 westward, because the inner clock runs slightly long.

concepts.title: What water does in the body
concepts.description: Water keeps temperature normal (evaporating sweat cools the skin), cushions joints, protects the spinal cord and carries waste away.

concepts.title: How much of the body is water
concepts.description: Water is about 75 percent of a newborn and 50 to 60 percent of an adult, less in old age and with more fat; almost two-thirds of it is inside cells.

concepts.title: Why babies have more bones
concepts.description: A newborn has roughly 270 to 300 bones (sources vary); many start as cartilage, and over childhood separate pieces fuse, from skull bones to the hip bones and sacrum, into the adult 206.

concepts.title: Growth plates
concepts.description: Long bones lengthen at growth plates, layers of cartilage near their ends that are turned into bone; when bone replaces the plate in early adulthood, growth in length stops.

concepts.title: Marrow, the blood factory
concepts.description: Red marrow, in the spaces of spongy bone such as in the hip and thigh bones, makes red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets; yellow marrow is mostly fat.

concepts.title: What bone is made of
concepts.description: Bone is living tissue: flexible collagen fibers hardened with calcium phosphate crystals, arranged as dense compact bone outside and a lattice of spongy bone inside.

concepts.title: The brain's energy budget
concepts.description: The brain is about 2 percent of body weight but uses about 20 percent of the body's energy at rest, and hard thinking adds very little.

concepts.title: Two hemispheres
concepts.description: The cerebrum has two hemispheres linked by the corpus callosum; each controls the opposite side of the body, and some jobs, like forming words, lean to one side.

concepts.title: The left-brained, right-brained myth
concepts.description: The popular idea that logical people are left-brained and creative people right-brained is not supported: a 2013 study of 1,011 brain scans found no one with a stronger side overall.

concepts.title: The four lobes
concepts.description: Each cerebral hemisphere has frontal, parietal, occipital and temporal lobes, each specializing in different work, from planning to vision to hearing and memory.

concepts.title: The main parts of the brain
concepts.description: The brainstem runs vital functions, the cerebellum coordinates movement, and the cerebrum, the largest part, handles conscious thought; the cerebellum holds most of the neurons.

concepts.title: Carbon dioxide drives the urge to breathe
concepts.description: A respiratory center in the brainstem runs breathing automatically; its main signal is rising carbon dioxide, which makes the brain more acidic. Low oxygen drives breathing only when it falls quite low.

concepts.title: Why breath-holding in water is dangerous
concepts.description: Hyperventilating or long breath-holding lowers carbon dioxide, delaying the urge to breathe while oxygen keeps falling, which can cause blackout and drowning; CDC warns against it, and strong swimmers have died this way.

concepts.title: What changes between a breath in and a breath out
concepts.description: Air going in is about 21 percent oxygen; air leaving the air sacs still holds about 16 percent, plus 4 to 5 percent carbon dioxide, so the body keeps only part of each breath's oxygen. Adults breathe 12 to 18 times a minute at rest.

concepts.title: Why cells need oxygen
concepts.description: Cells use oxygen to release energy from food, mostly in their mitochondria, and give off carbon dioxide as waste that the blood carries to the lungs to be breathed out.

concepts.title: How the diaphragm pulls air in
concepts.description: The dome-shaped diaphragm contracts and moves down, enlarging the chest; pressure in the lungs falls below the air outside, and air flows in, about 500 mL in a quiet breath.

concepts.title: The nose conditions the air
concepts.description: The nose (and mouth) warms and moistens incoming air, because cold, dry air irritates the lungs, and nostril hairs and the airways remove debris and germs.

concepts.title: Breathing out: recoil at rest, muscles at work
concepts.description: At rest, breathing out is passive: the muscles relax and the elastic lungs recoil like a balloon. During activity the rib muscles and extra muscles help force air in and out.

concepts.title: Measuring the energy in food and people
concepts.description: From 1896, Wilbur Atwater's respiration calorimeter showed energy is conserved in the human body and gave the 4, 9 and 4 Calories per gram used for food energy today.

concepts.title: Bodies need different amounts of energy
concepts.description: How much energy a body uses varies with age, sex, body size, activity and metabolic rate; the brain, about 2 percent of body weight, uses about 20 percent of the body's calories.

concepts.title: What a calorie is
concepts.description: A calorie is a unit of energy, the heat that warms 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius; the food Calorie is a kilocalorie; food energy is released in digestion and used by cells.

concepts.title: What a cell is
concepts.description: Cells are the basic building blocks of all living things; each takes in nutrients, makes energy and does a job, and the body is made of trillions.

concepts.title: How many cells make a body
concepts.description: A 2016 estimate puts a reference adult at about 30 trillion human cells, most of them red blood cells; counts vary with body size.

concepts.title: How many kinds of cell
concepts.description: The body's cells fall into about 400 types whose masses span seven orders of magnitude: red blood cells lead the count, muscle cells the mass.

concepts.title: The main parts of a cell
concepts.description: A cell has a plasma membrane that controls what enters and leaves, jelly-like cytoplasm, a nucleus that directs the cell, and mitochondria that supply energy.

concepts.title: The body renews its cells
concepts.description: About 330 billion cells, roughly 1 percent, are replaced every day, mostly blood cells; each new cell comes from an existing one and gets a full copy of the DNA.

concepts.title: One lap of the circulation
concepts.description: Blood runs two circuits, through the lungs and through the body, passing the heart twice per lap; at rest the heart pumps about an adult's whole blood supply each minute.

concepts.title: How blood clots
concepts.description: To stop bleeding, the vessel narrows, platelets form a plug, and clotting factors build a fibrin mesh; in hemophilia a missing clotting factor stops blood clotting properly.

concepts.title: Acquired immunity: antibodies and memory
concepts.description: Acquired immunity develops as you meet germs: B cells make antibodies against a specific antigen, T cells attack directly, and memory cells make the next response faster.

concepts.title: Why some people have allergies
concepts.description: Genes and environment both shape allergies, which run in families; about a third of US adults have a diagnosed seasonal allergy, eczema or food allergy, and anaphylaxis can be life-threatening.

concepts.title: How an allergy happens
concepts.description: An allergy is the immune system reacting to something harmless: IgE antibodies attach to mast cells, and on a later exposure the mast cells release histamine, which causes symptoms.

concepts.title: Why fever helps
concepts.description: Fever's heat stirs white blood cells and antibody production and slows some germs; it is costly but over 600 million years old, and even infected lizards seek warmth.

concepts.title: Fever: the thermostat turned up
concepts.description: In a fever, pyrogens in the blood make the hypothalamus raise the body's temperature set point, so you feel chilly as temperature climbs and warm and sweaty as it falls.

concepts.title: Three kinds of germ
concepts.description: Germs are microbes that cause infectious disease; bacteria are single living cells, most of them harmless, fungi include molds and yeasts, and viruses are not cells at all.

concepts.title: Handwashing today
concepts.description: The CDC calls soap and water the best way to remove germs in most situations: scrub at least 20 seconds, because friction lifts microbes off skin before hands carry them to your face. It cuts diarrheal illness by 23 to 40 percent.

concepts.title: Innate immunity and phagocytes
concepts.description: Innate immunity is the nonspecific defense you are born with: barriers like skin plus phagocytes, the "devouring cells" Metchnikoff found in starfish larvae in 1882.

concepts.title: Jenner and the first vaccine
concepts.description: Milkmaids with cowpox escaped smallpox. In 1796 Jenner inoculated James Phipps with cowpox, then with smallpox, and no disease developed; he named the method vaccination. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.

concepts.title: Lymph nodes, the immune system's meeting points
concepts.description: Lymph nodes sit along the lymph vessels in places like the neck, armpits and groin; with the spleen they are where white blood cells fight infection, which is why infections make them swell.

concepts.title: Florey, Chain and the Oxford team
concepts.description: Florey and Chain's Oxford team purified penicillin, grew it even in bedpans, cured infected mice in 1940 and treated a first patient in 1941; a British-American effort mass-produced it and the three men shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.

concepts.title: Fleming's moldy dish
concepts.description: In September 1928 Fleming saw Staphylococcus fail to grow near a Penicillium mold that had contaminated a dish left out during his vacation; he named the substance penicillin.

concepts.title: Semmelweis and childbed fever
concepts.description: In 1847 Semmelweis traced higher childbed fever deaths in the students' division to infection carried on hands from the dissecting room; chlorinated lime handwashing cut deaths from about 18 to about 1 percent, but he was rejected.

concepts.title: Skin's chemical and living shields
concepts.description: The skin surface is cool, dry and slightly acidic, oil from its glands kills bacteria, and resident microbes crowd out harmful ones.

concepts.title: Skin, the body's outer wall
concepts.description: Skin is the largest organ: an epidermis of epithelial cells over the dermis and hypodermis, topped by dead, keratin-packed cells that block germs and are replaced about every 4 weeks.

concepts.title: Vaccines are safe, effective and shared
concepts.description: Vaccines are tested in several trial phases and monitored after use; side effects are usually minor. They protect the unvaccinated around us and have saved at least 154 million lives since 1974.

concepts.title: How vaccines train immunity
concepts.description: A vaccine imitates an infection with a killed or weakened germ, a part of one or genetic instructions, so the immune system makes antibodies and memory without the disease.

concepts.title: Variolation before vaccines
concepts.description: Before vaccines, people in Africa, India and China deliberately infected healthy people with smallpox material; about 2 to 3 percent died, far fewer than from natural smallpox. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu brought it to England in 1721.

concepts.title: Viruses, the hijackers
concepts.description: Viruses are genetic material in a protein coat, far smaller than bacteria, and can multiply only by hijacking living cells; they were found in 1892 because they slipped through bacterial filters.

concepts.title: From food to a cell's energy
concepts.description: Digested sugars are absorbed into the blood, pass the liver, and are carried to cells, where mitochondria combine food molecules with oxygen to release their energy; spare fuel is stored.

concepts.title: Peristalsis moves food
concepts.description: Waves of muscle contraction, peristalsis, push food along the tract, so swallowing does not depend on gravity, even upside down or in orbit.

concepts.title: The route through the digestive tract
concepts.description: Food travels one tube, mouth, esophagus, stomach, small and large intestine, anus, while the liver, pancreas and gallbladder add juices; the small intestine absorbs most nutrients and the large intestine absorbs water.

concepts.title: DNA, the instruction book
concepts.description: DNA is the hereditary material, written in four chemical letters (A, C, G, T) whose order carries information; about 3 billion letters, over 99 percent shared.

concepts.title: Where the body keeps DNA
concepts.description: Nearly every cell holds the same DNA, mostly in the nucleus as 46 chromosomes, with a little in mitochondria; mature red blood cells have no nucleus.

concepts.title: Dreams and REM sleep
concepts.description: Rapid eye movements in sleep were discovered in the early 1950s and linked to dreaming; everyone dreams, most vividly in REM, though dreams occur in other stages too.

concepts.title: Theories of dreaming
concepts.description: Why we dream is not known. Leading ideas include Freud's disguised wishes, the activation-synthesis hypothesis, and dreams helping process emotions and memories.

concepts.title: Epigenetics: switches on the DNA
concepts.description: Chemical tags such as methyl groups switch genes on or off without changing the DNA letters; identical twins' tags drift apart with age.

concepts.title: Fertilization: egg and sperm make one cell
concepts.description: A sperm cell and an egg cell, each carrying 23 chromosomes, fuse into one cell, the zygote, with the full 46: one of each pair from each parent.

concepts.title: Fractures and how doctors see them
concepts.description: A fracture is a break in a bone; X-rays show it because calcium-rich bone absorbs X-rays, and a cast or splint keeps the bone still so it heals in line.

concepts.title: How a broken bone heals
concepts.description: A break heals in stages: a clot within hours, a cartilage callus within days, spongy bone over weeks, then remodeling into compact bone over months to years, faster in children.

concepts.title: What a gene is
concepts.description: A gene is a stretch of DNA; about 20,000 human genes code for proteins, filling under 2 percent of the genome, and most traits involve many genes.

concepts.title: From gene to protein
concepts.description: A gene is copied into messenger RNA, which leaves the nucleus; a ribosome reads it three letters at a time and links amino acids into a protein.

concepts.title: Harvey shows that blood circulates
concepts.description: Galen said the liver makes blood that the body uses up; in 1628 Harvey showed by arithmetic and a tied-off arm that the same blood circulates, pumped by the heart.

concepts.title: What activity does for the body
concepts.description: Regular activity improves fitness, heart and bone health, thinking and mental health; for adults it lowers heart disease risk and improves sleep, and some brain benefits come right after a session.

concepts.title: WHO's 2020 physical activity guidelines
concepts.description: WHO's 2020 guidelines recommend an average of 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity a day for ages 5 to 17 and 150 to 300 minutes a week for adults; the CDC's talk test tells moderate from vigorous.

concepts.title: Body myths debunked
concepts.description: We use far more than 10 percent of our brains, every part of the tongue with taste buds senses all tastes, spiders avoid sleeping people, hair and nails don't grow after death and the head isn't a special heat leak.

concepts.title: WHO's healthy-diet principles
concepts.description: WHO describes a healthy diet by four principles (adequacy, balance, moderation, diversity); the exact mix varies by person and culture, and it helps protect against malnutrition and diseases.

concepts.title: WHO's diet numbers
concepts.description: WHO recommends at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day for people over 10, free sugars under 10 percent of daily energy and salt under 5 g a day.

concepts.title: Testing myths with evidence
concepts.description: Donald Unger's 50-year one-hand experiment and a 2011 study found no link between knuckle cracking and arthritis; blinded trials show sugar doesn't make kids hyper, but expecting it changes what parents see.

concepts.title: Placebos, randomization and blinding
concepts.description: Trials compare a medicine with an inactive placebo, assign people at random and often blind patients and doctors, so that expectation and chance can be told apart from the drug's real effect.

concepts.title: Why sleep matters for health
concepts.description: Sleep helps learning and long-term memory, supports growth in young people, helps immune defenses and gives the heart a rest; enough sleep is linked to lower risk of several chronic diseases.

concepts.title: How much sleep people need
concepts.description: CDC recommendations, based on AASM consensus statements, are 9 to 12 hours for ages 6 to 12, 8 to 10 for teens and 7 or more for adults; most US high schoolers get less than 8.

concepts.title: Short-term and long-lasting stress
concepts.description: Short bursts of stress can help you meet a challenge, but stress that doesn't let up can affect sleep and several body systems; talking with a trusted adult or health professional can help.

concepts.title: The stress response
concepts.description: The amygdala alerts the hypothalamus; adrenaline speeds heart and breathing and releases stored fuel; cortisol keeps the body alert; the parasympathetic nervous system then acts as a brake.

concepts.title: Sunlight and vitamin D
concepts.description: Skin makes vitamin D from UVB in sunlight; vitamin D helps regulate calcium and phosphate for bones, teeth and muscles; glass blocks UVB, and winter sun in places like the UK is too weak.

concepts.title: Anesthesia ends the agony
concepts.description: On 16 October 1846 in Boston, William Morton showed that ether could make surgery painless, so surgeons no longer had to operate at speed on patients who felt everything.

concepts.title: From antisepsis to asepsis
concepts.description: Joseph Lister used carbolic acid from 1865 to kill germs in wounds and on instruments; modern surgery aims for asepsis, sterilizing everything that touches the surgical field.

concepts.title: The first successful transplant
concepts.description: On 23 December 1954, Joseph Murray's team moved a kidney from Ronald Herrick to his identical twin Richard; today one donor can save up to 8 lives.

concepts.title: Rejection and matching
concepts.description: The immune system can attack a donated organ's foreign antigens; doctors match blood and tissue types, and recipients take immunosuppressants, usually for life. Identical twins match almost perfectly.

concepts.title: Clinical-trial phases
concepts.description: New medicines go from preclinical lab tests to Phase 1 (safety and dose), Phase 2 (does it work, side effects), Phase 3 (large trials) and Phase 4 (monitoring after approval).

concepts.title: Too much UV and sun protection
concepts.description: Too much UV damages DNA, causes sunburn and raises risks of skin cancer, cataracts and skin ageing; WHO advises protection at UV Index 3 or above, and the CDC recommends SPF 15+ broad-spectrum sunscreen.

concepts.title: The heart's four chambers
concepts.description: The heart is a fist-sized muscular pump with four chambers: atria receive blood, ventricles pump it; the right side sends blood to the lungs, the left side to the whole body.

concepts.title: Coronary arteries and heart attacks
concepts.description: The heart muscle is fed by the coronary arteries; in coronary heart disease plaque narrows them, and a sudden blockage of blood to part of the heart muscle is a heart attack.

concepts.title: What public-health bodies say affects heart health
concepts.description: The WHO calls cardiovascular diseases the leading cause of death, mostly preventable by addressing risks like unhealthy diet, inactivity, tobacco and alcohol; the AHA tracks eight measures in Life's Essential 8.

concepts.title: How much the heart pumps
concepts.description: About 70 mL per beat, about 100,000 beats and 7,000 to 8,000 liters a day, nearly 2.9 billion beats and more than 200 million liters over 79 years.

concepts.title: Heart rate and the heart's pacemaker
concepts.description: Each beat starts at the SA node in the right atrium; a normal resting adult rate is 60 to 100 beats a minute, faster in young children and during exercise.

concepts.title: Heart valves keep blood moving one way
concepts.description: Four valves open to let blood through and close to stop it flowing backward; their closing makes the lub-dub sound.

concepts.title: Two versions of each gene, one from each parent
concepts.description: You inherit two alleles for each variable stretch of DNA, one from each parent; a dominant allele can mask a recessive one, and random sorting gives each egg or sperm a different mix.

concepts.title: Most traits involve many genes
concepts.description: Traits like height and skin color are polygenic and shaped by environment; even eye color involves several genes, not one where brown simply beats blue.

concepts.title: How the intestines absorb
concepts.description: The small intestine does most digestion and absorbs almost all nutrients through villi and microvilli; nutrients go in the blood to the liver first; the large intestine absorbs water, and its bacteria make vitamin K.

concepts.title: The gut's real surface area
concepts.description: Textbooks long said the gut's inner surface rivals a tennis court; a 2014 measurement found about 30 to 40 square meters, half a badminton court, mostly in the small intestine.

concepts.title: Joints sorted by how much they move
concepts.description: A joint is where bones meet; joints can be immovable (skull sutures), slightly movable (between vertebrae) or freely movable (synovial joints).

concepts.title: How much the kidneys filter
concepts.description: The kidneys filter about 150 to 180 liters of fluid a day and return about 99 percent to the blood, leaving about 1 to 2 liters of urine.

concepts.title: Kidneys and nephrons
concepts.description: Two fist-sized kidneys below the rib cage hold about a million nephrons each; a glomerulus filters the blood and a tubule returns what the body needs.

concepts.title: The oldest verified person
concepts.description: Jeanne Calment died in 1997 aged 122; a 2018 challenge to her record was rejected by its validators, and most researchers accept it.

concepts.title: Why life expectancy has risen
concepts.description: Global life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2024 (UN); it was once pulled down by child deaths, and it has risen at all ages thanks to nutrition, sanitation and health care.

concepts.title: The liver's many jobs
concepts.description: The liver, the body's largest gland, gets nutrient-rich blood from the gut first; it makes bile for fats, stores glycogen and vitamins, breaks down old red blood cells and clears wastes.

concepts.title: The liver grows back
concepts.description: Up to two-thirds of a healthy liver can be removed and the remaining cells multiply until it is back to about its original size, over weeks to months.

concepts.title: The airways: from windpipe to bronchioles
concepts.description: Air travels past the voice box, down the windpipe and through the branching bronchial tree to thousands of bronchioles; the right lung has three lobes and the left two; cilia sweep mucus and trapped dirt up to the throat to be swallowed.

concepts.title: The alveoli, where gas is exchanged
concepts.description: The lungs hold about 480 million tiny air sacs wrapped in capillaries; oxygen crosses their very thin walls into the blood and carbon dioxide crosses back.

concepts.title: Malpighi finds the missing link
concepts.description: Harvey could not see how blood crossed from arteries to veins; in 1661 Malpighi's microscope revealed the capillaries connecting them.

concepts.title: Forgetting and spacing
concepts.description: Ebbinghaus showed that most forgetting happens soon after learning; spacing study out over time makes memories last longer than cramming.

concepts.title: The hippocampus and new memories
concepts.description: The case of Henry Molaison showed that the hippocampus is needed to turn new experiences into lasting memories, while skills rely on other systems.

concepts.title: Bacteria and human cells, about one to one
concepts.description: A 2016 recount found about 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells, roughly one to one, weighing about 0.2 kg; a bowel movement can tip the ratio.

concepts.title: The microbes that live on you
concepts.description: Trillions of microbes, mostly gut bacteria of more than 10,000 species, live on and in the body; they help digest food and make vitamins.

concepts.title: Microscopes and cell theory
concepts.description: Hooke named cells in cork (1665), Leeuwenhoek first saw bacteria in his own tooth plaque (1683), and by the late 1830s cell theory said all life is made of cells.

concepts.title: Muscles only pull, so they work in pairs
concepts.description: A muscle can only contract and pull, so muscles work in opposing pairs: the biceps bends the elbow and the triceps straightens it.

concepts.title: Sliding filaments
concepts.description: Inside a muscle fiber, myosin heads grab thin actin filaments and pull them past thick filaments, re-cocking with ATP energy after each short pull.

concepts.title: The three kinds of muscle
concepts.description: Skeletal muscle is attached to bones and voluntary; smooth muscle lines hollow organs and is involuntary; cardiac muscle is found only in the heart and is involuntary.

concepts.title: Bones and muscles as levers
concepts.description: Bones are levers, joints are fulcrums and muscles supply the effort; most arrangements, like the bent arm, trade force for a large, fast movement.

concepts.title: Nerve signals and hormones
concepts.description: Nerves send fast, local chemical messages; hormones travel through the blood to distant targets and usually act more slowly; in an emergency the two work together.

concepts.title: Central and peripheral nervous system
concepts.description: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system; the nerves that reach everywhere else form the peripheral nervous system, carrying signals both ways.

concepts.title: Sense, decide, act
concepts.description: The nervous system has three basic jobs: sensation (taking in information), integration (weighing it against memories and circumstances) and response.

concepts.title: Voluntary and automatic control
concepts.description: The somatic nervous system runs voluntary responses such as moving skeletal muscles; the autonomic nervous system runs involuntary ones such as heart muscle, smooth muscle and glands.

concepts.title: Why we sleep
concepts.description: Sleep's exact purpose is still a mystery; it likely helps consolidate memories, and the idea that it flushes toxins from the brain is actively debated.

concepts.title: The stages of sleep
concepts.description: Sleep cycles through three non-REM stages, from light to deep, and REM sleep, when the eyes dart, the brain is nearly as active as awake and the limbs are paralyzed.

concepts.title: How many neurons
concepts.description: A 2009 count by Azevedo and colleagues found about 86 billion neurons in the adult human brain, replacing an unsupported round figure of 100 billion.

concepts.title: The parts of a neuron
concepts.description: A neuron has dendrites that receive messages, a cell body holding the nucleus, and an axon that sends messages on; information flows one way through it.

concepts.title: How a neuron sends a signal
concepts.description: A signal travels along the axon as electricity, sped up by insulating myelin, then crosses the synapse as chemical neurotransmitters that attach to the next cell.

concepts.title: Carbohydrates, proteins and fats
concepts.description: Carbohydrates, proteins and fats are the three main nutrients; digestion breaks them into simple sugars, amino acids, and fatty acids and glycerol, and glucose is cells' main fuel.

concepts.title: Vitamins and minerals
concepts.description: Vitamins and minerals are micronutrients, needed in very small amounts but critical for health; there are 13 essential vitamins, and minerals such as calcium and phosphorus keep bones, muscles, heart and brain working.

concepts.title: The body's organ systems
concepts.description: The body works as 11 organ systems, each a group of organs sharing a major job: wrapping and moving, supplying and cleaning, controlling and defending.

concepts.title: Levels of organization
concepts.description: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and the systems together make the organism.

concepts.title: From zygote to fetus in about 40 weeks
concepts.description: The zygote divides into a ball of cells that specialize into all the body's cell types; the embryo is called a fetus from week 10 of pregnancy, and pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks.

concepts.title: Growth spurts and a brain that matures last
concepts.description: The growth spurt peaks around 11.5 in girls and 13.5 in boys, body hair appears, and the brain keeps maturing until the mid-to-late 20s.

concepts.title: The hormone relay that starts puberty
concepts.description: Puberty begins when the hypothalamus releases GnRH, the pituitary releases LH and FSH, and the ovaries or testes release sex hormones; changes typically start between 8 and 14.

concepts.title: The reflex arc
concepts.description: In a withdrawal reflex, a signal runs from skin sensors to the spinal cord and straight out to a motor neuron, so the body acts before the brain registers pain.

concepts.title: The stretch reflex
concepts.description: When a muscle is stretched, a sensor in it triggers the muscle to contract, keeping it at a steady length; the knee jerk is the classic example.

concepts.title: James Lind's scurvy trial
concepts.description: In 1747 James Lind compared six remedies in 12 sailors and saw citrus work best, but he blamed scurvy mainly on damp air and poor digestion, recommended boiled rob, and the Navy adopted lemon juice only in 1795.

concepts.title: Vitamin C and scurvy
concepts.description: Vitamin C is needed to make collagen; humans cannot make it; without it connective tissue weakens into scurvy, with bleeding gums, loose teeth and poor healing.

concepts.title: When balance signals disagree
concepts.description: The brain builds balance from the eyes, inner ears and body sensors; when they disagree (after spinning, or below deck on a ship) you feel dizzy or motion sick.

concepts.title: Senses beyond the classic five
concepts.description: Aristotle listed five senses, but the body also senses balance, body position and movement, temperature, pain and inner states like hunger.

concepts.title: Hair cells in the cochlea
concepts.description: In the cochlea, hair cells ride a traveling wave, sorted by pitch; bending their bristles creates electrical signals. Human hair cells do not grow back.

concepts.title: Color blindness
concepts.description: Red-green color blindness, the most common kind, affects about 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women of Northern European ancestry, because its genes sit on the X chromosome; John Dalton first described it.

concepts.title: Cones and color
concepts.description: Rods work in dim light; cones work in bright light and give color. Three types of cone each respond best to different wavelengths, and the brain combines them.

concepts.title: How glasses and contacts fix focus
concepts.description: Concave lenses spread light so the focus moves back onto the retina (nearsightedness); convex lenses bring it together (farsightedness). Contacts do the same on the eye's surface.

concepts.title: How many senses? It depends how you count
concepts.description: There is no agreed number of human senses: proposals range from six or seven to between 22 and 33, depending on how a separate sense is defined.

concepts.title: How the eye focuses light
concepts.description: The cornea bends incoming light, the iris sets the size of the pupil, and the lens works with the cornea to focus light onto the retina.

concepts.title: Flavor is mostly smell
concepts.description: Smell cells high in the nose get aromas through the nostrils and, while you chew, from the back of the throat; flavor blends these smells with taste, temperature and texture.

concepts.title: The path of sound through the ear
concepts.description: Sound vibrates the eardrum; three tiny middle-ear bones (malleus, incus, stapes) amplify the vibrations and pass them to the fluid-filled cochlea.

concepts.title: Sensors for heat, cold and touch
concepts.description: David Julius used chili pepper capsaicin to find TRPV1, a sensor for painful heat; he and Ardem Patapoutian used menthol to find the cold sensor TRPM8, and Patapoutian found the touch sensor Piezo2 (2021 Nobel Prize).

concepts.title: Optical illusions
concepts.description: An optical illusion is a perception that contradicts reality, often because of how the brain interprets what the eyes send; the Muller-Lyer lines are a classic example.

concepts.title: Correcting for shadows
concepts.description: The visual system estimates the lighting and judges each surface's own shade despite shadows; Adelson's checker-shadow illusion shows this correction misfiring on a flat picture.

concepts.title: Nearsightedness and farsightedness
concepts.description: When the eye's shape keeps light from focusing on the retina, nearsighted eyes focus it in front (far things blur) and farsighted eyes focus it behind (near things blur).

concepts.title: From retina to brain
concepts.description: Photoreceptors turn light into electrical signals that the optic nerve carries to the brain, which builds the image, turns the inverted retinal image upright and fills in the blind spot.

concepts.title: Sensation, transduction and perception
concepts.description: Every sense starts with receptors converting a stimulus into a nerve signal (transduction); sensation is that detection, and perception is the brain organizing and interpreting it.

concepts.title: Sensory adaptation
concepts.description: We often stop perceiving stimuli that stay the same for a long time, which frees attention for change.

concepts.title: The skin's sensors, and why pain matters
concepts.description: Skin sensors come in families for touch, temperature, pain and chemicals, crowded most densely in fingertips and lips; pain is a warning signal, as people born without it show.

concepts.title: Taste buds and the five basic tastes
concepts.description: Taste cells in taste buds on the tongue, palate and throat detect at least five basic tastes (sweet, sour, bitter, salty, umami), and every taste area senses all of them: the tongue map is a myth.

concepts.title: The inner ear's balance organs
concepts.description: The vestibular system has three fluid-filled semicircular canals that sense head rotation and two pouches, the utricle and saccule, whose tiny grains sense gravity.

concepts.title: How many bones an adult has
concepts.description: An adult skeleton has 206 bones: 80 in the axial skeleton and 126 in the appendicular skeleton, with 106 of them in the hands and feet.

concepts.title: What the skeleton does
concepts.description: The skeleton supports the body, anchors muscles for movement, protects organs, makes blood cells in red marrow, stores fat in yellow marrow and banks minerals such as calcium.

concepts.title: Smoking and lung cancer
concepts.description: In the US about 80 percent of lung cancer deaths are linked to smoking, and smokers are 15 to 30 times more likely to get or die from it; WHO says there is no safe level of tobacco exposure; risk falls after quitting.

concepts.title: How smoking damages the lungs
concepts.description: Smoke stalls and damages the airway cilia and adds mucus; smoking is the main US cause of COPD, including emphysema, which damages the walls between air sacs.

concepts.title: How the stomach digests
concepts.description: Stomach glands release hydrochloric acid and pepsin, muscles churn food into chyme, and a bicarbonate-rich mucus coat plus a lining renewed every few days keep the stomach from digesting itself.

concepts.title: Beaumont's window into the stomach
concepts.description: After an 1822 gunshot left Alexis St. Martin with a permanent opening into his stomach, William Beaumont studied digestion through it, publishing in 1833 that acidic gastric juice dissolves food.

concepts.title: How freely movable joints work
concepts.description: Synovial joints cap bone ends with cartilage inside a capsule of lubricating synovial fluid; their shape (hinge, pivot, ball-and-socket) sets how they move.

concepts.title: Systems work as a team
concepts.description: No organ system works alone: breathing and circulation share oxygen delivery, nerves, bones and muscles share movement, and muscles and blood share keeping warm.

concepts.title: Tooth enamel
concepts.description: Enamel is the hardest substance in the body, about 95 percent mineral, mostly calcium phosphate; it holds no living cells once formed, so it cannot regrow.

concepts.title: The kinds of teeth
concepts.description: Incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars crush and grind; children have 20 primary teeth and adults 32 permanent ones, and digestion starts with chewing and saliva.

concepts.title: What tendons and ligaments connect
concepts.description: Tendons connect muscle to bone and carry its pull; ligaments connect bone to bone at a joint; the Achilles tendon is the thickest.

concepts.title: Why tendons and ligaments are strong but slow to heal
concepts.description: Tendons and ligaments are dense connective tissue of parallel collagen fibers that resist stretching; with little blood supply, they heal slowly. A sprain hurts a ligament; a strain, a muscle or tendon.

concepts.title: The four tissue types
concepts.description: The body has four main tissue types: epithelial covers and lines, connective binds and supports, muscle contracts, and nervous tissue carries signals.

concepts.title: Endurance changes and disuse
concepts.description: Endurance exercise can add mitochondria and capillaries to muscle; a muscle that is not used loses structural proteins and shrinks (atrophy), which exercise can often reverse.

concepts.title: How muscles grow stronger
concepts.description: Muscles grow without making new cells: resistance exercise adds myofibrils, the bundles of actin and myosin filaments, so each fiber gets thicker (hypertrophy).

concepts.title: What twins reveal about genes and environment
concepts.description: Identical twins have different fingerprints because womb conditions shape fine details; comparing identical and fraternal twins helps separate genes from environment.

concepts.title: Identical and fraternal twins
concepts.description: Identical twins come from one fertilized egg that splits and share the same DNA; fraternal twins come from two eggs and two sperm and are as alike as siblings.

concepts.title: Vesalius and human dissection
concepts.description: Galen's anatomy, drawn from animals, ruled into the 1500s; in 1543 Vesalius published anatomy from human dissections he did himself and corrected Galen.

concepts.title: Capillaries, where delivery happens
concepts.description: Capillaries link the smallest arteries to the smallest veins; they are so narrow red cells pass single file, and their thin walls let oxygen, nutrients and wastes cross.

concepts.title: Arteries and veins
concepts.description: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and have thick, elastic walls; veins carry it back at low pressure, with thinner walls, valves, and about two-thirds of the blood.

concepts.title: The appendix: vestigial but not useless
concepts.description: The appendix has immune tissue and may shelter helpful gut bacteria; it evolved independently over 30 times in mammals.

concepts.title: Vestigial traits: goosebumps and the tailbone
concepts.description: Vestigial structures are leftovers from ancestors with little apparent function, like the goosebump muscle and the embryo's lost tail, though some still do jobs.

concepts.title: What sets the pitch of a voice
concepts.description: Pitch is how fast the vocal folds vibrate, more than 100 times a second in speech; tightening them raises pitch like tuning a guitar string, and shorter, thinner folds give women and children higher voices.

concepts.title: How the vocal folds make a voice
concepts.description: The larynx holds two vocal folds that stay open for breathing and snap together to vibrate as air blows past; throat, nose and mouth shape the sound, and tongue and lips make it speech.

concepts.title: How a cut heals
concepts.description: After a clot and scab, a wound is swollen for 2 to 5 days while white cells fight germs, fills with new tissue over about 3 weeks, and leaves a smaller, weaker scar.

concepts.title: Abbasid Baghdad
concepts.description: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750 and ruled from Baghdad, founded by al-Mansur in 762 as the Round City.

concepts.title: Agincourt
concepts.description: At Agincourt in 1415 Henry V's archers, behind stakes on a narrow muddy field, beat a larger French army; the size of the armies is debated.

concepts.title: Alfred defends Wessex
concepts.description: Alfred of Wessex survived the Viking onslaught of 878, won at Edington, agreed a border with the Danelaw and defended his kingdom with burhs, ships and learning.

concepts.title: The Aztecs and Tenochtitlan
concepts.description: The Mexica (Aztecs) founded Tenochtitlan about 1325 on islands in Lake Texcoco; estimates of its 1519 population range from about 50,000 to 400,000.

concepts.title: Cahokia
concepts.description: Cahokia, near modern St. Louis, was the largest city north of Mexico, flourishing about 950-1350 with an estimated 8,000 to 40,000 people.

concepts.title: The Inca
concepts.description: The Inca ruled from Ecuador to central Chile with great roads and knotted-cord records (quipu); about 12 million people lived in the empire in 1532, though estimates vary.

concepts.title: The Maya
concepts.description: Maya cities flourished in the Classic period (about 250-900), with the only true writing system of the pre-Columbian Americas.

concepts.title: Anglo-Saxon England
concepts.description: Angles, Saxons and Jutes settled Britain after Roman rule ended and built several kingdoms; the Angles gave England its name.

concepts.title: Arabic names in the sky
concepts.description: Many bright stars carry names adopted from Arabic, passed to Europe through translations of al-Sufi's 10th-century update of Ptolemy's catalog.

concepts.title: From mail to plate
concepts.description: Mail of interlocking links gave way, from the late 13th century and fast after 1325, to full plate harness.

concepts.title: How heavy armour really was
concepts.description: Field armour weighed about 20 to 25 kg, spread over the body; knights were never hoisted by cranes.

concepts.title: How King Arthur grew
concepts.description: Arthur first appears in the Historia Brittonum (about 830) as a winner of 12 battles against the Saxons; Geoffrey of Monmouth, Chrétien de Troyes and Malory built him into the legend.

concepts.title: Benedict's Rule
concepts.description: Benedict of Nursia's Rule balanced prayer, work and reading, and became the standard for monasteries across western Europe.

concepts.title: How the Black Death reached Europe
concepts.description: The plague began in Central Asia, struck the Mongol siege of Caffa in 1346, and Genoese ships carried it to Messina in October 1347, from where it spread across Europe by 1350.

concepts.title: The Black Death's death toll
concepts.description: Death tolls are estimates: most put Black Death deaths at about 30-50% of Europe's population in 1347-1351, some higher; England lost around a third by 1349.

concepts.title: The Byzantine Empire
concepts.description: The eastern Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, lasted until 1453; its Greek-speaking people called themselves Romans.

concepts.title: How Byzantium lasted
concepts.description: Constantinople's layered land walls and a trusted gold coin, the solidus, helped the eastern empire survive for centuries.

concepts.title: Canossa, 1077
concepts.description: Excommunicated, Henry IV waited three days as a penitent at Canossa in January 1077 before Gregory VII absolved him.

concepts.title: Becket and Canterbury
concepts.description: Thomas Becket's murder in 1170 made Canterbury England's great shrine, the goal of Chaucer's pilgrims.

concepts.title: The caravel
concepts.description: The Portuguese developed the caravel, a light ship with triangular lateen sails that could sail against the wind, to explore Africa's coast.

concepts.title: The Carolingian Renaissance
concepts.description: Charlemagne revived learning: Alcuin ran his palace school, scholars copied classical texts, and a clear new script shaped the letters we read today.

concepts.title: Walls, gates and murder holes
concepts.description: Moats, curtain walls, arrow loops, portcullises and murder holes made the way in the deadliest place.

concepts.title: What a castle was for
concepts.description: A castle was a lord's or king's fortified home, used to control the land around it.

concepts.title: Stone keeps
concepts.description: Stone replaced timber; the keep was the castle's strongest point.

concepts.title: Heresy and the Cathars
concepts.description: Heresy was belief rejected by church authorities; the dualist Cathars were the best-known medieval example.

concepts.title: How cathedrals were built
concepts.description: Master masons, templates, shipped stone and treadwheel cranes built cathedrals over decades or centuries, as at Canterbury and Cologne.

concepts.title: Fairs and the Champagne fairs
concepts.description: Fairs met once a year on saints' days; the great Champagne fairs linked northern cloth and Mediterranean spices, used credit, and fair courts settled disputes on the spot.

concepts.title: Emperor in 800
concepts.description: On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor, reviving the title in the West, angering Byzantium and making popes the makers of emperors.

concepts.title: Charlemagne's empire
concepts.description: Charlemagne, king of the Franks from 768 to 814, came from the family that replaced the Merovingians and conquered much of western Europe.

concepts.title: Printing in Tang and Song China
concepts.description: Printing was invented under the Tang; the Diamond Sutra (868) is the first known dated printed book, and Bi Sheng made clay movable type around 1041-48.

concepts.title: The chivalric ideal
concepts.description: Chivalry first meant mounted knights and became an ideal of honour, loyalty, faith and protecting the weak.

concepts.title: Chivalry in practice
concepts.description: In practice mercy was for ransomable nobles, and historians like Kaeuper see chivalry as part of the problem of violence.

concepts.title: The tithe
concepts.description: Believers owed the Church a tithe, a tenth of their income, which paid clergy, churches, the poor and even cathedrals.

concepts.title: The Church and the two powers
concepts.description: Medieval thinkers divided Christendom into clergy and rulers, but the Church also held land, armies and learning.

concepts.title: Cloth as a badge of rank
concepts.description: Wool clothed almost everyone, from cheap russet to costly scarlet; pointed shoes were a fashion whose mark shows in medieval bones.

concepts.title: Clovis and the Franks
concepts.description: Clovis united the Franks, conquered most of Gaul and became a Catholic Christian, which won him the support of the bishops and most of his subjects.

concepts.title: Columbus's voyage of 1492
concepts.description: Funded by Ferdinand and Isabella, Columbus sailed from Palos in August 1492 and reached the Bahamas on October 12, believing he was in Asia.

concepts.title: Columbus and the round Earth
concepts.description: Educated Europeans already knew the Earth was a sphere; Columbus's error was underestimating its size. The flat-Earth story comes from Washington Irving's 1828 biography.

concepts.title: What 1492 cost the Taino
concepts.description: Columbus enslaved Taino people, and enslavement, starvation and imported disease reduced the Taino from perhaps one or two million to a few thousand by 1520.

concepts.title: Common law
concepts.description: English common law, consolidated under Henry II, was law common to all England, built from the decisions of the king's courts and followed as precedent.

concepts.title: Concentric castles
concepts.description: Rings of mutually supporting walls, as at Beaumaris, made attackers win again and again.

concepts.title: After the fall of Constantinople
concepts.description: Constantine XI died, Hagia Sophia became a mosque, Mehmed moved his capital from Edirne to Constantinople, and the Byzantine Empire ended.

concepts.title: The siege of Constantinople, 1453
concepts.description: Sultan Mehmed II, aged 21, used Urban's great cannon against the walls and hauled ships overland past the Golden Horn chain in the siege of April to May 1453.

concepts.title: The longbow at Crécy
concepts.description: At Crécy in 1346 English longbowmen, shooting far faster than crossbows, broke repeated French charges.

concepts.title: The First Crusade
concepts.description: The First Crusade reached a divided Muslim Near East, took Antioch in 1098 and stormed Fatimid-held Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, killing many of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.

concepts.title: The Fourth Crusade and 1204
concepts.description: In debt to Venice and lured by an exiled prince, the Fourth Crusade attacked Christian Zara and in April 1204 sacked Constantinople, setting up a Latin empire until 1261.

concepts.title: What the Crusades changed
concepts.description: After Acre fell in 1291, the Crusades left richer Italian trading cities, embittered Greeks, long memories among Jews and Muslims, and less influence on learning than once claimed.

concepts.title: The Reconquista
concepts.description: Over nearly eight centuries, Christian kingdoms took back the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule, from Covadonga around 718 to Granada in 1492.

concepts.title: The Rhineland massacres of 1096
concepts.description: In May 1096 crusader bands attacked the Jewish communities of Speyer, Worms and Mainz, a turning point in Jewish-Christian relations.

concepts.title: Richard I and the Third Crusade
concepts.description: Richard I took Acre and won at Arsuf in the Third Crusade (1189-1192) but never retook Jerusalem; he and Saladin agreed a truce in 1192 without ever meeting.

concepts.title: Saladin
concepts.description: Saladin, a Kurdish commander who became ruler of Egypt and Syria, destroyed the crusader army at Hattin and took Jerusalem by ransomed surrender in 1187; the West later made him a legend.

concepts.title: The Knights Templar
concepts.description: The Templars, founded around 1120 to protect pilgrims, were fighting monks and bankers; after Acre fell, Philip IV had them arrested in 1307 on baseless charges and the pope suppressed the order in 1312.

concepts.title: Urban II's call of 1095
concepts.description: A Byzantine appeal for help against the Turks led Pope Urban II to call Western knights east at Clermont in 1095, offering the remission of penance for sin.

concepts.title: The crusader states
concepts.description: The crusaders set up four states, called Outremer, ruled by a Christian minority; Bohemond kept Antioch despite his oath to Byzantium, and Edessa's fall in 1144 led to the failed Second Crusade.

concepts.title: The crusading era at a glance
concepts.description: From 1095 to 1291 the Crusades filled almost two centuries of the high Middle Ages and drew Rome's three heirs, the Latin West, Byzantium and the Islamic world, into one story.

concepts.title: The "Dark Ages" debate
concepts.description: Historians now rarely use "Dark Ages" because it passes a negative judgment on a whole era; evidence shows the period was not dark.

concepts.title: The Divine Office
concepts.description: Monks and nuns sang a daily cycle of services at set hours, from matins in the night to compline.

concepts.title: The Domesday Book
concepts.description: In 1086 William's commissioners surveyed who held England's land and what it was worth, for tax and defence; the record became Domesday Book.

concepts.title: The first caliphates
concepts.description: Caliphs ("successors") led the Muslim community after 632; within about a century their empire stretched from Spain to the Indus.

concepts.title: Knowledge flowing east and west
concepts.description: Paper, numerals, Greek learning and medicine moved between China, the Islamic world and Europe; under the Pax Mongolica, inventions went west and Islamic science went east.

concepts.title: 476: a convenient line
concepts.description: Odoacer deposed the last western emperor in 476, the traditional end of the Western Roman Empire, but he ruled as king and Roman government carried on.

concepts.title: Lords, vassals and fiefs
concepts.description: A lord granted a vassal a fief, usually land, in return for service; the bond was made by homage and fealty.

concepts.title: Feudalism: a debated label
concepts.description: Feudalism is a label coined centuries later; historians such as Brown and Reynolds showed the tidy pyramid is a simplification.

concepts.title: The first universities
concepts.description: Universities began as guilds of students and masters: Bologna late in the 11th century, then Paris and Oxford.

concepts.title: The four humours
concepts.description: Medieval medicine held that blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile had to stay in balance; the theory came from Hippocrates and Galen and left words like sanguine.

concepts.title: Genghis Khan and the Mongol empire
concepts.description: Temujin, born about 1162, was proclaimed Chinggis Khan in 1206; his heirs built the largest contiguous land empire in history.

concepts.title: Gothic engineering
concepts.description: Rib vaults, pointed arches and flying buttresses let Gothic builders go taller and open walls into windows, sometimes past the limit, as at Beauvais.

concepts.title: The Great Famine of 1315
concepts.description: Torrential rain from 1315 ruined harvests across northern Europe, causing the worst European famine by share of population.

concepts.title: Why the famine was so bad
concepts.description: Historian William Chester Jordan shows how animal diseases, repeated harvest failures, volatile prices and war worsened the weather's damage.

concepts.title: The stone city of Great Zimbabwe
concepts.description: Built by ancestors of the Shona between the 11th and 15th centuries, Great Zimbabwe's mortarless stone walls ruled a kingdom rich from the gold trade with the Indian Ocean coast.

concepts.title: Who built Great Zimbabwe: the colonial myth
concepts.description: Colonial-era Europeans falsely credited Great Zimbabwe to foreigners; archaeology in 1905 and 1929 showed it was medieval and African, yet Rhodesia's government censored the truth.

concepts.title: Apprentice, journeyman, master
concepts.description: Guild members climbed from apprentice (five to nine years, living with the master) to journeyman (paid by the day) to master, by way of a masterpiece.

concepts.title: What guilds did
concepts.description: Merchant and craft guilds grew up in busy towns; craft guilds held a local monopoly, set quality and prices, and had patron saints, chapels and charity.

concepts.title: Guns end the age of castles
concepts.description: Firearms improved so fast in the 15th and 16th centuries that French guns took castle after castle in Italy in 1494, ending the age of the medieval castle.

concepts.title: Gunpowder reaches Europe
concepts.description: Black powder, thought to originate in China, was used in European firearms from the 14th century, moving the power of weapons from muscle to chemistry; giant guns like Mons Meg followed.

concepts.title: Gutenberg's movable type
concepts.description: Around 1450 in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg printed with reusable metal letters and a press, producing the Gutenberg Bible about 1455.

concepts.title: Hagia Sophia
concepts.description: Justinian's great church, built 532-537 after a riot burned the old one, with a vast dome that seems to float.

concepts.title: Reading a coat of arms
concepts.description: Coats of arms used set metals and colours, a rule of contrast, and became hereditary.

concepts.title: Why heraldry began
concepts.description: Heraldry took shape in the 12th century to tell armoured men apart.

concepts.title: Hildegard of Bingen
concepts.description: Hildegard (born 1098), a German abbess, recorded visions, wrote on medicine, preached and corresponded with popes and an emperor.

concepts.title: Hildegard's music
concepts.description: Hildegard composed songs and the Ordo virtutum, the earliest known morality play, in which only the Devil does not sing.

concepts.title: The Holy Roman Empire
concepts.description: A German-centred empire, often dated from Otto I's crowning in 962 to 1806, whose name Voltaire mocked as neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire.

concepts.title: The House of Wisdom and the translators
concepts.description: Under al-Ma'mun, Baghdad sponsored translation of Greek works into Arabic; the House of Wisdom was a royal library whose scope historians debate.

concepts.title: Electing an emperor
concepts.description: Holy Roman Emperors were elected; the Golden Bull of 1356 fixed the electors at seven, and the empire became a loose federation.

concepts.title: Humanists hunt for lost classics
concepts.description: Humanists such as Poggio Bracciolini recovered ancient texts from medieval monastery libraries, and Poggio's humanist handwriting became the model for roman type.

concepts.title: Diagnosis and bloodletting
concepts.description: Physicians read urine for signs of imbalance and removed "excess" humours by bloodletting, often done by barber-surgeons; the practice was later discredited.

concepts.title: The Hundred Years' War
concepts.description: England and France fought on and off from 1337 to 1453, 116 years; England ended with only Calais.

concepts.title: Why the Hundred Years' War began
concepts.description: Edward III claimed the French crown through his mother, and English kings held Gascony as vassals of the French king.

concepts.title: Ibn Battuta
concepts.description: Ibn Battuta of Tangier set out on the hajj in 1325 and travelled some 120,000 km across the Islamic world and beyond, dictating his Rihla to Ibn Juzayy.

concepts.title: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine
concepts.description: Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980-1037) wrote the Canon of Medicine, translated into Latin in the 12th century and used as a textbook in Europe until the mid-17th century.

concepts.title: Numbers from India
concepts.description: Our digits originated in India and reached Europe through scholars of the Islamic world, with Fibonacci's Liber abaci spreading them after 1202.

concepts.title: The Investiture Controversy
concepts.description: Popes and kings fought over who installed bishops; Gregory VII excommunicated Henry IV, and the Concordat of Worms (1122) split the difference.

concepts.title: How Islam began
concepts.description: Muhammad, born in Mecca about 570, preached what Muslims believe are revelations from God, gathered in the Qur'an; the move to Medina in 622 begins the Islamic calendar.

concepts.title: The astrolabe in the Islamic world
concepts.description: A Greek instrument that reached the Islamic world by the 8th century, where it found prayer times and the qibla and was refined, as in al-Zarqali's universal astrolabe.

concepts.title: Hospitals of the Islamic world
concepts.description: Bimaristans in Baghdad, Damascus, Cordoba and Cairo admitted patients regardless of religion or rank; Qalawun's Cairo hospital treated rich and poor free.

concepts.title: Joan of Arc's rise
concepts.description: A farmer's daughter who heard saints' voices, Joan helped lift the siege of Orléans and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims in 1429.

concepts.title: Joan of Arc's trial
concepts.description: Captured in 1430, Joan was tried by a church court at Rouen; the record preserves her answers, including her escape from the grace-of-God trap. She was burned in 1431 and cleared in 1456.

concepts.title: The first juries
concepts.description: Henry II's Assize of Clarendon (1166) created juries that named suspects; after 1215, when ordeals ended, juries also came to decide guilt.

concepts.title: Justinian's law code
concepts.description: Justinian had centuries of Roman law sorted into the Corpus Juris Civilis, which became the foundation of civil law in continental Europe and Latin America.

concepts.title: Al-Khwarizmi and algebra
concepts.description: Al-Khwarizmi, working at the House of Wisdom, wrote the book on al-jabr that named algebra; his Latin name gave us algorithm.

concepts.title: Kings under law by 1450
concepts.description: By 1450 English kings had repeatedly reconfirmed Magna Carta, and Parliament used those reconfirmations to assert the king's duty to uphold the rule of law.

concepts.title: Dubbing a knight
concepts.description: The accolade made a knight; equipment was costly, and many knights held fiefs as vassals.

concepts.title: Page and squire
concepts.description: A future knight served as a page from about 7, then as a squire learning arms and courtly skills.

concepts.title: Crisis and resilience in the late Middle Ages
concepts.description: Famine, plague, financial collapse and war cut Europe's population for a time to about half of its 70 million of 1300, yet Europe proved resilient and recovered.

concepts.title: Magna Carta, 1215
concepts.description: In June 1215 rebel barons forced King John to agree to Magna Carta at Runnymede; its clauses 39 and 40 promised lawful judgment and justice for all.

concepts.title: Magna Carta's survival
concepts.description: The Pope annulled Magna Carta within ten weeks, but it was reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225, and three of its clauses are still English law.

concepts.title: The empire of Mali
concepts.description: Founded by Sundiata about 1230, Mali grew rich on the gold and salt trade and under Mansa Musa took in Timbuktu and Gao.

concepts.title: What peasants owed the manor
concepts.description: Villeins paid for their holdings with week-work on the lord's demesne, produce, and fees such as merchet and heriot.

concepts.title: Mansa Musa's hajj
concepts.description: On his 1324 pilgrimage, Mansa Musa gave away so much gold in Cairo that, al-Umari reported, its value fell for about twelve years; 'richest person ever' is a popular claim that cannot be measured.

concepts.title: Marco Polo
concepts.description: The Venetian Marco Polo spent 1271-95 in Asia, 17 years in China, and dictated his Travels to Rustichello; parts are exaggerated, but evidence shows he was in China.

concepts.title: Weekly markets
concepts.description: An English market met once a week on a set day and place, by royal charter, and from 1200 only if it did not harm its neighbours.

concepts.title: Food by rank
concepts.description: Bread quality, meat and drink all marked rank: fine wheat for lords, coarse loaves for servants, meat rarely for peasants, and fish on fast days.

concepts.title: When the Middle Ages ended
concepts.description: Historians end the Middle Ages at different dates, most often 1453 (Constantinople falls), 1492 (Columbus) or 1517 (Luther), all near 'about 1500'.

concepts.title: Holy days and festivals
concepts.description: Free time followed the Church calendar ("holiday" means holy day); at York the craft guilds staged a 48-play cycle on Corpus Christi.

concepts.title: The medieval inquisition
concepts.description: Papal inquisitors from 1227 tried suspected heretics; most received penances or prison, and those who refused to recant were burned.

concepts.title: Medieval inventions we still use
concepts.description: Eyeglasses (Italy, about 1290) and mechanical tower clocks are medieval inventions still in daily use.

concepts.title: Water and wind power
concepts.description: Thousands of watermills ground England's grain by 1086; windmills, first known in Persia, appear in English records in the 1180s as timber post mills.

concepts.title: Why "Middle" Ages
concepts.description: Renaissance scholars invented the Middle Ages as a gap between classical antiquity and their own revival; medieval means "middle age".

concepts.title: Games and songs
concepts.description: Folk football was a rowdy all-comers game that kings banned again and again, in vain; songs like "Sumer is icumen in" survive from the 1200s.

concepts.title: Early, high and late
concepts.description: Historians divide the Middle Ages into early (about 500-1000), high or central (about 1000-1300) and late (about 1300-1500) periods.

concepts.title: When the Middle Ages were
concepts.description: The Middle Ages run from the collapse of Roman rule in the West in the 5th century to the Renaissance: roughly 500 to 1500, about a thousand years.

concepts.title: Spices as status
concepts.description: Spices were costly imports for the rich, used in strong sauces to show wealth; historians reject the myth that they hid rotten meat.

concepts.title: Coverture and its limits
concepts.description: In England a married woman's legal existence was suspended under coverture, while a single woman could contract and sue in her own name.

concepts.title: What medieval women did
concepts.description: Examples by class and region: Christine de Pizan wrote for a living in France, Margaret Paston ran and defended Norfolk estates, English brewsters and Paris silkwomen worked in trade.

concepts.title: The lord's mill
concepts.description: Lords claimed the right to grind all their tenants' grain and took a toll for it, which is why Abbot Samson destroyed a rival windmill in 1191.

concepts.title: The cloister
concepts.description: The cloister, a square of covered walkways, linked the church, refectory, chapter house and dormitory and was used for study, exercise and burial.

concepts.title: Monks and books
concepts.description: In the early Middle Ages, monks copied books by hand in scriptoria, and figures like Cassiodorus made sure pagan classics were copied too.

concepts.title: The cost of the Mongol conquests
concepts.description: Estimates of the dead are rough but enormous: roughly 40 million for Genghis Khan's conquests (Britannica); in 1258 the Mongols sacked Baghdad.

concepts.title: The Pax Mongolica
concepts.description: In the 13th and 14th centuries Mongol rule revived the Silk Road with unprecedented security, the yam relay stations and paiza passes.

concepts.title: Motte and bailey
concepts.description: Early castles were earth mounds topped by timber towers beside a fenced yard, quick to build with forced labour.
In 1066 Harold beat a Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge, then lost to William of Normandy at Hastings; how Harold died is debated.

concepts.title: The Normans
concepts.description: The Normans were Vikings who settled in northern France after Rollo's 911 treaty, took up French language and Christianity, and later won lands in England and southern Italy.

concepts.title: Nuns and convents
concepts.description: Nuns lived by the Benedictine pattern under an abbess, in mostly small, enclosed houses.

concepts.title: Where the Ottomans came from
concepts.description: Founded about 1300 by Osman I, the Ottomans entered the Balkans as Byzantine allies, took Gallipoli in 1354 and built the Janissaries.

concepts.title: Near-collapse and recovery
concepts.description: In 1402 Timur defeated Bayezid I at Ankara and split Ottoman lands among his sons; after civil war Mehmed I reunited them in 1413.

concepts.title: Paper from China
concepts.description: Chinese craftsmen made the first paper from rags, first as medicine wrapping in the 2nd century BCE, and by the 3rd and 4th centuries CE wrote everything on it.

concepts.title: Paper's journey west
concepts.description: Paper reached Samarkand by trade, papermaking arrived there in 751 (the Talas prisoner story is a legend), Baghdad made paper by the 790s, and Europe had it by the 12th century.

concepts.title: The parish church in daily life
concepts.description: The parish church was normally the only place to receive the sacraments and be buried, and councils like Lateran IV (1215) set yearly duties for every believer.

concepts.title: The first parliaments
concepts.description: Parliaments grew from royal councils: León's assembly of 1188 included town representatives; in England the word appears in 1236, towns joined in 1265, the Model Parliament met in 1295 and the Commons sat apart from 1341.

concepts.title: Parliament and taxes
concepts.description: Parliament grew because kings needed its consent to extra taxes to pay for their wars.

concepts.title: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381
concepts.description: Angered by the Statute of Labourers and set off by the poll tax of 1380, rebels led by Wat Tyler and inspired by John Ball marched on London in 1381.

concepts.title: How the revolt ended
concepts.description: Richard II promised to abolish serfdom at Mile End; Wat Tyler was killed at Smithfield, the promises were forgotten, but no poll tax was levied for over 250 years.

concepts.title: Pilgrimage and its shrines
concepts.description: Medieval Christians made pilgrimages for penance, cures, vows and salvation, to Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago de Compostela and other shrines.

concepts.title: Faith, fear and blame
concepts.description: The plague drove flagellant processions and the false blaming of Jews, who were massacred across Europe, as at Strasbourg in 1349, though they died of plague too.

concepts.title: Plague, wages and work
concepts.description: With workers scarce after the Black Death, wages rose and labour services gave way to wages and rents; England's Statute of Labourers (1351) tried to freeze wages.

concepts.title: Rats or people? The transmission debate
concepts.description: The rat-flea story is challenged by Dean et al. (2018), whose human flea and louse model fit death records better in seven of nine outbreaks; the question is still debated.

concepts.title: What caused the plague
concepts.description: Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, confirmed for the Black Death by ancient DNA from victims' teeth; bubonic plague spreads by flea bites, pneumonic plague person to person.

concepts.title: Portugal's voyages around Africa
concepts.description: Prince Henry sponsored voyages down West Africa for gold and enslaved people; Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 and da Gama reached India in 1498.

concepts.title: From thousands of books to millions
concepts.description: Printing turned Europe's few thousand manuscript books into more than 9 million printed books by 1500, in editions larger than whole monastic libraries.

concepts.title: The Renaissance begins in Italy
concepts.description: The Renaissance, 'rebirth', began in 14th-century Italy as a revival of classical learning, funded by rich city-states and families such as Florence's Medici.

concepts.title: How Robin Hood grew
concepts.description: Robin Hood is known from rhymes and ballads, not records; Marian and his noble rank were added centuries later.

concepts.title: Rome's three heirs
concepts.description: After Rome fell in the West, its world passed to three heirs: the western kingdoms, the Byzantine Empire and the caliphate.

concepts.title: Bosworth and the Tudors
concepts.description: Henry Tudor defeated Richard III at Bosworth in 1485, married Elizabeth of York and founded the Tudor dynasty; Richard's skeleton was found in Leicester in 2012.

concepts.title: The Wars of the Roses
concepts.description: From 1455 to 1485 the houses of Lancaster and York, both descended from Edward III, fought for England's crown; the rose name came long afterward.

concepts.title: A round Earth in the classroom
concepts.description: Medieval universities taught a spherical Earth from Sacrobosco's Sphere; the flat-Earth Middle Ages is a 19th-century myth.

concepts.title: The excommunications of 1054
concepts.description: In 1054 a papal legate and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other, the traditional date of the East-West split; the sentences were lifted in 1965.

concepts.title: Why East and West drifted apart
concepts.description: Disputes over papal authority, the Creed, celibacy and bread widened a gap that grew from the 5th to the 11th century.

concepts.title: What a serf was
concepts.description: A serf was bound to a hereditary plot and to his lord's will: not a slave, but not free to leave, marry or change work without permission.

concepts.title: How to attack a castle
concepts.description: Ladders, siege towers, rams, mines and counterweight trebuchets.

concepts.title: How sieges ended
concepts.description: Most sieges ended by treachery, starvation or disease; Rochester in 1215 fell to a pig-fat mine and then hunger.

concepts.title: The Silk Road
concepts.description: A network of routes about 6,400 km long, travelled in stages by middlemen; silk went west, wool, gold and silver east, and religions travelled too.

concepts.title: Gunpowder, compasses and paper money
concepts.description: Chinese gunpowder was used in fireworks and signals by the 10th century; the Song improved compasses for sea trade and pioneered paper money.

concepts.title: Kingdoms after Rome
concepts.description: Germanic kingdoms replaced Rome in the West: Ostrogoths in Italy, Visigoths in Spain, Vandals in North Africa, Franks in Gaul, Anglo-Saxons in Britain.

concepts.title: Sumptuary laws
concepts.description: Laws such as England's of 1363 set what each rank could wear, to stop people dressing above their station, but proved hard to enforce.

concepts.title: Sutton Hoo
concepts.description: The 1939 ship burial at Sutton Hoo, probably King Rædwald's, revealed a rich, well-connected Anglo-Saxon world.

concepts.title: Pray, fight, work
concepts.description: Early 11th-century bishops described society as three orders: those who pray, fight and work.

concepts.title: Charters and "city air"
concepts.description: Self-governing towns (communes) held charters from bishops, counts or kings, and many offered freedom to settlers who stayed a year and a day.

concepts.title: Town dwellers: the first bourgeois
concepts.description: Medieval France called a walled-town dweller a bourgeois, as distinct from a peasant; the word later named the middle class.

concepts.title: Why towns grew after 1000
concepts.description: Once raids ended, western European towns revived: Europe's population nearly doubled between 1000 and 1340, and new walled towns were founded.

concepts.title: Trial by combat
concepts.description: In trial by combat the two sides or their champions fought, trusting God to give victory to the right; it came to England with the Normans and was abolished only in 1819.

concepts.title: Trial by ordeal
concepts.description: Ordeals of hot iron and cold water asked God to reveal guilt; the Church's 1215 ban on priests blessing them ended them in England.

concepts.title: From Northmen to Normans
concepts.description: Charlemagne built defences against the Northmen, but Vikings raided and settled anyway, and a Viking leader's descendant, William, conquered England.

concepts.title: No horns
concepts.description: Vikings did not wear horned helmets: the best-preserved Viking helmet has none, no Viking-age writer mentions them, and the image came from 19th-century artists.

concepts.title: Viking longships
concepts.description: Clinker-built longships with a square sail and oars drew so little water that they could run onto beaches, go up rivers and be dragged overland.

concepts.title: Viking voyages
concepts.description: Vikings travelled east down Russian rivers to Kyiv and Constantinople, and west to Iceland, Greenland and Newfoundland, where they were present in 1021.

concepts.title: Who the Vikings were
concepts.description: The Vikings were Scandinavians who raided, traded and settled from the late 8th century; most were farmers, and the Age is dated from the Lindisfarne raid of 793.

concepts.title: Africa across the Equator
concepts.description: The Equator nearly halves Africa, the only continent crossed by the Equator and both tropics, so its climate zones are largely mirrored north and south.

concepts.title: Africa's young population
concepts.description: About 19% of the world's people live in Africa, the youngest continent (median age about 19); Nigeria has the most people.

concepts.title: Africa, the second-largest continent
concepts.description: Africa is the second-largest continent, covering about one-fifth of Earth's land, and flat maps often undersell it.

concepts.title: Africa's great cities
concepts.description: Cairo, Lagos and Kinshasa are among Africa's largest cities; Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other across the Congo River.

concepts.title: Africa's countries
concepts.description: Africa has 54 countries, more than any other continent; Algeria has been the largest since South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011.

concepts.title: The Alpide belt
concepts.description: A second great earthquake belt runs from the Atlantic through the Mediterranean and the Himalayas to Indonesia, along the Alpine-Himalayan ranges.

concepts.title: The Alps, Europe's crumpled water tower
concepts.description: The Alps are fold mountains pushed up by a fragment of the African plate colliding with Eurasia, and their water feeds rivers flowing to four seas.

concepts.title: Air cools as you climb
