levels.title: The Sea Peoples
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the raiders who struck around 1177 BCE.
levels.summary: Around 1177 BCE Ramesses III beat off the Sea Peoples, a mix of raiders whose identity is still debated. Egypt won, but came out of the Late Bronze Age collapse much diminished.

cards.headline: Around 1177 BCE, raiders hit Egypt by land and by sea. Egypt won.
cards.body: So why do historians file that victory under the start of Egypt’s decline? And who were the raiders, anyway? Both answers are messier than the battle.

cards.headline: Ramesses III’s big win
cards.body: Historian Eric Cline dates it to 1177 BCE, the eighth year of Pharaoh Ramesses III’s reign. Warriors reached Egypt’s edge, some marching overland, others in ships. Ramesses beat them in battles on land and at sea, probably in or near the Nile Delta. Then he did what pharaohs did best: he advertised. The walls of his mortuary temple at Medinet Habu, near Thebes, show the fighting and rows of captives. Egypt’s side of the story, carved in stone.

cards.headline: Who were they?
cards.body: Egyptian texts name the groups one by one. The Peleset are generally believed to be the Philistines; the Sherden were probably from Sardinia. The carvings show feathered headdresses next to horned helmets, which suggests many peoples from many places, not one nation. Beyond that, their exact origins are uncertain. “Sea Peoples” is less a name than a label on a mystery box.
cards.callout: Many peoples, many places, one label

mascot.line: The most visible villain in a story isn’t always the whole explanation.

cards.headline: Winning the battle, losing the era
cards.body: Scholars once blamed the Sea Peoples for wrecking the great powers of the day, such as the Hittite empire. Recent research sees the Late Bronze Age collapse as having many causes, climate change among them, and the raiders’ role is debated. Egypt was the only major power to fight them off. Yet afterward, New Kingdom Egypt was much diminished. It survived the storm, but the whole neighborhood had changed.

levels.title: Priests and Kings
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Egypt split between priests and kings.
levels.summary: After the New Kingdom, the high priests of Amun ruled the south from Thebes while kings ruled the north from Tanis. The priests also rescued robbed royal mummies.

cards.headline: After about 1069 BCE, kings ruled Egypt’s north and priests ran the south.
cards.body: The New Kingdom was over. Egypt didn’t fall; it split. And the most powerful man in the south wore a priest’s robes.

cards.headline: A priest takes the title
cards.body: Herihor was high priest of the god Amun at Karnak, in Thebes. Late in the 20th dynasty, as Egypt became disunited, he took the full title of a pharaoh and founded a line of priest-kings who ruled the south. Picture your local archbishop quietly adding “King” to his business card.

cards.headline: Two capitals
cards.body: In the 21st Dynasty the split settled in. Kings ruled Lower Egypt from Tanis, in the Delta, while the High Priests of Amun at Thebes grew more and more powerful. Remember Level 1’s valleys between the peaks? This is the third: the Third Intermediate Period, when the land was divided again. Later a Libyan leader, Shoshenq, founded a new dynasty at Tanis. The one who finally took all of Egypt would come from Kush, in the south.
cards.callout: North: kings at Tanis. South: priests at Thebes.

cards.headline: Rescuing the dead kings
cards.body: Meanwhile, the royal tombs at Thebes were being robbed. Priests and officials of the 21st Dynasty gathered damaged royal mummies, rewrapped them and hid several New Kingdom kings together in a secret cache at Deir el-Bahari. It worked: nobody found it until 1881. Among the kings inside was Ramesses II. Ramesses the Great, sharing a hiding place, saved by priests.

levels.title: The Nubian Pharaohs
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the kings of Kush who ruled Egypt.
levels.summary: Kush, a Nubian kingdom south of Egypt, conquered Egypt in the 8th century BCE and ruled it as the 25th Dynasty. Driven out by Assyria, Kush lasted another thousand years.

cards.headline: In the 700s BCE, a kingdom from the south conquered Egypt.
cards.body: Many people have never heard of it. But Kush was no small neighbor. It was one of Africa’s earliest civilizations, and for nearly a century its kings ruled Egypt as pharaohs.

cards.headline: The kingdom up the river
cards.body: Kush was the southern part of Nubia, a region stretching south from near the Nile’s first cataract, in what is now Sudan. Remember Level 5’s rapids at Aswan, Egypt’s southern border? Kush lay beyond them, upstream. Its kings ruled from Napata, near Mount Barkal, and the cult of Egypt’s god Amun was strongly rooted there. Egypt’s new pharaohs would already know its gods.

cards.headline: Piye marches north
cards.body: In the 8th century BCE, King Piye marched into Egypt, ended its petty kingdoms and took Memphis. By about 715 BCE, under Piye and then Shabaka, all of Egypt was ruled from Kush. How do we know Piye’s side? He recorded his conquest on a great stone stela, found back home at Mount Barkal. The Kushite kings ruled as Egypt’s 25th Dynasty. The pharaohs now came from the south.

mascot.line: More pyramids than Egypt. Kush deserves a much bigger spot in the story.

cards.fact: Sudan has some 255 ancient pyramids, more than twice as many as Egypt built.
cards.context: Kushite kings were buried in pyramids. Their rule in Egypt ended after the Assyrians invaded in 671 BCE; by 654 BCE the Kushites were back in Nubia. But Kush didn’t fade. It lasted about another thousand years, later ruling from Meroe, until the king of Aksum destroyed Meroe in 350 CE. Losing Egypt was one chapter in Kush’s story, not the end.

levels.title: Persian Rule
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Persia conquered Egypt.
levels.summary: Persia’s Cambyses II conquered Egypt in 525 BCE and was crowned pharaoh. Egypt won back its independence in 404 BCE, but Persia returned in 343 BCE.

cards.headline: In 525 BCE, a Persian king put on the crown of the pharaohs.
cards.body: Kush had taken Egypt from the south. Now the Persian king Cambyses II took it, and he didn’t just seize the land. He took the job title too.

cards.headline: Crowned by the conqueror
cards.body: Cambyses II won the Battle of Pelusium in the Nile Delta, took Memphis, and Egyptian resistance collapsed. Then he had himself crowned as pharaoh. A later Persian king, Darius I, restored the priests’ privileges, had Egyptian law written down and completed or repaired a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea. Foreign rulers, wearing Egyptian titles.

mascot.line: When the writer is famous and the story is juicy, check it twice.

cards.headline: Don’t believe every travel writer
cards.body: Remember Herodotus from Level 2? His 5th-century BCE visit came while Egypt was Persian. He accused Cambyses of atrocities in Egypt and put them down to madness. But Egyptian sources from Cambyses’ own time suggest those accusations must largely be discounted. A famous writer with a great story still needs checking against the evidence.

cards.headline: The last native pharaoh
cards.body: Egypt rebelled near the end of Darius’s reign, and in 404 BCE it won its independence under Amyrtaeus of Sais. Egyptian kings ruled again, but not for long. The last of them, Nectanebo II, reigned from 360 until 343 BCE, when Persia reconquered Egypt. He fled south, and after that nothing more is known of him. The line of native pharaohs didn’t end with a funeral. It simply went quiet.

levels.title: Alexander in Egypt
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Alexander the Great took Egypt.
levels.summary: In 332 BCE Egypt welcomed Alexander the Great and the Persian satrap surrendered. Alexander was crowned at Memphis, hailed as son of Amun at Siwa, founded Alexandria and was buried there.

cards.headline: In 332 BCE, Egypt welcomed a foreign conqueror as its deliverer.
cards.body: Alexander the Great took Egypt without a real fight. Then he set about becoming a proper pharaoh.

cards.headline: No battle needed
cards.body: Egypt was still under Persian rule when Alexander, king of Macedonia, arrived in November 332 BCE. The Persian governor, the satrap Mazaces, surrendered, and the people welcomed Alexander as their deliverer. Picture tenants throwing a party for the new landlord. After Persia, the bar was low.

cards.headline: Playing pharaoh
cards.body: At Memphis, Alexander sacrificed to the sacred Apis bull and was crowned with the double crown of the pharaohs. Remember it from Level 6? White and red together: Upper and Lower Egypt under one king. Then he went to the oracle of Amun in the Siwa oasis, where the priest greeted him as “son of Amun,” the traditional greeting for a pharaoh. A Macedonian, hailed in the pharaohs’ own words.
cards.callout: Crowned at Memphis, greeted as son of Amun at Siwa

cards.headline: A city, and a body
cards.body: Alexander founded a new city near the Nile’s western arm, between the sea and Lake Mareotis, sheltered by the island of Pharos: Alexandria. He didn’t stay to see it grow. He died in Babylon in 323 BCE, and his general Ptolemy diverted his body to Egypt. It ended up in a golden coffin in Alexandria. Alive, Alexander left Egypt behind. Dead, he came back to stay.

levels.title: Alexandria
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Alexandria’s lighthouse and library.
levels.summary: Alexandria’s Pharos lighthouse was one of the Seven Wonders, and its library tried to collect every book in the world. The library faded slowly over centuries, not in one fire.

cards.headline: One city had antiquity’s most famous lighthouse and its most famous library.
cards.body: One burned a fire every night. The other, whatever you’ve heard, didn’t vanish in one great blaze.

cards.headline: A tower with a fire on top
cards.body: On the island of Pharos stood a lighthouse finished in about 280 BCE, one of the Seven Wonders of the World. It rose more than 110 metres; only the pyramids of Giza would have been taller. A spiral ramp led to the top, where a fire burned at night. It stood until an earthquake in the 1300s, and in 1477 a sultan, Qaitbay, built a fort from its ruins. Ancient recycling, on a grand scale.

cards.headline: All the books in the world
cards.body: Around 295 BCE, Ptolemy I had Demetrius of Phaleron found a library and the Mouseion, a research institute for scholars. The goal: all the books in the world. Ships entering Alexandria’s harbor were searched, and books found aboard were confiscated or copied for the collection. Imagine landing at an airport and having your paperback copied at customs.

mascot.line: Big fires make great stories. Slow neglect makes real history.

cards.headline: A slow goodbye, not one fire
cards.body: The popular story is one great fire. The evidence is messier. In 48 BCE, during Julius Caesar’s civil war, at least part of the library was damaged, yet scholars seem to have kept working there. Historians describe a slow decline through neglect and several blows over centuries, and they still debate the causes. A later tale blaming the Arab conquerors is, modern historians say, a myth. No single villain, no single night.

levels.title: The Ptolemies
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a Greek family ruled Egypt for 300 years.
levels.summary: Ptolemy, Alexander’s Macedonian general, founded a dynasty that ruled Egypt for almost 300 years. They appeared as pharaohs on temple walls while keeping their own Greek ways.

cards.headline: For almost 300 years, Egypt’s kings were Macedonian Greeks named Ptolemy.
cards.body: How does a foreign family hold a country that long? By being two kinds of ruler at once.

cards.headline: Ptolemy takes charge
cards.body: When Alexander died in 323 BCE, his Macedonian general Ptolemy became governor of Egypt, and in 305 BCE he proclaimed himself king. His dynasty ruled until 30 BCE. Naming the heirs was easy: the kings ran from Ptolemy I to Ptolemy XV. If you’ve ever lost track of which one is which, you’re in good company.

cards.headline: Two faces of one crown
cards.body: To their Egyptian subjects, the Ptolemies looked like proper pharaohs: they backed Egyptian temples and appeared on temple walls in the traditional pharaonic style. Ptolemy I also promoted Serapis, a god with Egyptian roots and Greek features, whose cult blended both religions. Remember Manetho from Level 9? He wrote his history of Egypt in Greek around 300 BCE, early in Ptolemaic rule.
cards.callout: Pharaohs on the temple walls, Greeks at home

cards.headline: Only one learned Egyptian
cards.body: Behind the temple images, the family kept its own ways. Ptolemy II married his full sister, Arsinoe II, and brother-sister marriage became a feature of the dynasty. And according to the ancient writer Plutarch, of all the Ptolemies only Cleopatra VII took the trouble to learn Egyptian. Nearly three centuries on the throne, and one ruler who could chat with Egyptians in their own language.

levels.title: Rome's Breadbasket
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Egypt became the grain supply of Rome.
levels.summary: From 30 BCE Egypt was the Roman emperor’s own province, closed to senators without permission. Its Nile-fed grain fed Rome for about four months a year.

cards.headline: For four months of every year, one ancient writer said, Rome ate Egyptian grain.
cards.body: No wonder the emperors kept Egypt on a very short leash.

cards.headline: The emperor’s own province
cards.body: In 30 BCE Egypt became a Roman province, but not an ordinary one. Octavian, the future emperor Augustus, treated it as his own private kingdom, as heir to the Ptolemies. A prefect he appointed ran it, and Roman senators were forbidden to visit without the emperor’s permission. Egypt wasn’t just conquered. It was fenced off.

cards.headline: Four months of bread
cards.body: Why the fuss? Grain. Egypt’s granaries now belonged to Rome, and Egypt became the empire’s breadbasket. The historian Josephus, writing in the 1st century CE, said Egypt sent Rome enough grain to feed it for four months of the year, on top of its tax money. Four months out of twelve: a third of the city’s year, from one province.
cards.callout: Egypt fed Rome a third of the year

mascot.line: Same river, same silt. Only the address on the grain sacks changed.

cards.headline: The Nile pays Rome’s bills
cards.body: Remember Level 2’s flood? Its silt was a natural fertilizer that let Egypt feed a dense population, and now Rome took the harvest. Josephus even noted that Egypt was walled round by near-impassable deserts and harborless seas, the defenses you met in Level 3, and still it submitted to Rome. The walls that guarded the pharaohs didn’t keep out the tax collector.

levels.title: The End of the Old Gods
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Christianity and later Islam replaced the old religion.
levels.summary: Christianity spread through Egypt, and the temples closed, the Serapeum in 391 CE and Philae under Justinian. After the Arab conquest of 640 to 642 CE, Egypt became Muslim gradually.

cards.headline: Egypt’s gods outlasted every conqueror. They didn’t outlast a change of faith.
cards.body: The old religion didn’t fall in one battle. It went quiet temple by temple, from the Serapeum in 391 CE to Philae in the 6th century.

cards.headline: A new faith
cards.body: Christianity, tradition says, was brought to Alexandria by St. Mark in the first half of the 1st century CE, and it spread quickly through Egypt. Egypt’s Christians came to be called Copts, and they spoke Coptic, a late form of the Egyptian language. The old tongue lived on. It just had new prayers to say.

cards.headline: The temples close
cards.body: In 391 CE the patriarch of Alexandria and his followers destroyed the city’s Serapeum, the great temple of Serapis, with Emperor Theodosius I’s encouragement, and other temples fell too. One famous holdout was Isis’s temple on the island of Philae, where the last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in 394 CE. It wasn’t closed until Emperor Justinian’s reign, in the 6th century, and was then made into a church.
cards.callout: Serapeum destroyed 391 CE; Philae closed in the 6th century

cards.headline: Then, slowly, Islam
cards.body: Between 640 and 642 CE, Arab forces under ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ beat the Byzantine armies and entered Alexandria. Even then, change was slow. Egypt was mostly Christian at the conquest and became Muslim gradually over centuries; historians can’t pin down when Muslims became the majority. By the 12th century the Coptic church itself had adopted Arabic alongside Coptic. Faiths and languages rarely switch overnight.

cards.headline: One story
cards.body: Egypt beat the Sea Peoples and still came out weaker. It split between kings at Tanis and priests at Thebes, and outsiders stepped in: Kushites who worshipped Amun, a Persian crowned pharaoh, Alexander greeted as son of Amun, Ptolemies carved as pharaohs, Romans who shipped its grain home. Native kings returned only once, and Nectanebo II was the last. Libraries faded slowly and temples closed. The crown kept changing heads; the land kept feeding whoever wore it.

levels.title: Forgetting Hieroglyphs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how knowledge of hieroglyphs was lost.
levels.summary: The last known hieroglyphs were carved at Philae in 394 CE. Egyptians switched to a Greek-based alphabet, and later scholars like Horapollo misread the signs as symbols.

cards.headline: For more than 1,400 years, nobody on Earth could read a hieroglyph.
cards.body: The signs never went anywhere. They stayed carved on temple walls and tombs the whole time. What vanished was anyone who knew what they said. So how does a whole civilization’s writing get forgotten?

cards.headline: The last hieroglyph
cards.body: The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in 394 CE, at the Temple of Isis at Philae. That’s more than four centuries after Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BCE (remember the end of Level 1’s timeline?). The old script had outlived the pharaohs by a long way. Its final signs are roughly cut but still clear enough to read. There was just no one left to read them.

mascot.line: Same language, new letters. Hold on to Coptic: it comes back to help later in this chapter.

cards.headline: A new alphabet
cards.body: Why stop? As Christianity spread in Egypt, people dropped hieroglyphs for an adapted form of the Greek alphabet. The language itself lived on as Coptic, the final stage of Egyptian, written in Greek letters plus seven letters borrowed from demotic. So Egyptians kept speaking their ancestors’ language while the old signs fell silent. It’s like keeping your family’s recipes but losing the handwriting they were written in.

cards.headline: Reading riddles
cards.body: Without readers, people guessed. In the 5th century CE, a Greco-Egyptian scholar named Horapollo wrote the Hieroglyphica, explaining each sign as a symbol or an allegory. He couldn’t actually read hieroglyphs himself. Renaissance scholars loved his book anyway, and the idea stuck: hieroglyphs were picture riddles, not sounds. That one wrong idea kept the door locked until the 1820s.
cards.callout: Wrong assumption: pictures, not sounds

levels.title: The Rosetta Stone
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Rosetta Stone was found and why it mattered.
levels.summary: French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone in 1799. It carries one decree in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802.

cards.headline: In 1799, soldiers digging a fort’s foundations hit the key to a lost script.
cards.body: They were French troops of Napoleon’s campaign in Egypt, working near the port of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta. The broken slab they dug up was covered in writing, in three different scripts. That was the whole point.

cards.headline: One message, three scripts
cards.body: The stone carries the same decree three times. First in hieroglyphs. Then in demotic, the everyday Egyptian handwriting. Then in ancient Greek, the language of Egypt’s Macedonian Greek rulers. Nobody could read the first two, but scholars could still read Greek. So here was a lost script with a translation stapled on. Picture a menu printed in a language you can’t read, right beside one you can.
cards.callout: Hieroglyphs + demotic + Greek = one message

mascot.line: The key to a whole lost script is, word for word, a bit of priestly paperwork.

cards.headline: What it actually says
cards.body: Don’t expect a treasure map. The decree was issued in 196 BCE by priests of a temple in Memphis, confirming the Macedonian king Ptolemy V as a divine ruler. It’s official temple business. The words were never the exciting part. The exciting part was hearing the same thing said three ways.

cards.headline: From Rashid to London
cards.body: The French didn’t keep their find. After the French surrender in Egypt in 1801, the stone passed to the British. It has been on display in the British Museum since 1802, leaving only once, when it was moved to safety during the First World War. Whether it should stay there is a live argument, and it gets its own level later in this chapter.

levels.title: Champollion Cracks the Code
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Champollion deciphered hieroglyphs.
levels.summary: Thomas Young read the sounds of Ptolemy’s name; in 1822 Champollion showed that hieroglyphs mix sound signs with signs for ideas.

cards.headline: In 1822, a scholar burst in on his brother, cried “I’ve got it!” and fainted.
cards.body: In French, he said “Je tiens mon affaire!” The scholar was Jean-François Champollion, and what he’d got was the key to hieroglyphs. But he wasn’t the first to get a foot in the door. An English scientist had already shown that some signs spelled the sounds of a name.

cards.headline: Thomas Young’s head start
cards.body: Thomas Young was an English physicist, also famous for his work on light, who began studying the Rosetta Stone in 1814. He showed that some hieroglyphs on the stone spelled out the sounds of a royal name: Ptolemy. He also made major advances in reading demotic. That was a real crack in the wall. Most of the wall was still standing.

mascot.line: Sometimes the breakthrough isn’t a flash of genius. It’s just counting carefully.

cards.headline: Too many signs
cards.body: Champollion tried counting. The hieroglyphic text on the Rosetta Stone uses 1,419 signs, while the Greek version has only 486 words. If every sign were a whole idea, those numbers should be much closer. So many signs had to stand for sounds, mixed with others that stood for whole ideas or objects. Hieroglyphs weren’t picture riddles after all. They were writing down a spoken language.
cards.callout: 1,419 signs for 486 words: too many for pictures alone

cards.headline: Not just foreign names
cards.body: Maybe sound signs were only a trick for foreign names like Ptolemy? Champollion knew Coptic, the last stage of Egyptian, which helped him hear the sounds behind the signs. With it he read the name of Ramesses, a native Egyptian king. Egyptians had been writing sounds all along. On 27 September 1822 he announced it in Paris, with Thomas Young in the audience. The door locked since 394 CE was open.

levels.title: Egyptomania
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the craze for all things Egyptian in Europe.
levels.summary: Napoleon’s scholars and their Description de l’Égypte, then Champollion’s decipherment, set off Egyptomania: Egyptian-style buildings and real obelisks shipped to London and New York.

cards.headline: Napoleon invaded Egypt with an army and about 150 artists and scientists.
cards.body: The army’s campaign ended in surrender. The scholars did better: they helped set off a craze for ancient Egypt that swept Europe and America.

cards.headline: A country in picture books
cards.body: The 1798 invasion doubled as the first large-scale scientific expedition to Egypt. The scholars measured and drew everything they could. Back in France, their record became the Description de l’Égypte, published from 1809 with huge prints of pyramids, temples and other antiquities. For readers at home, it was like having Egypt delivered to the library in giant installments.

mascot.line: Next time you see an Egyptian-style gate or column far from Egypt, you’ve spotted a bit of Egyptomania.

cards.headline: Egyptomania
cards.body: Then came Champollion’s decipherment in 1822 (Level 93), and interest surged again. The craze got a name: Egyptomania. Architects mined the Description for Egyptian designs. In the United States the first wave was mostly buildings, including cemetery architecture and the Washington Monument, begun in 1848. Some of that craze is still standing in Washington.

cards.headline: Cleopatra’s Needles
cards.body: Some people wanted the real thing. Two granite obelisks, carved about 3,500 years ago for Thutmose III, were given away by Egypt’s government: one was raised in London in 1878, the other in New York’s Central Park in 1881. They’re called Cleopatra’s Needles because the Romans moved them to Alexandria, to a temple conceived by Cleopatra. They were already more than a thousand years old in her day.
cards.callout: Named for Cleopatra, carved for Thutmose III

levels.title: Finding Tutankhamun
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Howard Carter's discovery in 1922.
levels.summary: Funded by Lord Carnarvon, Howard Carter found Tutankhamun’s largely intact tomb in November 1922 and spent about ten years recording its 5,398 objects.

cards.headline: By 1922, the man paying for the dig was ready to give up.
cards.body: Lord Carnarvon had funded Howard Carter’s digging for years with little to show for it. Carter talked him into one final season. It began on 1 November 1922, and three days later, a step appeared.

cards.headline: A step under a hut
cards.body: On 4 November, Carter’s team found a step cut into the bedrock beneath the remains of ancient workmen’s huts, about four metres below the entrance of Ramesses VI’s tomb. Soon they had exposed a sealed doorway. Carter covered it back up and cabled Carnarvon in England: “At last have made wonderful discovery in Valley.” The tomb had spent centuries under a building site.

mascot.line: Even the most famous line in archaeology got a second draft.

cards.headline: Wonderful things
cards.body: On 26 November, with Carnarvon beside him, Carter made a small hole in a second sealed doorway, stamped with Tutankhamun’s seals, and held up a candle. Carnarvon asked if he could see anything. That night Carter’s journal recorded his reply: “Yes, it is wonderful.” His later popular account polished it into the line everyone quotes: “Yes, wonderful things.”

cards.headline: Ten years of homework
cards.body: The tomb was largely intact, the first known intact royal burial from ancient Egypt. Carter’s team numbered its 5,398 objects and spent about ten years clearing and recording them. Their notes, photographs and drawings are kept at the Griffith Institute in Oxford. The gold made the headlines. The paperwork made it science.

levels.title: Studying Egypt Today
levels.objective: After this level you can describe modern tools like scans and satellite images.
levels.summary: Muon detectors find hidden spaces in the Great Pyramid, CT scans unwrap mummies digitally, and infrared satellite images reveal buried mud-brick buildings.

cards.headline: Archaeologists can now look inside a pyramid without moving a single block.
cards.body: They can unwrap a pharaoh without touching a thread, and spot buried buildings from orbit. Egypt is still giving up secrets. What’s changed is the tools.

cards.headline: An X-ray lit by the sky
cards.body: Muons are particles made when cosmic rays hit our atmosphere, and they rain down constantly. Stone absorbs some of them, so detectors can map empty spaces inside a pyramid. In 2017 the ScanPyramids team reported a big void at least 30 metres long above the Great Pyramid’s Grand Gallery. In 2023, muons located a corridor about 9 metres long behind the north face, and a camera pushed inside confirmed it.

mascot.line: No scissors, no unrolling: just a scanner and a lot of patience.

cards.headline: Unwrapping without unwrapping
cards.body: Amenhotep I’s mummy was so finely wrapped, with flower garlands and a lifelike mask, that no one opened it in modern times. In 2021, radiologist Sahar Saleem and Egyptologist Zahi Hawass unwrapped it digitally with CT scans. Inside was a man about 35 years old, with good teeth and 30 amulets tucked into his wrappings. The mask stayed on. The secrets came out.

cards.headline: Archaeology from orbit
cards.body: Sarah Parcak of the University of Alabama at Birmingham processes satellite images to see in infrared, which your eyes can’t. In the desert, it picks up moisture differences in the ground above buried mud bricks, tracing the outlines of vanished buildings. Her team mapped the street grid of Tanis, once a capital in the Nile Delta, and tracked tomb looting after 2011. Some of the best new digging starts with no digging at all.

levels.title: Who Owns the Past?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain debates over returning ancient objects to Egypt.
levels.summary: Zahi Hawass wants the Rosetta Stone and Nefertiti bust returned; the museums in London and Berlin defend how they got them. Egypt opened the Grand Egyptian Museum in 2025.

cards.headline: The Rosetta Stone has sat in London since 1802. Many want it back.
cards.body: Who should keep objects taken from Egypt long ago? It’s a real argument, and both sides have reasons. Here are both cases, who makes them, and one very large new building.

cards.headline: The case for return
cards.body: In 2022, Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, launched a petition for the Rosetta Stone’s return that passed 100,000 signatures. He also wants the bust of Nefertiti back from Berlin and the Dendera Zodiac from the Louvre, saying these unique objects belong in Egypt. On Nefertiti he goes further: he argues the bust, found in 1912 and taken to Berlin in 1913, left Egypt illegally.

mascot.line: When two sides tell the same story differently, it helps to know exactly who is saying what.

cards.headline: The museums’ case
cards.body: The British Museum says the Rosetta Stone came to Britain under an 1801 treaty signed by a representative of Egypt. It adds that Egypt’s government has made no formal request, and that most known copies of the decree are already in Egypt. Berlin’s museum points out that the Nefertiti bust left through an official division of finds in 1913, overseen by an inspector of Egypt’s antiquities service. Same objects, very different stories.

cards.headline: A new home by the pyramids
cards.body: Egypt has also made its point in concrete. The Grand Egyptian Museum, near the Great Pyramid at Giza, officially opened on 1 November 2025 with about 100,000 artifacts. For the first time since its discovery, Tutankhamun’s entire collection is shown together. Remember Carter’s 5,398 numbered objects from Level 95? They’re finally all in one place.

levels.title: Myths About Egypt
levels.objective: After this level you can debunk common myths, like aliens building the pyramids.
levels.summary: Paid workers, not slaves, built the Giza pyramids; Merer’s logbook shows human crews at work; the curse and Cleopatra’s looks rest on thin evidence.

cards.headline: Ancient Egypt collects myths the way a pyramid collects sand.
cards.body: Take the famous curse on Tutankhamun’s tomb: Howard Carter, the man who opened it in 1922, lived until 1939. Some myths started with ancient writers, and some with Hollywood. The fix is always the same: check the evidence.

cards.headline: Myth: slaves built the pyramids
cards.body: The picture of whipped slaves comes from Herodotus (yes, Level 2’s “gift of the river” man), misreadings of the Bible’s book of Exodus, and Hollywood films. The ground tells another story. Near the Giza pyramids, archaeologists found workers’ districts with bakeries and workshops, and workers’ tombs close to the pyramids, some naming the dead. Most archaeologists now think paid laborers built them.

mascot.line: The best answer to a wild theory is often a very boring document.

cards.headline: Myth: aliens did it
cards.body: The builders left paperwork. In 2013, archaeologists at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea found the oldest known inscribed papyri, including the logbook of an official named Merer. His crew shipped limestone by boat from the Tura quarries to Giza for Khufu’s pyramid, and he logged the work in half-day entries. Aliens, as far as anyone knows, don’t fill in timesheets.

cards.headline: Myth: we know Cleopatra’s face
cards.body: People argue hotly about Cleopatra’s looks, but the evidence is thin. She belonged to a Macedonian Greek dynasty, yet even her mother’s identity is uncertain, and her coins and portrait busts don’t all agree. Plutarch, writing long after, said her beauty was “not altogether incomparable,” but that talking with her had “an irresistible charm.” Egypt’s most famous face is one of its least certain.

levels.title: Egypt's Legacy
levels.objective: After this level you can name what the modern world still owes to ancient Egypt.
levels.summary: Our calendar descends from Egypt’s solar calendar via Julius Caesar, the letter A from an ox-head sign, and the word paper from papyrus.

cards.headline: You use ancient Egypt daily: in your calendar, your alphabet and your paper.
cards.body: Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BCE, but pieces of it never left. Here are three hiding in plain sight.

cards.headline: Your calendar
cards.body: In 46 BCE, Julius Caesar reformed Rome’s calendar by adopting the Egyptian solar calendar, advised by Sosigenes, an astronomer from Alexandria. The year became 365 and a quarter days, with an extra day every fourth year. Pope Gregory XIII fine-tuned it in 1582, and his Gregorian calendar gradually replaced Caesar’s. Every leap day has an Egyptian ancestor.
cards.callout: Egypt, then Caesar, then Gregory, then your wall

mascot.line: A for ox. Once you see the horns, you can’t unsee them.

cards.headline: Your alphabet
cards.body: Look at the letter A. The inventors of the alphabet were influenced by Egyptian writing, and A goes back to a sign shaped like an ox’s head. Early Semitic writing in Sinai adopted it around 1500 BCE. The Phoenicians called it aleph, meaning “ox,” and the Greeks renamed it alpha and used it for a vowel. Turn a capital A upside down and imagine the horns.

cards.headline: Your paper
cards.body: The word “paper” comes from papyrus, the Egyptian writing material. The Greeks adopted papyrus, and the Roman Empire used it widely. Books and documents on papyrus were still being made, now and then, until about the 12th century. So whenever you ask for a sheet of paper, you’re naming an Egyptian invention.

levels.title: Rome in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the three big eras of Roman history and roughly when each began and ended.
levels.summary: Rome went from Kingdom to Republic (509 BCE) to Empire (27 BCE). It ringed the Mediterranean; the West fell in 476 and the East in 1453.

cards.headline: Rome tried kings, then a Republic, then emperors. Then it fell. Twice.
cards.body: That’s the whole plot. It took more than a thousand years to play out, and even the ending was in no hurry.

cards.headline: Kingdom, Republic, Empire
cards.body: Romans dated their city’s founding to 753 BCE, and at first it was ruled by kings: the Kingdom. In 509 BCE the Romans threw out their last king and ran things as a Republic instead. That lasted until 27 BCE, when Augustus took sole power and the Empire began. Same city, three very different answers to one question: who’s in charge here?
cards.callout: Kingdom → Republic (509 BCE) → Empire (27 BCE)

cards.headline: An empire around a sea
cards.body: At its height, Rome held every coast of the Mediterranean, stretching from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to the Middle East. Picture it on a map: a giant ring of land with a sea in the middle. So Romans simply called the Mediterranean Mare Nostrum, “our sea.” Sail anywhere on it, and wherever you landed, you were still in Rome’s empire.

cards.fact: Rome fell twice.
cards.context: The western half of the empire ended in 476 CE, when its last emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed. The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, kept going until 1453, almost a thousand years later. So if someone asks you when Rome fell, the honest answer is another question: which half?

levels.title: Romulus and Remus
levels.objective: After this level you can retell Rome’s founding legend and explain why Romans valued it.
levels.summary: Legend says twin sons of Mars, nursed by a she-wolf, founded Rome, and Romulus killed Remus. Historians treat it as legend, not history.

cards.headline: Rome’s origin story: twins, a wolf and a murder.
cards.body: Not exactly a bedtime story. Yet the wolf became a symbol of Rome itself.

cards.headline: Raised by a wolf
cards.body: In the legend, the twins Romulus and Remus were sons of the god Mars. They were abandoned as babies, and a she-wolf found them and nursed them. Rome turned that moment into its emblem: the she-wolf feeding the twins became one of the city’s best-known symbols. Most cities don’t put a wild predator in the family photo. Rome made it the cover shot.

cards.headline: A city named in blood
cards.body: The twins grew up, and their new city came between them. They quarreled over it, and Romulus killed Remus. The winner got the naming rights: the city was named Rome, after Romulus. Imagine your hometown being named after whichever sibling won the argument. Romans didn’t have to imagine it.

cards.headline: Legend, not history
cards.body: Romans had a second origin story, too. They traced their ancestry to Aeneas, a Trojan prince who, in legend, fled the fall of Troy to Italy. Historians treat both stories as legend, because they were written down centuries after the events they describe. So why learn them? Because they show how Romans saw themselves. A legend won’t tell you what happened, but it tells you who a people wanted to be.

levels.title: What the Ground Remembers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what archaeology shows about Rome’s earliest villages.
levels.summary: Latin farmers built huts on the Palatine by about the 8th century BCE. Hilltop villages merged, and the marshy Forum valley was drained.

cards.headline: Forget the wolf for a moment. What does the ground say?
cards.body: Under the ruins on Rome’s Palatine Hill lie traces of the city’s first huts. They tell a quieter story than twins and a she-wolf.

cards.headline: Huts on a hill
cards.body: The first Romans were Latins, a people of the region of Latium in central Italy. On the Palatine Hill, archaeologists have found traces of their Iron Age huts from around the 8th century BCE. Now hold that next to the traditional founding date, 753 BCE. The huts sit close to the traditional founding: the shovel and the storytellers land in the same century. Not bad for a tale with a wolf in it.

cards.headline: From villages to a town
cards.body: Early Rome wasn’t one city. It was a cluster of small hilltop villages that gradually merged into one community. Down between the hills lay a marshy valley. It was drained, and that soggy low ground became the Roman Forum, the center of Roman public life. Before it was famous, it was a bog.

cards.fact: Rome’s great drain still works.
cards.context: The Cloaca Maxima, Rome’s great drain, helped dry out that marshy Forum valley. Parts of it still carry water today. Somewhere under the modern city, a very old drain is still doing its job.

levels.title: Seven Hills and a River
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Tiber and the seven hills shaped where and why Rome grew.
levels.summary: Rome grew at a crossing of the Tiber on a trade route, on hills that were easy to defend and stayed dry. Ostia became its port.

cards.headline: Why build a city right here? Follow the river and the salt.
cards.body: Rome sits where it does for reasons you can still see on a map: a river you can cross, a road for salt, and hills that keep your feet dry.

cards.headline: A river crossing
cards.body: Rome grew where the Tiber River could be crossed, near an island in the river, about 25 km from the sea. An ancient salt route, later called the Via Salaria, passed right through, linking the coast with inland Italy. So anyone moving goods between the two came this way. Own the crossing, and trade has to walk past your front door.
cards.callout: River crossing + trade route = a place worth holding

cards.headline: Seven hills
cards.body: The city spread across seven hills beside the Tiber, among them the Capitoline and the Palatine, where those first huts stood. The hills made sense twice over. They were easier to defend, and they stayed dry when the Tiber flooded the low ground between them. Enemies and floods: the hills handled both.

cards.fact: Rome had its own port.
cards.context: Rome sat about 25 km inland, so its harbor was downstream. Ostia, at the mouth of the Tiber, became Rome’s port. Grain and other goods came in there and traveled up the river to the city. The same river that gave Rome its crossing also delivered dinner.

levels.title: The Etruscans Next Door
levels.objective: After this level you can describe who the Etruscans were and what Rome borrowed from them.
levels.summary: The Etruscans of Tuscany were early Italy’s great power. Rome had Etruscan kings and borrowed the fasces and haruspicy from them.

cards.headline: Before Rome was a great power, it lived next to one.
cards.body: The Etruscans were among the most powerful peoples of early Italy. Rome borrowed a lot from them, even, tradition says, some of its kings.

cards.headline: Rome’s powerful neighbors
cards.body: North of Rome, in Etruria, mostly what is now Tuscany, lived the Etruscans. They weren’t one kingdom but a set of independent cities, and they were among the most powerful peoples of early Italy. Their language was unrelated to Latin, and it is still only partly understood. Rome’s big neighbors next door, and we still can’t fully read their mail.

cards.headline: Etruscan kings
cards.body: Here’s the twist. According to Roman tradition, the last three kings of Rome were Etruscans. Historians can’t vouch for every detail, but the bigger picture holds: young Rome grew up under strong Etruscan influence. For a while, the neighbors weren’t just next door. They were on the throne.

cards.headline: What Rome borrowed
cards.body: Some of Rome’s most Roman-looking things were imports. Take the fasces, a bundle of rods around an axe. Attendants carried it in front of officials as a sign of their authority, and it came from the Etruscans. So did haruspicy: reading omens in the organs of sacrificed animals. A way to show power and a way to read the gods, both borrowed from next door.
cards.callout: Fasces: rods and an axe, the symbol of authority

levels.title: The Seven Kings
levels.objective: After this level you can outline Rome’s age of kings and how kingship worked there.
levels.summary: Seven kings ruled from 753 to 509 BCE, each chosen with the Senate’s and people’s approval. Numa founded religion; Servius, the census.

cards.headline: Rome had seven kings, if you trust the legends. Not the kind you picture.
cards.body: No crown passed neatly from father to son. Most of the time, Rome had other ideas about who got the job.

cards.headline: Seven kings
cards.body: Roman tradition counted seven kings, from Romulus in 753 BCE to Tarquin the Proud in 509 BCE, the last three of them Etruscans. But this wasn’t a family business. Kingship was not simply inherited: tradition says most kings were chosen with the approval of the Senate and the people. Being the old king’s son didn’t get you the job. Getting approved did.

cards.headline: Remembered for different things
cards.body: Each king came with a reputation, like a line on a résumé. Numa Pompilius, the second king, was remembered as the founder of Rome’s religious institutions and its calendar. Servius Tullius, the sixth, was credited with the first census, which sorted citizens by wealth. Ask a Roman who started a custom, and there was often a king ready to take the credit.

cards.fact: The Senate started as the king’s advisers.
cards.context: It began as a council of elders who advised the king. Keep an eye on it. The kings would go, but the Senate would stay, long after the last king was gone.

levels.title: Gods of the Household and the State
levels.objective: After this level you can describe early Roman religion, from household spirits to state priests and omens.
levels.summary: Romans kept peace with the gods through correct ritual: household spirits at home, Jupiter on the Capitoline, Vesta’s fire and augury.

cards.headline: Romans rarely asked whether the gods existed. They asked what the gods wanted.
cards.body: Get the ritual right, and the gods stayed on your side. Get it wrong, and even a few birds could hold up the city’s business.

cards.headline: Keeping peace with the gods
cards.body: Roman religion was less about what you believed and more about doing the rituals correctly. The goal had a name: the pax deorum, peace with the gods. Think of it as a contract where the fine print really matters. It started at home. Every household honored the Lares and Penates, guardian spirits of the home and its food store, at a small shrine. Even the pantry had protection.

cards.headline: Gods of the state
cards.body: The city had its own gods to keep happy. On the Capitoline Hill stood Rome’s greatest temple, dedicated to Jupiter, king of the gods, together with Juno and Minerva. Meanwhile, the Vestal Virgins tended the sacred fire of Vesta, goddess of the hearth, day and night. That fire was never allowed to go out. Every home had its little shrine. Rome had a fire nobody was allowed to let die.

cards.fact: Birds could put Roman politics on hold.
cards.context: Before major public decisions, Romans consulted augurs, priests who read the will of the gods in the flight of birds. An unfavorable sign could delay public business. Imagine a big vote postponed because the wrong birds flew by.

levels.title: The Roman Family
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the power of the paterfamilias and how Roman families were organized.
levels.summary: The paterfamilias held legal power over his descendants, even adults. The familia included the whole household, enslaved people too.

cards.headline: In Rome, a 40-year-old could still be under his father’s legal power.
cards.body: Growing up didn’t make you your own boss. Meet the paterfamilias.

cards.headline: The father’s power
cards.body: Every Roman family had a paterfamilias: its oldest living male. He held legal power over his children and grandchildren, even when they were grown adults with children of their own. In early Roman law this power, patria potestas, in theory reached as far as life and death. So if your grandfather was alive, he wasn’t just your boss. He was your dad’s boss too.

cards.headline: More than relatives
cards.body: To a Roman, familia meant more than relatives. It meant the whole household, including the enslaved people who lived and worked in it. The family reached back in time, too. Noble families kept wax masks of their ancestors and carried them in funeral processions. At a noble Roman funeral, the ancestors came along.

cards.fact: Roman names came in three parts.
cards.context: Take Gaius Julius Caesar. Gaius was his personal name, Julius his clan name, and Caesar the name of his family’s branch of that clan. Say a Roman man’s full name, and you’ve recited a small family tree.

levels.title: The Last King
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Rome overthrew Tarquin the Proud and why it rejected kings.
levels.summary: Tarquin the Proud ruled as a tyrant. After the Lucretia scandal, Brutus led the Romans to expel him in 509 BCE and swear off kings.

cards.headline: Rome’s kings ended with a crime, an uprising and an oath never to have another.
cards.body: The seventh king pushed too far. What came next left Romans with a lasting horror of one word: king.

cards.headline: A tyrant king
cards.body: The seventh king, Tarquin the Proud, was remembered as a tyrant who ruled by force and ignored the Senate, the very council that had begun as the king’s advisers. Then, according to tradition, the king’s son assaulted a noblewoman named Lucretia. That was the spark. The crime set off an uprising, and not just against one bad king, but against the monarchy itself.

cards.headline: No more kings
cards.body: According to tradition, the Romans, led by Lucius Junius Brutus, drove out their king in 509 BCE and ended the monarchy. Then Brutus had them swear never again to let anyone be king in Rome. Not just “no more Tarquin.” No more kings, ever.
cards.callout: The end of the monarchy: 509 BCE

cards.fact: Romans hated the word “king.”
cards.context: After the tyrant kings, the title rex, king, became so hated that even Rome’s most powerful later leaders avoided it. They could hold enormous power. They just couldn’t call it that.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: what Romans said, and what the ground says.
cards.body: Romans had a great story about how their city began. Archaeologists have shovels. Let’s see where they meet.

cards.headline: One story
cards.body: Put it together and early Rome makes sense. The site sat on a crossing of the Tiber, on the route between the coast and inland Italy: a place worth holding. Latin villages on its hills merged into a town. Powerful Etruscan neighbors shaped it, and tradition says its last three kings were Etruscan. Founding legends told Romans who they were. Then, in 509 BCE, Rome drove out its seventh king and swore off kings for good. Which leaves a big question: what do you build instead?

levels.title: A Republic Is Born
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a republic is and what SPQR stood for.
levels.summary: After the kings, Rome became a res publica: elected magistrates with limited terms, the Senate and People of Rome, from 509 to 27 BCE.

cards.headline: Rome’s answer to tyranny was to share power, and keep it short.
cards.body: Rome had just sworn never to have another king. Now it needed a government where nobody could turn into one.

cards.headline: The public thing
cards.body: No king? Then who owns the state? Rome’s answer was res publica, Latin for “the public thing,” and the root of our word republic. Instead of a king, citizens elected officials called magistrates, and every one of them held power only for a limited term. Think of it as renting power, never owning it. The state belonged to the public, not to a king.

cards.headline: SPQR
cards.body: Romans called their state by four letters: SPQR, Senatus Populusque Romanus, “the Senate and People of Rome.” Read it again: there’s no king anywhere in the name. That arrangement lasted almost five centuries, from 509 BCE until Augustus took sole power in 27 BCE.
cards.callout: SPQR: the Senate and People of Rome

cards.fact: “The People” came with fine print.
cards.context: Only adult male citizens could vote. Women, enslaved people and foreigners had no vote at all. So when SPQR said “the People,” it meant a smaller crowd than everyone who lived in Rome.

levels.title: Two Consuls, One Year
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how consuls shared power and why their terms were short.
levels.summary: Two consuls led Rome for one year each, commanded its armies and could block each other. Emergencies allowed a dictator for six months.

cards.headline: Rome’s top job came with a partner and an expiry date.
cards.body: Rome wanted a leader strong enough to run the state, but never strong enough to become a king. Its fix was simple and sneaky.

cards.headline: Two at the top
cards.body: The Republic was led by two consuls, elected by the citizens every year. Each could block the other’s actions, so neither could rule alone. Picture a car with two steering wheels and two brake pedals: nobody goes on a joyride. And after one year, both stepped down. However good you were at the job, no one held supreme power for long.

cards.headline: Generals and calendars
cards.body: Consuls also commanded Rome’s armies in war. They were so central to Roman life that Romans didn’t count their years by number. They named each year after its two consuls. Imagine dating your birthday by who happened to be in charge that year. For a Roman, that was simply the date.

cards.fact: Emergencies came with a six-month limit.
cards.context: In a crisis, Rome could appoint a dictator with supreme power. Even that came with a timer: six months at most. Rome’s emergency brake had an expiry date too.

levels.title: The Senate
levels.objective: After this level you can describe who sat in the Senate and how it steered the Republic.
levels.summary: The Senate was about 300 former magistrates, usually serving for life. It only gave advice, but that advice was almost always followed.

cards.headline: The Senate couldn’t pass laws. It ran Rome anyway.
cards.body: Consuls came and went every year. So who remembered how things were done?

cards.headline: A council of former officials
cards.body: Remember the council of elders that advised the kings back in Level 6? It outlived them. In the Republic, the Senate was made up of former magistrates, men who had already held office, and they usually stayed senators for life. For most of the Republic there were about 300 of them. The only way into the room was to have helped run Rome already.

cards.headline: Advice that was obeyed
cards.body: Formally, the Senate only gave advice to the magistrates. In practice, its advice was almost always followed, especially on foreign policy and money. Why? A consul had one year. The senators facing him had all held office before and would sit there for life. When a room like that “suggests” something, you listen.

cards.fact: The Senate met in the middle of everything.
cards.context: Its usual home was the Curia, a building in the Roman Forum, the center of Roman public life. Rome’s most powerful advisers met a short walk from the markets and law courts.

levels.title: Patricians and Plebeians
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Conflict of the Orders between Rome’s old families and ordinary citizens.
levels.summary: Plebeians won rights from the patricians over two centuries, starting with a walkout in 494 BCE and ending with the Hortensian law of 287.

cards.headline: What if the workers and soldiers of a city simply walked out?
cards.body: In Rome, they did. It was the opening move in a fight over who got a say, and it lasted about two centuries.

cards.headline: Two kinds of citizen
cards.body: Every Roman citizen was one of two kinds. Patricians belonged to Rome’s old aristocratic families. Plebeians were all the rest. In the early Republic, patricians held the priesthoods and, by tradition, the magistracies too, though some historians think a few plebeians also held early offices. Either way, the top jobs belonged mostly to one side. Rome had thrown out its king, but not its old families.

cards.headline: The walkout
cards.body: In 494 BCE, according to tradition, the plebeians tried something bold: they walked out of Rome in protest. They refused to work or fight until they won concessions. A city nobody will work or fight for is just a pile of buildings. Their long struggle for political rights, about two centuries of it, is called the Conflict of the Orders.

levels.title: The Twelve Tables
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Rome wrote down its laws and what that changed.
levels.summary: Around 450 BCE Rome wrote its laws on the Twelve Tables in the Forum, so patrician judges could no longer bend unwritten custom.

cards.headline: A law you can’t read is a law someone else controls.
cards.body: The plebeians knew it. So they demanded that Rome’s laws be written down.

cards.headline: Law in public
cards.body: Roman law used to be unwritten custom, and patrician judges could interpret it as they pleased. Imagine playing a game where only the other team knows the rules. Plebeians demanded written laws, and around 450 BCE they got them: the Twelve Tables, Rome’s first written laws, displayed in the Forum. Now anyone could check the rules, at least in principle.

cards.headline: Everyday rules
cards.body: The Twelve Tables weren’t grand speeches about liberty. They covered ordinary life: debt, property, family and damage to others. In other words, the everyday arguments neighbors actually have. Centuries later, Cicero remembered memorizing them as a boy at school, then noted that boys no longer did. Kids these days.

cards.fact: The original tablets are lost.
cards.context: They were probably destroyed when the Gauls sacked Rome. The laws survive only because later writers quoted them. So the laws written down for everyone to read are the ones nobody today can read in the original.

levels.title: Tribunes of the Plebs
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the tribunes’ power to protect plebeians, including the veto.
levels.summary: Tribunes, elected by plebeians, could veto other magistrates and were sacrosanct. Ten of them protected ordinary citizens.

cards.headline: The most powerful word in Roman politics meant “I forbid.”
cards.body: The plebeians had officials of their own, and those officials could stop the powerful with a single word.

cards.headline: Protectors of the plebs
cards.body: The tribunes of the plebs were officials elected by plebeians to protect them from abuses by magistrates. Their number eventually rose to ten: ten officials whose whole job was to take the plebeians’ side. And a tribune’s door was expected to stay open day and night, so any plebeian could come and ask for help. Think of a 24-hour help desk with real political muscle behind it.

cards.headline: I forbid
cards.body: Remember how each consul could block the other in Level 12? A tribune could block them both. He could stop the acts of other magistrates, consuls included, simply by declaring “Veto,” Latin for “I forbid.” (A dictator was probably out of reach.) So why didn’t an angry consul just arrest him? Tribunes were sacrosanct: harming one was a religious crime. And because plebeians elected them, tribunes answered to ordinary citizens rather than to the old families.

levels.title: Cincinnatus and the Citizen Ideal
levels.objective: After this level you can retell the story of Cincinnatus and explain the Roman idea of civic duty.
levels.summary: Called from his plow in 458 BCE to save Rome, Cincinnatus won and gave up power after 16 days: the model Roman citizen.

cards.headline: Rome handed a farmer supreme power. He gave it back in about 16 days.
cards.body: Remember the dictator’s six-month limit from Level 12? One man didn’t need anywhere near that.

cards.headline: Called from the plow
cards.body: In 458 BCE, according to tradition, a Roman army was trapped by its enemies. The Senate needed a rescuer, so it made Cincinnatus dictator, with supreme power. The messengers didn’t find him in a palace or a war tent. They found him plowing his farm. For the moment, the most powerful man in Rome was standing behind a plow.

cards.headline: Power returned
cards.body: Cincinnatus won the war. Then he resigned as dictator after about 16 days, far short of his six months, and went back to his farm. He gave up supreme power the moment the crisis was over. His story shows what Romans prized, the mos maiorum, “the custom of the ancestors”: duty, discipline and service to the state. Cincinnatus managed all three and still got the plowing done.

cards.fact: An American city carries his name.
cards.context: Cincinnati is named after the Society of the Cincinnati, which took its name from Cincinnatus. So a whole city is named, at one remove, after a man remembered for giving power back.

levels.title: The Gauls Sack Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Gallic sack of Rome and how it changed Roman defense.
levels.summary: Around 390 BCE Gauls under Brennus won at the Allia and sacked Rome. “Woe to the conquered.” Rome answered with a great stone wall.

cards.headline: Around 390 BCE, Rome learned it could be captured.
cards.body: It began with a battle at a river and ended with an enemy army inside the city.

cards.headline: Disaster at the Allia
cards.body: In about 390 BCE (387 by some counts), an army of Gauls led by Brennus crushed the Romans at the Allia River. Then came the unthinkable: the Gauls marched into Rome itself and sacked it. The damage reached even Rome’s laws. The original Twelve Tables from Level 15 were probably destroyed in the sack.

cards.headline: Woe to the conquered
cards.body: According to Livy, when the Romans protested the ransom, Brennus threw his sword onto the scales and said “Vae victis”: woe to the conquered. In other words, losers don’t get to argue. Legend gives Rome one bright moment: the sacred geese of Juno warned the defenders of the Capitoline of a night attack by the Gauls. Saved by geese. Rome would take it.

cards.fact: Rome’s answer: a wall.
cards.context: After the sack, Rome surrounded itself with a strong stone wall, later called the Servian Wall. A city that had just learned it could be captured gave itself a shell.

levels.title: Conquering Italy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Rome came to control the Italian peninsula, and the role of roads and alliances.
levels.summary: Rome beat the Samnites, built the Via Appia from 312 BCE and made defeated peoples allies. By about 264 BCE it controlled Italy.

cards.headline: Rome won Italy with armies, roads and allies.
cards.body: Swords can win land. Roads and allies help you keep it.

cards.headline: Wars in the hills
cards.body: From 343 to 290 BCE, Rome fought the Samnite Wars against the hill peoples of central and southern Italy, a struggle for control of the peninsula. Rome came out on top. By about 264 BCE it controlled nearly all of Italy south of the Po Valley. The little town on the Tiber now ran almost the whole boot, minus the top.

cards.headline: Roads and allies
cards.body: In 312 BCE Rome began the Via Appia, its first great road, built to move armies quickly to the south. But the smarter move was what Rome did with the people it beat. Defeated Italian peoples became allies who supplied soldiers instead of paying tribute, and some were granted citizenship. So every war Rome won made its next army bigger. Lose to Rome, and you ended up marching for it.

cards.fact: A victory that cost too much.
cards.context: King Pyrrhus of Epirus beat Roman armies, but at such a cost that his name became a warning. A “Pyrrhic victory” now means a win that costs too much.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How the Republic Worked

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale. How do you stop anyone from becoming a king?
cards.body: You spread power around and let each part hold the others back. Here’s the whole machine.

items.label: Consuls
points: Two, elected every year, each able to block the other

items.label: Citizens and tribunes
points: Assemblies elected magistrates and passed laws

cards.headline: Checks and balances
cards.body: It took an outsider to name the design. Polybius, a Greek historian taken to Rome as a hostage, wrote his history to explain how Rome came to dominate the Mediterranean world. Along the way he praised Rome’s government as a mix of three kinds of rule: the consuls were the monarchy, the Senate the aristocracy, and the assemblies the democracy. Each part checked the others, so none could take over. Rome kept a piece of a king, a piece of the nobles and a piece of the people, and let none of them win.

levels.title: Carthage, Queen of the Sea
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Carthage and why it clashed with Rome.
levels.summary: Carthage, founded by Phoenicians in 814 BCE, ruled the western seas. In 264 BCE it and Rome went to war over Sicily: the Punic Wars.

cards.headline: Once Rome held Italy, it looked across the water and found a rival.
cards.body: By about 264 BCE Rome controlled nearly all of Italy south of the Po Valley. Across the sea waited a city that was older than Rome and far better at sea.

cards.headline: A city of traders
cards.body: Carthage began as a colony. Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded it, traditionally in 814 BCE, on the coast of what is now Tunisia. It grew rich from trade, and it guarded that trade with ships, becoming the leading naval power of the western Mediterranean. Rome was a land power with a new peninsula. Carthage was a trading house with a fleet.

cards.headline: Sicily in between
cards.body: Look at a map and the trouble is obvious. Sicily sits between Italy and North Africa, like a stepping stone in the middle of a stream. Rome now held Italy and faced Carthage, the great sea power, across the water. In 264 BCE the two went to war over control of Sicily. Romans called these wars Punic, from the Latin Punicus, “Phoenician.” The name remembers where Carthage came from.
cards.callout: Punic = Phoenician

cards.fact: Carthage was older than Rome.
cards.context: Carthage’s traditional founding date, 814 BCE, comes 61 years before Rome’s own, 753 BCE. So when the two met in Sicily, Rome was the newcomer, taking on an older city that already ruled the western sea. The upstart against the old sea power: that’s the story of the Punic Wars.

levels.title: The First Punic War
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Rome built a navy and won the First Punic War.
levels.summary: In 264–241 BCE a land power learned to fight at sea. With a new fleet and the corvus, Rome beat Carthage and took Sicily.

cards.headline: To beat a sea power, Rome had to become one, almost from scratch.
cards.body: Rome’s enemy was the leading navy of the western Mediterranean. Rome’s answer was simple and slightly outrageous: build a navy of its own.

cards.headline: A navy from nothing
cards.body: The First Punic War lasted from 264 to 241 BCE, and Rome started it with a problem. It had little experience at sea, and Carthage was the leading naval power of the western Mediterranean. So Rome built a large war fleet. Picture a team of wrestlers signing up for a swimming race against the champions. Bold. Also, on paper, a terrible idea.

cards.headline: Turning sea battles into land battles
cards.body: Rome’s trick was to change the game. Roman ships carried the corvus, a boarding bridge with a spike at its end. Drop it onto an enemy deck, and Roman soldiers could storm across and fight on enemy decks as if they were on solid ground. A sea battle became a fight between soldiers, the kind of fight Rome was good at. Can’t win the swimming race? Turn it into a wrestling match.

cards.fact: Sicily became Rome’s first province.
cards.context: Winning the war in 241 BCE gave Rome the island the fighting had started over, and with it Rome’s first overseas province. Remember that word, province. Rome was about to start collecting them.

levels.title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps
levels.objective: After this level you can retell Hannibal’s march over the Alps with his army and elephants.
levels.summary: In 218 BCE Hannibal led an army with war elephants from Spain over the Alps into Italy, beginning the Second Punic War.

cards.headline: The attack Rome never expected came over the mountains, with elephants.
cards.body: Rome now had a war fleet of its own. The next Carthaginian invasion didn’t come by sea. It came over the Alps.

cards.headline: A general sworn against Rome
cards.body: According to tradition, Hannibal’s father made him swear as a boy never to be a friend of Rome. He kept that promise on a grand scale. As a Carthaginian general based in Spain, Hannibal attacked Saguntum, a Roman ally, sparking the Second Punic War, which lasted from 218 to 201 BCE. Then he invaded Italy itself, taking the war straight to Rome’s home ground.

cards.headline: Over the Alps
cards.body: In 218 BCE Hannibal led his army, war elephants included, from Spain over the Alps into Italy. The mountains were brutal: he lost many men on the march. Oddly, most of the elephants survived the crossing, only for nearly all of them to die in the cold soon after. Still, he reached Italy and won early victories. Then he stayed. For about 15 years, Rome could not drive him out of its own backyard.

levels.title: Disaster at Cannae
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happened at Cannae and why it is still studied.
levels.summary: At Cannae in 216 BCE Hannibal encircled a much larger Roman army and destroyed it. Rome lost tens of thousands, yet refused to make peace.

cards.headline: A much larger Roman army walked into a trap it couldn’t escape.
cards.body: More soldiers usually means a better chance. At Cannae, Hannibal made Rome’s numbers work against it.

cards.headline: The trap
cards.body: At Cannae in 216 BCE, Hannibal faced a much larger Roman army. He let the center of his line fall back as the Romans pushed forward, so every step forward carried them deeper in. Then his wings and cavalry closed around them from both sides. The army doing the pushing was suddenly surrounded. This is a double envelopment: think of a hand closing into a fist, with the Romans inside.
cards.callout: Center falls back, wings close in

cards.headline: A catastrophe, and a refusal
cards.body: Ancient sources report Roman losses in the tens of thousands, one of the worst defeats in Roman history. After a blow like that, you’d expect Rome to ask for terms. It refused to make peace. Hannibal had won a battle. He had not won the war. Officers still study Cannae as the classic example of encirclement. Rome was the first to learn that lesson, the hard way.

levels.title: Fabius the Delayer
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Fabius Maximus’s strategy of avoiding battle and why it worked.
levels.summary: Fabius shadowed Hannibal and cut his supplies instead of fighting. Mocked as the Delayer, he was proved right as Italy’s allies held firm.

cards.headline: Sometimes the best way to beat a genius is to refuse to fight him.
cards.body: Hannibal kept winning battles in Italy. One Roman general’s answer sounded almost cowardly: stop giving him battles to win.

cards.headline: Don’t fight, follow
cards.body: Fabius Maximus avoided pitched battles with Hannibal. Instead he shadowed Hannibal’s army and cut off its supplies, like a shadow that also steals your lunch. Romans first used his nickname as an insult: Cunctator, “the Delayer.” After the disaster at Cannae in 216 BCE, a little delay looked a lot wiser, and the insult became praise.

cards.headline: Why it worked
cards.body: Hannibal was far from home. To keep going, he needed supplies and new allies: Italian cities willing to switch sides and send him men. But Rome had bound the peoples it defeated as allies who supplied soldiers, and most of them stayed loyal. With Fabius cutting his supplies and no new allies joining, Hannibal never got the reinforcements he needed. Time was on Rome’s side.

cards.fact: His name became a strategy.
cards.context: A “Fabian strategy” still means wearing down a stronger enemy by avoiding a decisive battle, exactly as Fabius did. Not bad for a man once mocked as the Delayer.

cards.headline: Delay: vindicated

levels.title: Scipio and Zama
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Scipio Africanus defeated Hannibal at Zama.
levels.summary: Scipio took Spain, invaded Africa and beat Hannibal at Zama in 202 BCE. Carthage lost its empire and fleet and paid a huge indemnity.

cards.headline: Rome finally beat Hannibal by making him come home.
cards.body: For years, Rome couldn’t drive Hannibal out of Italy. So it went somewhere he wasn’t.

cards.headline: Take the war to Africa
cards.body: Publius Cornelius Scipio drove the Carthaginians out of Spain, Hannibal’s old base. Then he made a bold move: he invaded Africa and threatened Carthage itself. Carthage called Hannibal home to defend the city, and he was forced to leave Italy. Years of Roman armies couldn’t push him out. One threat to his own city did it.

cards.headline: Zama, 202 BCE
cards.body: At the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE, Scipio defeated Hannibal and won the Second Punic War, the war Hannibal had started back at Saguntum. Carthage paid heavily. It lost its overseas territories and most of its fleet, and it owed Rome a huge indemnity. The old queen of the sea was left with hardly a navy.

cards.fact: He was named for his victory.
cards.context: Scipio was given the name Africanus, after the continent where he won the war. Hannibal had carried the war into Italy. Scipio won it by carrying it to Africa, and the name stuck.

levels.title: Rome Turns East
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how Rome came to dominate Greece and the Hellenistic kingdoms.
levels.summary: Rome beat Macedon and came to control Greece, destroying Corinth in 146 BCE. Meanwhile Greek culture conquered Rome from within.

cards.headline: Rome conquered Greece. Then Greece conquered Rome right back.
cards.body: Rome won the wars in the east. Greek art, books and ideas won over the Romans.

cards.headline: Wars with Macedon
cards.body: In the east, Rome’s opponent was the kingdom of Macedon. In a series of wars ending in 148 BCE, Rome came to control Greece. Along the way, in 196 BCE, the Roman general Flamininus proclaimed the Greek cities free. Free, on paper. Roman influence over them only kept growing, like a guest who says he’s just visiting and keeps unpacking.

cards.headline: Captive Greece
cards.body: Then the conquered started conquering back. Greek art, literature and philosophy deeply shaped Roman culture, changing how Romans made art, wrote and thought about the world. The poet Horace put it perfectly: captive Greece took its fierce conqueror captive. Rome took the land. Greece took the Romans, one statue and one book at a time.

cards.fact: Corinth was destroyed in 146 BCE.
cards.context: The Greek cities’ freedom had limits. In 146 BCE Rome destroyed the Greek city of Corinth. Hold on to that year: in the same year, Rome destroyed Carthage too.

cards.headline: One senator ended every speech the same way: Carthage must be destroyed.
cards.body: Carthage had lost its overseas lands and most of its fleet. For one Roman senator, that still wasn’t the end of the story.

cards.headline: A rival that survived
cards.body: After Zama, Carthage had lost its overseas territories and most of its fleet, and owed Rome a huge indemnity. But it was still standing. In the Senate, Cato the Elder was said to end his speeches with the same demand: Carthage must be destroyed. Picture a coworker who closes every single meeting with the same line. Subtle, he was not.

cards.headline: The end of Carthage
cards.body: In the Third Punic War, from 149 to 146 BCE, Rome captured and destroyed Carthage. Its lands became the Roman province of Africa. And in that same year, 146 BCE, Rome destroyed Corinth in Greece. One year, two great cities gone, one on each side of the sea.

cards.fact: The salted earth is a myth.
cards.context: You may have heard that the Romans sowed salt on Carthage’s fields. That story is a much later invention. Carthage didn’t even stay empty: it was later refounded as a Roman colony and became one of the great cities of the empire. Destroyed by Rome, then rebuilt by Rome.

levels.title: The Legion
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how a Roman legion was organized, equipped and trained.
levels.summary: Republican legions had 4,000 to 5,000 citizen infantry in flexible maniples, three lines deep, armed with the gladius and pila.

cards.headline: Rome’s real weapon was organization.
cards.body: Cannae showed what happened when a legion got trapped. Here’s how it was built to fight.

cards.headline: Citizens under arms
cards.body: In the Republic, a legion had roughly 4,000 to 5,000 infantry: picture a small town, all on foot. In the earlier Republic, those soldiers were property-owning citizens who supplied their own equipment. War was very much bring-your-own. Each man carried a short stabbing sword, the gladius, and heavy throwing javelins called pila.

cards.headline: Flexible blocks
cards.body: A legion didn’t fight as one giant block. It fought in maniples, small flexible units arranged in three lines. The youngest men, the hastati, stood in front. The principes came next. The veterans, the triarii, stood at the back. So the least experienced soldiers met the enemy first, with the most experienced waiting behind them.
cards.callout: Hastati → principes → triarii

cards.fact: The pilum was hard to throw back.
cards.context: Its long, thin iron shank could bend or lodge in a shield, so an enemy couldn’t easily throw it back. Historians still debate whether the bending was deliberate or a happy accident. Either way, return to sender was off the table.

levels.title: The Gracchi Brothers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the land reforms of the Gracchi and why they ended in violence.
levels.summary: As estates swallowed small farms, the tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus pushed land and grain reforms. Both were killed.

cards.headline: Two brothers tried to give land to the poor. Both were killed for it.
cards.body: Rome’s rich were getting richer while its small farmers lost their land. Two brothers tried to fix that, and found out what fixing it would cost.

cards.headline: Rich estates, poor farmers
cards.body: Picture your family farm next to a giant estate worked by enslaved people. By the 2nd century BCE, wealthy Romans had built huge estates like that, while many small farmers lost their land. In 133 BCE a tribune named Tiberius Gracchus proposed an answer: give public land to poor citizens. Remember Level 16? Tribunes of the plebs were elected to protect ordinary Romans. This one took the job literally.

cards.headline: Politics turns deadly
cards.body: The argument didn’t end with a vote. A mob of senators and their supporters killed Tiberius, the first great outbreak of political bloodshed in Rome in centuries. His brother Gaius picked up the cause and pushed even wider reforms, including cheap grain for citizens. In 121 BCE, Gaius was killed too. Two brothers, two reform plans, two funerals.

cards.fact: After the Gracchi, Roman political fights could be settled with violence.
cards.context: That was the real turning point. Not the land, but the lesson: if you couldn’t win the argument, you could get rid of the person making it. Disputes that used to be settled by votes could now be settled by violence. Watch for that lesson in the levels ahead. Rome learned it far too well.
