levels.title: Instinct and Learning
levels.objective: After this level you can tell instinct from learned behavior.
levels.summary: Instincts are innate, like a gull chick pecking its parent's red bill spot; learning changes with experience. Imprinting mixes both, as Tex the crane showed.

cards.headline: A whooping crane named Tex thought she was a person.
cards.body: Tex hatched at the San Antonio Zoo and grew up around people. As an adult, she wouldn't pair with another whooping crane. So in spring 1976, biologist George Archibald started dancing with her, because dancing is how whooping cranes begin mating. In 1982 she finally hatched a chick, Gee Whiz. How does a bird get so confused about who she is?

cards.headline: Born knowing
cards.body: Some behavior comes preinstalled. A newly hatched herring gull chick pecks at the red spot on its parent's bill, and the parent brings up food for it. Nobody teaches it that. Biologists call this instinct: innate behavior with a strong genetic component, no practice needed. Its big advantage is that there's no risk of learning it wrong. The chick doesn't need a lesson. It needs a red spot.

cards.headline: Learned on the job
cards.body: Learned behavior is shaped by experience, so it can change when the world does. Prairie dogs give alarm calls when danger comes near. But they learn to ignore human footsteps that never bring harm, while still calling at predators. Learning is flexible, and that flexibility is its whole point. A prairie dog that screamed at every hiker would never get lunch.

mascot.line: Somewhere a duckling is following a cardboard box with total confidence. Respect.

cards.fact: Imprinting: learning that has a deadline.
cards.context: In an early critical period, a newly hatched duckling learns to follow the first moving object it sees, whether its mother, a person or even a cardboard box. In 1935, Konrad Lorenz quacked like a mother duck at newly hatched ducklings, and they treated him as their mother. Tex had imprinted on people. Today keepers raise crane chicks in crane costumes, so the chicks imprint on cranes. No behavior is purely innate or purely learned; imprinting is both at once.

levels.title: Animal Communication
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how animals send signals to each other.
levels.summary: Animals signal by smell (pheromones), sound, sight and touch. Vervet monkeys give different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, and displays like bared teeth can replace a fight.

cards.headline: One monkey shouts, and the whole troop looks at the sky.
cards.body: Vervet monkeys don't have just one alarm call. They have different calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, and the troop reacts to each one differently. Is that a scream of fear, or something closer to a word?

cards.headline: Four ways to send a message
cards.body: A signal is information one animal gives off that another can use to decide what to do. Signals travel by smell, sound, sight and touch. A pheromone is a chemical signal released to get a response from another member of the same species, to attract mates, sound an alarm or mark a food trail. Primates groom each other; a signal can be instinctive, learned or both. If someone reacts, it counts as a message.

mascot.line: Up for eagles, down for snakes, trees for leopards. Not bad for a vocabulary of three.

cards.headline: Leopard, eagle, snake
cards.body: In a 1980 study in Amboseli, Kenya, Robert Seyfarth, Dorothy Cheney and Peter Marler recorded vervet alarm calls, then played them back with no predator anywhere. The monkeys still did the right thing: they ran into trees at a leopard alarm, looked up at an eagle alarm and looked down at a snake alarm. Each call pointed to a kind of danger. The call alone was enough.

cards.fact: Some signals exist to prevent a fight.
cards.context: A dog bares its teeth to make another dog back down. Displays like this let rivals judge each other's fighting ability, so a weaker animal can back off before anyone gets hurt, and real fights happen less often. Some displays even overstate an animal's strength: a bluff. A snarl is cheaper than a scar.

levels.title: The Bee Dance
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how honeybees tell each other where food is.
levels.summary: Bees do a round dance for nearby food and a waggle dance for far food: angle from up gives direction from the sun, duration gives distance. Von Frisch: Nobel 1973.

cards.headline: A bee finds flowers, flies home, and gives directions.
cards.body: Inside the hive, her sisters can't see the flowers, and there's no map on the wall. Yet after she dances on the comb, other bees know where to fly. Karl von Frisch worked out how she does it. So how do you give directions with your hips?

cards.headline: Two dances, two messages
cards.body: A forager with news of food dances on the comb while nestmates crowd around her. If the food is near the hive, she does a round dance, which sends them searching nearby. If it's farther away, she switches to the waggle dance: she runs straight ahead, waggling her abdomen, loops back to the start and repeats. The round dance says "somewhere close." The waggle dance gives an address.

cards.headline: The sun on the ceiling
cards.body: The straight waggle run is the map. On the vertical comb, straight up stands for the sun's direction. A run pointing straight up means "fly toward the sun"; a run tilted to the right of up means fly that far to the right of the sun. Distance is in the timing: the longer the waggle run lasts, the farther away the food. Clouds don't stop it, because bees can find the hidden sun using polarized light.

mascot.line: Even bees do better with a good dance teacher.

cards.fact: The dance won a Nobel Prize in 1973.
cards.context: Karl von Frisch shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Konrad Lorenz, of Level 71's ducklings, and Nikolaas Tinbergen. The 1973 announcement called the dance genetically programmed and not learned. A 2023 study added a twist: bees that never got to follow experienced dancers made messier dances and got distances wrong. Practice helped, but they never got distance right. The steps are inborn; the polish is learned.

levels.title: Packs and Herds
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why many animals live in groups.
levels.summary: Groups dilute risk and help hunters, at a cost. Wild wolf packs are families; the 'alpha' came from captive, unrelated wolves, as Mech showed in 1999.

cards.headline: The snarling "alpha wolf" came from wolves that had never met.
cards.body: The picture of a pack ruled by a top wolf that fought its way up came mostly from studies of captive wolves, such as Schenkel's in 1947: unrelated animals thrown together in an enclosure. Wild packs turned out to be something far more ordinary. First, though: why live in a group at all?

cards.headline: Safety in numbers
cards.body: If a predator takes one animal per attack, your odds of being the one shrink as the group grows. Alone, it's you. In a group of 100, it's 1 in 100. Animals in the middle of a group, like a fish school, are safer still, and a group that scatters unpredictably can confuse a predator. A crowd is the cheapest bodyguard around.

cards.headline: Teamwork, and the bill
cards.body: Groups help hunters too. Lions, hyenas and wolves that cooperate can corner and bring down prey more easily than one animal could. But group life has costs. Everyone competes for the same food, and if a group attracts too many predators, a single animal may be better off alone. Every herd is a deal that has to pay for itself.

cards.headline: A pack is a family
cards.body: In 1999, L. David Mech of the U.S. Geological Survey described wild packs as families: a breeding pair and their offspring from the previous 1 to 3 years. The alpha picture came from captive, unrelated wolves, who did form a pecking order. Mech had once used words like alpha himself. Now he says calling a wolf an alpha is like calling a human father one.

mascot.line: Top wolf turns out to mean "parent." Every family dinner makes more sense now.

cards.fact: In 13 summers, Mech saw no fights for the top spot.
cards.context: Watching a wild pack on Ellesmere Island, Canada, he found the parents simply lead. The mother mainly cares for and defends the pups; the father mainly leads hunting and brings food. Dominance displays showed up mostly over food, when parents steered it to the youngest pups. The "alpha" was just Mom or Dad.

levels.title: Courtship
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how animals attract mates, from bright feathers to birdsong.
levels.summary: Often one sex chooses and the other competes, so showy traits spread. Courtship runs on signals: song, step-by-step displays and the bowerbird's blue bower.

cards.headline: A bird in Australia collects blue bottle tops to impress a date.
cards.body: The male satin bowerbird gathers blue things: bottle tops, drinking straws, clothes pegs, parrot feathers, flowers. He arranges them around a structure of sticks he built on the ground. Why would a bird go to all that trouble?

cards.headline: The chooser decides
cards.body: In many species, one sex chooses and the other competes to be chosen. Peahens are the classic choosers: they tend to mate with the peacock showing the brightest, most elaborate plumage. A trait like that can make survival harder, but if it wins mates, it gets passed on anyway. A peacock's tail is a love letter he has to drag everywhere.

cards.headline: Songs and steps
cards.body: Courtship uses the signal channels from Level 72. Birdsong tells listeners which species is singing and helps attract a mate. Visual courtship displays often run as a series of steps: one partner displays, the other responds. If a step goes wrong or the response never comes, the courtship is abandoned. It's a duet where one missed cue ends the date.

mascot.line: He builds the stage, then she builds the actual home. Classic.

cards.fact: A bower is a stage, not a nest.
cards.context: The satin bowerbird's bower is two parallel walls of sticks, which he even paints with chewed plant matter mixed with saliva. When a female arrives, he struts and bows with quivering wings, buzzing and rattling, often holding a decoration in his bill. If she mates with him, she leaves to build a nest and raise the young on her own.

levels.title: Animal Parents
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how animals care for their young.
levels.summary: Care costs future young, so animals trade numbers for care. Orangutans raise only 4 or 5 young in a lifetime; seahorse fathers carry the eggs.

cards.headline: An orangutan mother may raise only 4 or 5 babies in her whole life.
cards.body: She has a baby only about every 7 to 9 years, and each one gets years of her attention. A seahorse father, meanwhile, gives birth to a brood and gives them no further care. Two very different bets on the same goal. Why?

cards.headline: Care has a price
cards.body: Every hour spent guarding one batch of eggs is an hour not spent producing the next. So parents face a trade-off: more young with little care, or fewer young with lots of it. Mammal mothers are locked onto the care side: they feed their young milk, and most carry them through pregnancy first. Parenting is paid for in babies not made.

cards.headline: The longest childhood
cards.body: Orangutans sit at the far end. Infants cling to their mothers from birth and can nurse until they're 6 or 7 years old. A mother has a baby only about every 7 to 9 years, so she raises just 4 or 5 in her lifetime. Daughters may stay close into their teens, watching their mother raise younger siblings. That's how they pick up the job themselves.

mascot.line: Dad does the pregnancy, then everyone swims off. Short parenting, very dramatic.

cards.fact: In seahorses, the father gets pregnant.
cards.context: The female places her eggs in a brood pouch at the base of the male's tail. He carries them for between 10 days and six weeks, depending on the species, then pushes the young out through an opening in the pouch. Care by the father alone is rare, but seahorse and pipefish males carry the eggs. Once born, the babies are on their own.

levels.title: Tool Use
levels.objective: After this level you can describe animals that use tools, from chimpanzees to crows.
levels.summary: In 1960 Goodall saw chimps make and use termite-fishing tools. Sea otters crack prey with rocks; veined octopuses carry coconut shells for later shelter.

cards.headline: In 1960, a chimpanzee got humans to rethink what makes them human.
cards.body: Making and using tools was thought to set people apart from every other animal. Then, at Gombe in Tanzania, Jane Goodall watched a chimp she had named David Greybeard sitting at a termite mound.

cards.headline: Fishing for termites
cards.body: David Greybeard poked a stem of grass into the termite mound, then raised it to his mouth. Soon after, Goodall saw chimps pick leafy twigs and strip off the leaves before fishing with them. That was tool making, never seen before. When she told her mentor, Louis Leakey, he replied that we must now redefine man or accept chimpanzees as human.

cards.headline: Otters with hammers
cards.body: A 2024 study followed 196 radio-tagged southern sea otters in California. They use rocks, shells and even trash to crack open prey. Tool users, mostly females, could eat harder and larger prey and had less tooth damage, which matters: badly worn teeth can mean starvation. Researchers think females make up for smaller bodies and weaker bites this way, since raising pups takes a lot of energy. A rock is cheaper than a dentist.

mascot.line: Packing your house for later. That's planning, with eight arms.

cards.fact: An octopus that carries its house.
cards.context: Veined octopuses in Indonesia dig up coconut shell halves, carry them under their bodies while walking awkwardly on stiffened arms, and later join them into a shelter. A hermit crab's shell doesn't count as a tool, because it's useful all the time. The coconut only pays off later, once the octopus needs a hiding place. Reported in 2009, it was the first known tool use by an invertebrate.

levels.title: How Smart Are Animals?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how scientists test animal intelligence.
levels.summary: Gallup's 1970 mirror test marks an animal where only a mirror shows it. Few species pass, often not every individual, and it is a sight test that dogs fail.

cards.headline: A chimp reaches for a red mark on its face that it can see only in a mirror.
cards.body: In 1970, psychologist Gordon Gallup Jr. marked chimpanzees with red dye, then gave them a mirror. The chimps used it to examine the marks on their own bodies. So does that mean they know who's in the mirror? And what about animals that fail?

cards.headline: How the mark test works
cards.body: The test runs in stages. First, the animal gets used to the mirror; many attack their reflection, as if it's a rival. Next, they often make odd movements, as if checking who controls the image. Finally, a colored mark goes where the animal can only see it in the mirror. If it pokes at the mark while watching its reflection, it passes.

cards.fact: Few species pass, and not every individual.
cards.context: Great apes, dolphins, elephants and magpies are on the short list. In 2006, researchers at the Bronx Zoo tested three Asian elephants. Only Happy clearly passed, repeatedly touching a white X painted on one side of her head. An invisible mark on the other side checked that she wasn't just reacting to feel or smell. One elephant out of three is a result, not a verdict on every elephant.

mascot.line: Good science: even the test's inventor stays skeptical of a surprising pass.

cards.headline: A test built for eyes
cards.body: Passing is impressive; failing proves less. Dogs usually fail, but dogs live by smell more than sight. In a 2017 smell version of the test, dogs sniffed their own urine longer when an extra odor had been added to it. And when cleaner wrasse fish scraped at marks in 2019, Gallup himself doubted it: they might just be reacting to what looked like a parasite. The mirror asks one question, in one sense.

levels.title: Play
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why young animals play.
levels.summary: Play costs energy yet young animals do it. Canids bow to invite play and keep it fair. Play-deprived rats grow up anxious, so play seems to train social judgment.

cards.headline: Play looks like a waste of energy. Young animals do it anyway.
cards.body: Play has no obvious immediate purpose. It burns energy, and it's noisy and conspicuous: two play-fighting rats could easily catch a hungry hawk's eye. So why does it exist?

cards.headline: "This is just a game"
cards.body: Play fighting uses bites and body slams that could be mistaken for the real thing, so players signal first. Dogs, wolves and coyotes bow: front legs down, back end up. The bow is used almost only in play and always looks the same. After a bow, even growls and bites draw submission or avoidance only about 15 percent of the time. The bow is a promise.

cards.headline: Playing fair
cards.body: Players also hold back. A stronger coyote may not bite as hard as it can, and a dominant animal may roll onto its back to let a weaker partner win for a while. Young rats with the upper hand often give it up the same way. A game where one side always wins stops being a game.

mascot.line: So recess is brain training. I always suspected.

cards.fact: Rats that never play grow up anxious.
cards.context: The old idea was that play is practice for fighting. But play fighting often skips the real moves: young elk lock horns in play, yet never butt heads, which is saved for serious fights. Young rats kept from play fighting grow up anxious, overreact to other rats, and later handle courtship poorly. Researchers think play trains the brain to adjust behavior to the situation.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Animal Behavior
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how instinct, learning and groups shape animal behavior.
levels.summary: The 1973 Nobel honored von Frisch (bee dances), Lorenz (imprinting) and Tinbergen, whose dummy bills showed exaggerated features make supernormal stimuli.

cards.headline: Animal Behavior finale: one prize, three scientists, three animals.
cards.body: In 1973, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to three people who studied animal behavior: Karl von Frisch, Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen. You've met two of them already. Let's line them up, then see Tinbergen's trick with fake beaks.

items.label: Karl von Frisch
points: Decoded the round and waggle dances

mascot.line: A cardboard bill outscoring a real parent. Instinct is a fast shortcut, not a careful judge.

cards.fact: A fake can beat the real thing.
cards.context: Lorenz found that many instinctive acts are set off only by specific key stimuli. Tinbergen tested which features of a gull's bill trigger a chick's begging pecks, using dummies and varying shape, colors and contrasts. Exaggerate the right features and you get a supernormal stimulus: a fake that draws a stronger response than the real parent. That's why Level 71's chick aims at the red spot: the spot is the key, not the whole parent. The chick isn't recognizing Mom. It's answering a few key signals.

levels.title: Darwin's Voyage
levels.objective: After this level you can describe what Darwin saw on the voyage of the Beagle.
levels.summary: Darwin sailed on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836. He dug up giant sloths related to living ones and saw Galápagos mockingbirds differ by island. The Origin followed in 1859.

cards.headline: In 1831, a 22-year-old boarded HMS Beagle for a five-year trip.
cards.body: Charles Darwin sailed as a companion to the ship's captain, Robert FitzRoy. He came back in 1836 with plants, animals, fossils and notebooks full of field notes. Hidden in that luggage were the clues to one of the biggest ideas in biology. What did he see?

cards.headline: Giant sloths in the ground
cards.body: In Argentina, Darwin dug fossil skulls, thighbones and armor plates out of the ground. Among them were giant ground sloths such as Megatherium, which weighed up to four tonnes. Yet this extinct giant was related to the sloths alive today. Why would the dead giants of a place be family of its living animals?

mascot.line: Every scientist has a box of unlabeled samples. Darwin's just became the most famous one.

cards.fact: Darwin labeled his mockingbirds by island. His finches, not so much.
cards.context: The Beagle reached the Galápagos Islands in September 1835. Darwin noticed the mockingbirds differed on four islands, so he tagged each one with its island. His other birds, which he took for wrens, finches and 'gross-beaks', went home without island labels. Neighboring islands, different mockingbirds: that detail would matter.

cards.headline: The verdict from London
cards.body: Back in England, the bird expert John Gould sorted the specimens. In 1837 he reported that the mockingbirds were three species, each unique to different islands, and that Darwin's mixed bag of wrens, finches and 'gross-beaks' were all ground finches. Neighbors, but not the same species. Darwin began asking how they had diverged from ancestors that arrived from the mainland. His answer came out in 1859: On the Origin of Species.

levels.title: Natural Selection
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how natural selection works.
levels.summary: Natural selection needs variation, differential reproduction and heredity. The Grants saw a 1977 drought favor big-beaked finches, whose young inherited bigger beaks.

cards.headline: Two biologists planned a two-year finch study. It ran for 40.
cards.body: In 1973, Peter and Rosemary Grant began catching and measuring Darwin's finches on Daphne Major in the Galápagos. They expected a short project. Instead, a drought gave them a front-row seat to the idea Darwin's voyage started. First, the idea.

cards.headline: Three ingredients, no chef
cards.body: The National Academies define natural selection as organisms with helpful variations leaving more offspring than others. It needs three ingredients. Variation: some beetles are green, some brown. Differential reproduction: birds eat more green beetles, so brown ones leave more young. Heredity: the young inherit their parents' color. Repeat for generations and brown takes over. Nobody plans it. The birds just keep eating.

mascot.line: Same island, same birds, different menu. The beak that fits the food wins.

cards.fact: In 1977, only 24 millimeters of rain fell on Daphne Major.
cards.context: The small seeds ran out. Medium ground finches, whose short beaks suit small seeds, faced a menu of big, hard ones, and most of the island's finches died. The survivors were the medium ground finches with larger beaks, strong enough to crack the larger seeds. Variation and unequal survival, in one dry year.

cards.headline: The next generation
cards.body: Now the third ingredient. Beak size is inherited, so the survivors' young had measurably larger beaks. The population had changed in about two years. Then the heavy rains of 1982-83 brought plentiful small seeds, smaller-beaked finches fed better, and the average beak slid back down. Selection doesn't aim for bigger. It follows the food.

levels.title: Fossils
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how fossils form and what they show.
levels.summary: Fossils are rare; quick burial lets minerals turn bone to stone, so around 99% are sea animals. Lower rock layers are older, and dated ash layers give ages.

cards.headline: Most living things vanish without a trace when they die.
cards.body: They rot away completely. Yet Darwin could still pull a giant sloth out of the ground. So what does it take for a body to turn to stone, and how can a stack of rock tell you when it lived?

cards.headline: How bone becomes stone
cards.body: The usual route is petrification. An animal dies and its soft parts rot, often leaving only bones and teeth, like the vertebrae of Level 3's backbone. Mud, sand or silt buries them before they vanish. More layers pile on and press down until they become sedimentary rock, while water seeping through leaves minerals in the bones, turning them to stone. It takes thousands or even millions of years. Slow cooking, extreme edition.

mascot.line: Somewhere in a museum drawer, very old poo is being handled with great respect.

cards.fact: Around 99% of the fossils we find are from sea animals.
cards.context: Shellfish and sharks lived where sand or mud could bury them quickly, and quick burial is the whole trick. Not every fossil is a body part, either. Bones, teeth and shells are body fossils. Footprints, skin impressions and fossil dung are trace fossils. Yes, fossil dung has a name: coprolites.

cards.headline: Reading the layers
cards.body: Rock builds up like laundry in a hamper: the newest lands on top. So in undisturbed layers, lower fossils are older than higher ones, a rule called superposition. For real dates, geologists measure radioactive elements, which decay at known rates, in volcanic ash above and below a fossil. That's how one set of trilobites was pinned between 520 and 545 million years old. Compare layers worldwide and you get the geologic timescale.

levels.title: The Age of Dinosaurs
levels.objective: After this level you can describe when dinosaurs lived and how varied they were.
levels.summary: Non-bird dinosaurs lived about 245 to 66 million years ago, through the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous. As Pangaea split, they evolved apart and diversified.

cards.headline: Tyrannosaurus lived closer in time to you than to Stegosaurus.
cards.body: Posters love to put them side by side. They never met. Stegosaurus had been extinct for about 80 million years before Tyrannosaurus appeared. The Age of Dinosaurs wasn't one scene. It was a story long enough to need chapters.

events.label: Triassic: the first dinosaurs, around 245 million years ago
Jurassic: giant sauropods and Stegosaurus

cards.headline: One supercontinent, then many
cards.body: When dinosaurs first appeared, all the land was one supercontinent, Pangaea, so animals in different places were much alike. After a mass extinction at the end of the Triassic, the dinosaurs survived and spread into new forms. Then Pangaea broke apart. Dinosaurs ended up on separate continents and evolved independently, like cousins raised in different countries. The result: more and more kinds of dinosaur.

mascot.line: Dinosaurs own the walking record. The whale owns the whole trophy cabinet.

cards.fact: Some sauropods were among the largest animals ever to walk the Earth.
cards.context: Plentiful Jurassic plants fed plant-eaters like Diplodocus and Brachiosaurus, and in the Cretaceous the titanosaurs grew bigger still. Yet Level 9's title holder keeps its crown: the blue whale is the largest animal known to have lived. The giants of the land walked. The biggest of all swims today.

levels.title: Birds Are Dinosaurs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the evidence that birds descend from dinosaurs.
levels.summary: Birds evolved from small theropod dinosaurs. Archaeopteryx mixed feathers with teeth and a bony tail; Sinosauropteryx had feathers. Birds outlived the other dinosaurs.

cards.headline: The pigeon on your windowsill is a dinosaur.
cards.body: Not dinosaur-ish. A dinosaur, from the same group of meat-eaters as Tyrannosaurus rex. It sounds like a joke until you see the fossils. So what's the evidence?

cards.fact: Archaeopteryx had feathers, teeth and a long bony tail.
cards.context: Its fossils, about 150 million years old, turned up in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany starting in 1861, two years after Darwin's Origin. It had feathered wings like a bird, but also well-developed teeth, three clawed fingers and a long bony tail like smaller dinosaurs. Its skeleton shares many features with a group of theropods. Part bird, part dinosaur, right on the line.

mascot.line: Picture a fluffy little dinosaur. Now you've pictured it correctly.

cards.headline: Feathers came first
cards.body: In 1996, a fossil hunter in China found Sinosauropteryx, a small meat-eating theropod covered in thin, hair-like feathers. It wasn't directly related to birds. It was the first feathered dinosaur discovered outside the bird line. So feathers weren't a bird invention at all. They were already on dinosaurs.

cards.headline: The dinosaurs that made it
cards.body: Birds evolved from small theropods, the meat-eating group that includes T. rex. The oldest bird-like fossils, over 150 million years old, still had sharp teeth; beaks came later. When the end-Cretaceous extinction struck 66 million years ago, every other dinosaur died out. Birds didn't. So the birds on Level 1's list of five vertebrate groups are living dinosaurs too. You've probably heard one this morning.

cards.headline: The clue in the clay
cards.body: In 1980, physicist Luis Alvarez and his geologist son Walter studied a thin layer of clay found around the world at the end of the Cretaceous. It was rich in iridium, a metal rare on Earth but more abundant in meteorites. Their idea: a huge asteroid impact. It was controversial at first. Then there's the crater, Chicxulub, centred on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula and the same age as the extinction. Today it's the most widely accepted explanation.

mascot.line: One bad afternoon for the dinosaurs, a very long one for the food chain.

cards.fact: The asteroid was about 10 to 15 km wide.
cards.context: It hit so hard it vaporised, throwing debris and soot into the sky. Less sunlight meant less plant growth, and the damage climbed Level 7's food chain: fewer plants, then starving herbivores, then hungry carnivores. Volcanic eruptions in India were already stressing life, but the asteroid was the final blow.

levels.title: From Water to Land
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how fish-like animals first came onto land.
levels.summary: Tiktaalik, a 375-million-year-old fish, had gills and scales plus a neck and wrist-like fin bones. It was found in rocks of the age its finders predicted.

cards.headline: Every time you bend your wrist, thank a fish.
cards.body: So says Neil Shubin, and he means a real fish that lived in streams 375 million years ago. He helped find it, and his team knew roughly where to look before they started digging.

cards.headline: They predicted where to dig
cards.body: Earlier research suggested the move onto land happened about 375 million years ago, in rivers. So the team hunted in 375-million-year-old rocks that had preserved a river delta. In 2004, on Ellesmere Island in Arctic Canada, a team led by Neil Shubin, Edward Daeschler and Farish Jenkins found it: Tiktaalik. The National Academy of Sciences cites it as a prediction of evolutionary theory confirmed. Not dig and hope. Dig where the theory points.

cards.headline: A fish that did push-ups
cards.body: Tiktaalik was still a fish. But its sturdy fin bones let it prop itself up in shallow water, and its neck let it turn its head while its body rested on the bottom. Its shoulder, elbow and wrist use the same bones as your upper arm, forearm and wrist. It sits on the path to the four-legged vertebrates: amphibians, dinosaurs, birds and mammals, you included.

levels.title: Whales Once Walked
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how whales evolved from land mammals.
levels.summary: Whales' ancestors walked on land about 50 million years ago. Pakicetus had a whale-like ear, Ambulocetus paddled, Dorudon kept tiny hind legs; hippos are cousins.

cards.headline: The blue whale's ancestors walked on four legs.
cards.body: About 50 million years ago, the family that would one day produce the largest animal known to have lived was on land. How did a land mammal end up in the open ocean, and what gives the secret away?

cards.headline: The giveaway is in the ear
cards.body: From the outside, Pakicetus looked like a typical land mammal: long skull, large meat-eating teeth, four legs. But the inner ear region of its skull, wrapped in a bony wall, strongly resembles living whales' and no other mammal's. Ambulocetus adds a chemical clue: oxygen isotopes in its bones show it drank both salt water and fresh, just right for an estuary. Small details, big family secret.

mascot.line: Next time a whale waves its tail, picture a dog mid-gallop. Same backbone move.

cards.fact: A whale's tail beats up and down, like a running dog's back.
cards.context: Fish swim by swinging their tails side to side. Whales move theirs up and down, because they evolved from walking land mammals whose backbones bend that way. And their closest living relatives? Hippos, but as cousins, not ancestors. The ancestors of both lived on land.

levels.title: Peppered Moths
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the peppered moth as evolution people could watch.
levels.summary: Dark peppered moths spread as soot hid them from birds, then declined as the air cleaned. Majerus's experiment, published in 2012, confirmed bird predation.

cards.headline: In 1848, a black peppered moth turned up in Manchester.
cards.body: Peppered moths were normally light-colored. By 1898, dark moths there outnumbered light ones 99 to 1. That's evolution fast enough to watch from a city window. What happened?

cards.headline: Soot changes the hiding game
cards.body: Peppered moths rest on tree bark by day, and birds hunt them there. Then the Industrial Revolution coated trees in coal soot and killed the pale lichens. A light moth on black bark stood out; a dark one blended in. Birds ate more light moths and fewer dark ones, and the dark form took over. It's Level 82's beetles again, with wings.

cards.headline: Then the air cleaned up
cards.body: Once the soot eased, the story ran in reverse: since about 1970, dark peppered moths in Britain have rapidly become rarer. But some scientists attacked the classic experiments and doubted that birds were really the cause. Someone had to test it properly.

mascot.line: Six years of moth-watching, finished by friends. Science can be a team sport.

cards.fact: Michael Majerus released 4,864 moths to settle the question.
cards.context: Over six years near Cambridge, the largest experiment of its kind, he let moths settle naturally at low density and watched the birds. Birds took dark moths more often than pale ones, enough to explain their decline. Majerus died in 2009 before publishing, so colleagues analysed his data and published it in 2012: the most direct evidence yet for camouflage and bird predation.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Evolution
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how natural selection and fossils show that life changes over time.
levels.summary: In science a theory is an explanation backed by vast evidence. This chapter caught evolution being watched (finches, moths) and dug up (Archaeopteryx, Tiktaalik, Pakicetus).

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: 'Evolution is just a theory.' Yes, in the science sense.
cards.body: In everyday talk, a theory is a hunch. In science, it's the top of the ladder. This chapter gave you the evidence. Here's what the word really means, and how the pieces fit.

cards.headline: A hunch or a heavyweight?
cards.body: When you say 'I have a theory', you usually mean a guess. In science, a theory is a comprehensive explanation of some part of nature, backed by a vast body of evidence, like the theory that living things are made of cells. Evolution is a theory in that sense. The National Academy of Sciences says there is no scientific controversy about its basic facts: it has survived testing by many thousands of scientists for more than a century.

levels.title: Domestication
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how people tamed dogs, cattle and horses.
levels.summary: Taming changes one animal; domestication changes a line over generations. All cattle trace to about 80 aurochs; modern horses to the Volga-Don steppe around 2200 BCE.

cards.headline: Every farmed cow on Earth descends from about 80 wild animals.
cards.body: They were aurochs, wild oxen, and they were no pushovers: just keeping them captive was hard work. So how does a wild animal become a farm animal, and what did people change along the way?

cards.headline: Tame is not the same as domesticated
cards.body: A tamed animal is one individual that has learned to put up with people. Its heredity hasn't changed. Domestication goes deeper: over many generations, people choose which animals breed, and choosing calm, docile animals has been central to it. The changes pass from parent to young. Dogs came first, domesticated by hunter-gatherers before anyone farmed. Taming takes one lifetime. Domestication takes many.

mascot.line: Eighty ancestors for every cow alive. That's one very crowded family tree.

cards.fact: All domestic cattle trace back to a small herd of aurochs.
cards.context: DNA from ancient cattle bones dug up in Iran points to about 80 aurochs, domesticated in the Near East about 10,500 years ago. Their wild relatives didn't last. The aurochs survived in central Poland until 1627, then vanished. The wild ox is gone; its farmyard descendants are the line that stayed.

cards.headline: Horses: bred for calm and a strong back
cards.body: Ancient DNA from 273 horses shows where today's domestic horses began: the western Eurasian steppes, especially the lower Volga-Don region, around 2200 BCE. From there they spread across Eurasia and replaced other horses. Two genetic changes stand out in them: one linked to more docile behavior, one pointing to a stronger backbone. People weren't just catching horses. They were breeding better ones to ride.

levels.title: Farm Animals
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the animals that help feed the world.
levels.summary: Livestock are about 60% of Earth's mammals by mass, and poultry outweighs wild birds. Chickens come from the red junglefowl; cattle are ruminants that chew cud.

cards.headline: Weigh every mammal on Earth, and most of the scale is farm animals.
cards.body: A 2018 census of life measured living things by their carbon mass. Wild mammals barely register. So which animals fill the farms, and what do they do for us?

mascot.line: The most successful bird on the planet may have started its career as a fighter.

cards.fact: Chickens outweigh all the world's wild birds, almost three times over.
cards.context: The same 2018 census found domestic poultry, mostly chickens, has almost three times the mass of every wild bird combined. And chickens may not have started out as food. They descend from the red junglefowl, a wild bird of Asia, and the first ones may have been kept for religious reasons or as fighting birds. Dinner came later.

cards.headline: A cow chews its lunch twice
cards.body: Cattle give us meat, milk, hides and pulling power. Early domestic cows made only enough milk for their calves; big dairy yields came much later, through selective breeding. Their fuel is grass, which is tough stuff. Like Level 6's panda, a cow can't digest cellulose on its own. Cattle, sheep and goats are ruminants: they bring swallowed food back up as cud and chew it again.

levels.title: Endangered Species
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why species become endangered.
levels.summary: The IUCN Red List ranks species from Least Concern to Extinct; three rungs count as threatened. In 2025, 47,187 of 169,420 evaluated species were. Habitat loss leads.

cards.headline: 47,187 species are officially threatened with extinction.
cards.body: That's the count in the IUCN Red List, version 2025-1, from March 2025: the world's main scorecard for species at risk. What do its labels mean, and why do species end up on it?

cards.headline: A ladder from safe to gone
cards.body: The Red List puts each assessed species on one rung of a ladder: Least Concern, Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild, Extinct. Three middle rungs, Vulnerable, Endangered and Critically Endangered, together count as threatened. Two extra labels sit off the ladder: Data Deficient (not enough is known) and Not Evaluated. Threatened isn't one label. It's three rungs of the same ladder.

cards.fact: About 41 percent of amphibian species are threatened.
cards.context: That's IUCN's best estimate in version 2025-1, against about 27 percent of mammals. Across all 169,420 species evaluated, 47,187 are threatened. Remember Level 2's 1.5 million named animals, a million of them insects? Only about 1 percent of described insect species have been evaluated at all. The list is a partial census, not a full one.

mascot.line: One rung up is real progress. It's also a reminder of how many rungs are left.

cards.headline: Why species slide down the ladder
cards.body: The most pervasive threat is habitat loss: land cleared for farms, logging and building. Introduced species, climate change, pollution, overhunting and disease pile on. Level 6's giant panda shows both sides. Logging and clearing broke its forest into patches, isolating small groups, and as few as 1,864 live wild. Yet in 2016 IUCN moved it from Endangered to Vulnerable. One rung up, still on the ladder.

levels.title: Gone in Our Time
levels.objective: After this level you can describe animals lost in recent centuries, like the dodo.
levels.summary: The dodo was gone by the late 1600s; passenger pigeons fell from billions to Martha (1914); the thylacine was protected in July 1936, two months before the last one died.

cards.headline: The last passenger pigeon had a name: Martha.
cards.body: She died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914, and her species died with her. She wasn't the first animal lost in modern times, or the last. Here are three, and in every one, people played the leading part.

cards.fact: The dodo was a flightless relative of pigeons.
cards.context: It lived only on Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean. When sailors arrived, they hunted it, and the animals they brought ashore, pigs, dogs, cats and rats, preyed on it too. A bird that couldn't fly, on an island it couldn't leave, had nowhere to go. It was gone by the late 1600s.

mascot.line: A huge number is not the same as a safe number.

cards.headline: From billions to one
cards.body: When Europeans arrived in North America, there were an estimated 3 to 5 billion passenger pigeons, and migrating flocks darkened the sky for days. People slaughtered them by the millions each year and shipped them by the railway carload to city markets. Martha outlived them all. When she died in 1914, her body was frozen in a block of ice and sent to the Smithsonian.

cards.headline: A 'tiger' that was really a marsupial
cards.body: The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, wasn't a cat. It was the largest meat-eating marsupial of recent times, with dark stripes across its back, and in historic times it lived only in Tasmania. Settlers there hunted it as a threat to their sheep.

cards.headline: Protection came two months too late

levels.title: Saving Species
levels.objective: After this level you can describe conservation successes, like the bald eagle.
levels.summary: DDT left 417 bald eagle pairs in 1963; after the 1972 ban they recovered. Condors bred in captivity now number over 500. Humpbacks rebounded after whaling stopped.

cards.headline: By 1987, every wild California condor had been caught on purpose.
cards.body: North America's largest land bird, with a 9.5-foot wingspan, was down so far that all the remaining wild ones went into a captive breeding program. A last resort. Did it work? And what saved the bald eagle and the humpback whale?

cards.headline: The eagle and the eggshell
cards.body: The pesticide DDT washed into rivers and lakes, where water plants and fish absorbed it. Bald eagles ate the fish and took in the poison too. It made their eggshells so thin that eggs often broke during incubation. By 1963, only 417 nesting pairs were known in the lower 48 states. The poison didn't have to kill the adults. It just had to stop the next generation.

mascot.line: From 417 pairs to more than 71,000. That's a comeback worth saluting.

cards.fact: Bald eagles: from 417 nesting pairs to about 316,700 birds.
cards.context: The US banned DDT in 1972, and the eagles rebuilt. In 2007, the bald eagle came off the list of threatened and endangered species. A USFWS estimate from 2018 and 2019 surveys counts about 316,700 bald eagles in the lower 48 states, including 71,467 breeding pairs. Remove the poison, and the eagles did the rest.

cards.headline: Condors and humpbacks
cards.body: Captive-bred condors have been going back to the wild since 1992, and the total population is now more than 500. Their top known killer is lead, from ammunition fragments scavenging condors swallow. Humpback whales needed something simpler: people had to stop hunting them. Whaling had cut most populations by more than 95 percent before a final moratorium in 1985. In 2016, NOAA found 9 of 14 humpback populations no longer needed listing.

levels.title: Invasive Species
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how animals brought to new places can harm them.
levels.summary: An invasive species harms a place where it isn't native. Cane toads missed Queensland's beetles and spread; brown treesnakes helped wipe out 9 of Guam's 11 forest birds.

cards.headline: In 1935, Australia imported toads to eat beetles. The beetles barely noticed.
cards.body: Queensland's sugarcane farmers had a beetle problem, so cane toads were released to eat them. The toads thrived; the beetles carried on. Today cane toads number in the millions. So when does a newcomer become a problem?

cards.headline: In the wrong place, doing harm
cards.body: An invasive species is one that causes ecological or economic harm in a place where it isn't native. Most get there with people's help, on purpose or by accident. Once there, they can compete with native animals for food and space, change habitats and even drive native species extinct. Being new isn't the problem. Doing damage is.

mascot.line: Hired to fix one problem, became a much bigger one. We've all had a week like that.

cards.fact: Cane toads now number in the millions in Australia.
cards.context: In 1935, 2,400 were released on Queensland sugarcane farms to control beetles. They had little or no effect on the beetles, but they spread across northeastern Australia, and they're still moving west about 40 to 60 km a year. Their poison kills many native predators that try to eat them. The pest control became the pest.

cards.headline: A stowaway on Guam
cards.body: The brown treesnake is native to places such as New Guinea and Australia. During or soon after World War II, it reached Guam hidden in cargo. There it helped wipe out 9 of the island's 11 native forest bird species. It even climbs power lines and causes expensive outages. Guam's forests lost most of their native birds to one hitchhiker.

levels.title: Zoos and Wildlife Parks
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what modern zoos try to do.
levels.summary: The Arabian oryx returned from zoo and royal herds to reach Vulnerable in 2011. AZA sees zoos as conservation centers; Born Free argues such successes are rare.

cards.headline: The Arabian oryx vanished from the wild in 1972. Zoo herds brought it back.
cards.body: The last wild one is believed to have been shot in Oman. Ten years later, oryx were running free there again. It's one of the strongest cases for zoos, and it's also where the argument about zoos begins.

cards.headline: Nine oryx in Phoenix
cards.body: As the oryx disappeared, some of the last ones were captured to start a 'World Herd'. It began at the Phoenix Zoo with nine animals. With royal herds in Arabia, it supplied oryx for reintroduction: first in Oman in 1982, then in other countries. By 2011 about 1,000 lived wild, and IUCN moved the species to Vulnerable. No species once Extinct in the Wild had climbed three full categories before.

cards.headline: One success, read two ways
cards.body: The Association of Zoos and Aquariums counts conservation breeding, like the oryx herds, among zoos' core jobs. The Born Free Foundation argues that pointing to a handful of reintroductions risks suggesting there are many more, and that such cases can't justify keeping large numbers of animals that aren't threatened. One side sees a model; the other sees an exception.

levels.title: Animals in Space
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the animals that flew in space before humans.
levels.summary: Fruit flies went first (1947). Laika was the first creature in orbit (1957) and died within hours. Belka and Strelka came home in 1960; Ham flew in 1961, before Gagarin.

cards.headline: The first animals in space were fruit flies.
cards.body: In 1947 they rode a rocket up and came back alive. Why send animals into space before people, and what did it cost them?

cards.headline: Could a body survive up there?
cards.body: Nobody knew what spaceflight would do to a living body. One big worry was that people might not survive long periods of weightlessness. Radiation was another unknown. So on 20 February 1947, fruit flies went up on a V-2 rocket; they were small, light and easy to store. Back on the ground, scientists found no radiation-caused changes to their genetics. The tiniest passengers cleared the way.

cards.fact: Laika was the first living creature to orbit Earth.
cards.context: She was a stray from the streets of Moscow, launched on Sputnik 2 on November 3, 1957. The spacecraft had no way to bring her home, and she died from overheating about five to seven hours into the flight. For years, Soviet officials said she had lived for days; the truth came out in 2002. Today a statue honors her in Moscow.

levels.title: Ideas From Animals
levels.objective: After this level you can name inventions inspired by animals, like Velcro.
levels.summary: Biomimicry copies nature's designs: Velcro from burdock burrs, a Shinkansen nose from a kingfisher's beak, and NASA grippers from gecko toe hairs.

cards.headline: Velcro began as burrs stuck in a dog's fur.
cards.body: Burrs come from burdock, a plant, not an animal. But the idea behind Velcro, copying designs that living things already use, has a name: biomimicry. And animals have handed engineers some brilliant designs.

cards.headline: Hooks meet loops
cards.body: Near Lausanne, Switzerland, George de Mestral came home from a walk with burdock burrs stuck to his clothes and his dog's fur. Under a microscope, each burr was covered in tiny hooks. He paired hooks with fabric loops and patented the fastener in 1955. The name blends two French words: velours, velvet, and crochet, hook. Nature drew the plans; he did the sewing.

mascot.line: Diving into water, entering a tunnel: same problem, same solution.

cards.fact: A bird's beak quieted a bullet train.
cards.context: Early Shinkansen trains made a loud 'tunnel boom' as they left tunnels, disturbing people nearby. Engineers turned to the kingfisher, whose long, pointed beak lets it dive into water with barely a splash. JR West's 500 Series, in service from 1997, got a nose shaped like that beak. The booms stopped, and the train ran faster on less electricity.

cards.headline: Sticky without glue
cards.body: Geckos are small reptiles that climb smooth walls on toe pads covered in tiny hairs, the smallest hundreds of times thinner than a human hair. They stick by van der Waals forces: weak, temporary attractions between atoms. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory copied the trick with synthetic hairs that grip when pressed and let go when the force is removed. They even work in a vacuum, handy for grabbing things in space.

levels.title: Your Cosmic Address
levels.objective: After this level you can state Earth's address: third planet from the Sun, a star in the Milky Way.
levels.summary: The Sun is a star, Earth is planet three, and our whole solar system lives in the Milky Way.

cards.headline: Every star you see at night is a sun. Ours is just the closest one.
cards.body: That little twinkle you wish on? It's a sun. It looks tiny for one reason only: it's unbelievably far away.

cards.headline: Your cosmic mailing address
cards.body: If aliens wanted to mail you a postcard, they'd need a long address. Line one: Earth. Line two: the third planet from the Sun, with two neighbors closer in and five farther out. Line three: the solar system, which is just the Sun plus everything swinging around it. And we're not done yet.
cards.callout: Earth → planet 3 → the solar system

mascot.line: You're always seeing the Sun a little late. I've been late my whole life, so this one I love.

cards.fact: The Sun you see is 8 minutes old.
cards.context: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us, so the Sun in the sky is the Sun from 8 minutes ago. If it vanished right now, you'd keep seeing it for about 8 more minutes. Light is the fastest thing there is. The Sun is just that far away.

cards.headline: Last line: the Milky Way
cards.body: The final line on the envelope is the Milky Way, a spiral of at least 100 billion stars. We live out in the suburbs, about 26,000 light-years from downtown. On a dark night, that hazy stripe across the sky is the rest of our galaxy. You're looking at your own neighborhood from the sidewalk.

levels.objective: After this level you can explain what powers the Sun and how dominant it is in the solar system.
levels.summary: The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, holds 99.8% of the solar system's mass, and is about 4.6 billion years old.

cards.headline: The Sun isn't on fire. It's doing something far stranger.
cards.body: Picture the Sun as a giant bonfire? Wrong picture. It has been shining for about 4.6 billion years, and no fire lasts that long. Something much stranger is going on inside.

cards.headline: A star that squeezes atoms
cards.body: Deep in the Sun's core it's about 15 million °C. At that heat, hydrogen atoms slam together so hard that they fuse into helium, and every crash releases a tiny spark of energy. One spark is nothing. But the core does this an almost unimaginable number of times every second, and all those sparks add up to every bit of sunshine you've ever felt.
cards.callout: Hydrogen → helium + energy

cards.fact: The Sun holds about 99.8% of the solar system's mass.
cards.context: Every planet, moon, asteroid and comet put together? That's the other 0.2%. We're the crumbs. If the Sun were as tall as your front door, Earth would be about the size of a nickel. No wonder everything circles it: the Sun's gravity is what holds the whole solar system together.

cards.headline: Middle-aged, not old
cards.body: 4.6 billion years sounds ancient, until you learn that a star like ours can keep fusing hydrogen for about 10 billion years. So the Sun isn't old at all. It's middle-aged, with billions of good years of shining still ahead of it.

levels.title: The Rocky Four
levels.objective: After this level you can name the rocky planets and explain why Venus, not Mercury, is the hottest.
levels.summary: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are rocky. Venus is the hottest planet thanks to its heat-trapping atmosphere, and Mars is red because of rust.

cards.headline: Mercury is closest to the Sun. So why is Venus hotter?
cards.body: You'd bet on Mercury, right? It's the closest planet to the Sun. You'd lose that bet. The winner is hiding under a thick blanket next door.

cards.headline: The rocky four
cards.body: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are small worlds of rock and metal. You could stand on any of them. You wouldn't enjoy most of them. Take Mercury: about 430 °C in the day, then about −180 °C at night. It's the closest planet to the Sun, and it still can't keep warm.
cards.callout: Mercury · Venus · Earth · Mars

cards.headline: Venus: a runaway greenhouse
cards.body: Venus wears a thick blanket of carbon dioxide. Sunlight gets in, but the heat can't get back out, so it piles up. The result is a surface over 450 °C, hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun. The air is so heavy that the pressure on the ground is about 90 times Earth's. Mercury gets the sunshine. Venus keeps the heat.

cards.fact: Mars is red because it's rusty.
cards.context: Seriously. Iron oxide, the same stuff as the rust on an old bike, coats Martian dust and rocks, and fine red dust in the air tints the whole planet. That air is thin, too: less than 1% of Earth's air pressure. Venus's air would crush you. Mars's barely shows up.

levels.title: Giants of the Outer Dark
levels.objective: After this level you can tell gas giants from ice giants and describe Jupiter's and Saturn's standout features.
levels.summary: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. Jupiter outweighs every other planet combined, and Saturn's rings are mostly ice.

cards.headline: Past Mars, the planets stop being rocky and start being enormous.
cards.body: Level 3's four worlds were small and rocky. Past Mars, the rules change. The next four planets are giants, and you couldn't land on a single one of them.

cards.fact: Jupiter has more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined.
cards.context: Remember the crumbs from Level 2, the 0.2% of the solar system that isn't the Sun? Jupiter is the biggest crumb by far. Put it on one side of a giant scale and every other planet on the other side. Jupiter wins. Double the pile and Jupiter still wins. If the planets were a team, Jupiter would be carrying it.

cards.headline: Saturn's rings are ice
cards.body: Those famous rings aren't a solid hoop you could walk around on. They're countless separate chunks of water ice, with a little rock mixed in. Some are as small as specks of dust. Others are as big as a house. So Saturn's rings are basically a giant field of hail. Some of the ice cubes are just the size of your home.

levels.title: Why We Have Seasons
levels.objective: After this level you can explain that seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun.
levels.summary: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. Each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun, which is why seasons are opposite north and south.

cards.headline: Most people get this one wrong: summer isn't when Earth is closest to the Sun.
cards.body: It's the obvious guess: summer is hot because Earth swings closer to the Sun. Nice guess. The calendar disagrees.

cards.fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
cards.context: That's the middle of winter in the Northern Hemisphere. If distance ran the seasons, New Year's Day would be beach weather in New York. Instead, northern summer arrives when Earth is farther from the Sun. So distance can't be what makes summer. Something else is in charge.

cards.headline: It's the tilt
cards.body: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. When your half of the planet leans toward the Sun, sunlight hits the ground more directly and days last longer, so more energy lands on each patch of ground. That's summer. Lean away, and the same sunlight arrives at a slant and spreads thin, like a flashlight beam tipped across a table. That's winter. Same Sun, different angle.
cards.callout: Tilt → angle of sunlight → season

cards.headline: Opposite seasons
cards.body: Here's the proof it's the lean. The two hemispheres tilt opposite ways, so they take turns. In December, New York shivers while Sydney has summer. In July it flips: summer up north, winter in Australia. Same planet, same trip around the Sun, opposite seasons. Somewhere on Earth, someone is always wearing a scarf.

levels.title: The Moon's Changing Face
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Moon phases and why we only ever see one side of the Moon.
levels.summary: Phases show how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces us, over a ~29.5-day cycle. The Moon is tidally locked, so the same side always faces Earth.

cards.headline: The Moon doesn't change shape. You're just seeing it from a different angle.
cards.body: Tonight a thin crescent, next week a full circle. The Moon seems to grow and shrink, but it's the same Moon the whole time. What changes is how you're looking at it.

cards.headline: Half lit, always
cards.body: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that sunlit half: a thin crescent, a half, the full face, then back again. Nothing is covering the Moon; only our viewing angle changes. Try it with a lamp and a ball held at arm's length, turning slowly, and you'll get phases in your living room.
cards.callout: One full cycle of phases: about 29.5 days

cards.fact: We always see the same side of the Moon.
cards.context: The Moon is tidally locked: it rotates exactly once per orbit, so the same face always points at us. Walk a circle around a chair while always facing it, and you'll have turned all the way around once too. And the 'dark side'? Not dark at all. The far side gets as much sunlight as the near side. We just never get to see it from Earth.

levels.title: Eclipses and a Cosmic Coincidence
levels.objective: After this level you can tell solar from lunar eclipses and explain why the Moon can exactly cover the Sun.
levels.summary: A solar eclipse is the Moon blocking the Sun; a lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow on the Moon. The Sun is ~400× wider and ~400× farther than the Moon.

cards.headline: By pure luck, the Moon is exactly the right size to blot out the Sun.
cards.body: The Sun is enormous and the Moon is small, yet the Moon can cover the Sun completely. It isn't design. It's a coincidence of two numbers.

cards.headline: Two kinds of eclipse: who's blocking whom?

The Moon's shadow falls on Earth

items.label: Lunar eclipse

Only happens at full Moon, when the Moon is on the far side of us

cards.fact: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, and about 400 times farther away.
cards.context: Those two numbers cancel out, so the Sun and Moon look almost exactly the same size in our sky. It's the same trick as hiding a faraway building behind your thumb. That's why, in a total solar eclipse, the Moon can cover the Sun's bright disc and reveal its faint outer glow, the corona. The Sun is 400 times bigger. It's also 400 times farther. Tie.

levels.title: Light-Years: Measuring the Unmeasurable
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a light-year measures and how far the nearest star is.
levels.summary: A light-year is a distance: about 9.46 trillion km. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

cards.headline: A light-year sounds like a unit of time. It isn't.
cards.body: It has 'year' right there in the name, so it's a fair guess. But a light-year is a ruler, not a clock.

cards.headline: Distance, measured in light
cards.body: A light-year is how far light travels in one year: about 9.46 trillion kilometers. So it's a distance, the way a mile is. Kilometers are great for a road trip. Out among the stars they pile up into numbers nobody can read, so astronomers switched to a bigger ruler.
cards.callout: 1 light-year ≈ 9.46 trillion km

cards.headline: Why measure space in light?
cards.body: Light is the fastest thing there is, which makes it a handy measuring tape. It crosses from the Moon to Earth in just over a second. From the Sun, it takes about 8 minutes (Level 1's slightly late Sun). So the Moon is about one light-second away and the Sun about 8 light-minutes. Past the Sun, even light needs years, and the ruler grows to match.

cards.fact: The closest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away.
cards.context: So its light takes about 4.2 years to reach us. Moon: a second. Sun: 8 minutes. Next star: more than four years. And that's the closest one; every other star is even farther. Proxima is our next-door neighbor. The street is just very, very long.

levels.title: The Life of a Star
levels.objective: After this level you can read a star's temperature from its color and outline how the Sun will end.
levels.summary: Stars are born in clouds of gas and dust. Blue stars are hottest, red coolest. The Sun will become a red giant and then a white dwarf; massive stars can go supernova.

cards.headline: Stars have a life story: birth, a long middle age, and a very dramatic ending.
cards.body: Level 2 told you the Sun is middle-aged. So what comes next? Here's the Sun's whole story, plus a trick for reading any star's temperature just by its color.

cards.headline: Color is temperature
cards.body: Look closely and stars have colors, and each color is a thermometer reading. Blue stars are the hottest; red stars are the coolest. That's backwards from your kitchen tap, where red means hot. The Sun sits in the middle: it shines white from space, and our air scatters away some of its blue light, so it looks yellowish from the ground.
cards.callout: Blue = hot · Red = cool

cards.headline: The Sun's life, in four stops

cards.headline: Bigger stars, bigger endings
cards.body: Relax: the Sun won't explode. It isn't massive enough. Stars much more massive than the Sun get a far louder exit: a supernova, an explosion that can briefly outshine a whole galaxy. Picture one dying star, for a moment, brighter than every other star in its galaxy put together. The Sun's quiet ending sounds better already.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Your Place in the Universe
levels.objective: After this level you can trace Earth's address from our planet all the way out to the observable universe.
levels.summary: The Milky Way is ~100,000 light-years across, Andromeda is ~2.5 million light-years away, and the observable universe holds billions of galaxies in a ~13.8-billion-year-old cosmos.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale. Let's zoom all the way out.
cards.body: Remember the cosmic mailing address from Level 1? Earth, the solar system, the Milky Way. Time to find out how big that last line is, and what lies beyond it.

cards.headline: Our galaxy
cards.body: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across. A light-year is a distance, so light leaving one edge would take about 100,000 years to reach the other. In Level 8, Proxima Centauri at 4.2 light-years felt far. Our galaxy is more than 20,000 times wider than that. The suburbs are big.

cards.fact: Andromeda, the nearest large spiral galaxy, is about 2.5 million light-years away.
cards.context: You could line up 25 Milky Ways in that gap. Yet on a dark night you can see Andromeda with the naked eye, as a faint smudge. That smudge is a whole galaxy, and the light reaching your eye took about 2.5 million years to get here.

cards.headline: And then everything else
cards.body: Andromeda is just one galaxy. The observable universe holds billions of galaxies, many with billions of stars each. And the universe itself is about 13.8 billion years old, about three times the Sun's age. So here's the full address: one planet, around one star, in one galaxy among billions.

levels.title: Why the Sky Turns
levels.objective: After this level you can explain that day and night, and the stars rising and setting, come from Earth spinning.
levels.summary: Earth spins once a day from west to east, so the Sun and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

cards.headline: The sky isn't turning. You are.
cards.body: Every sunrise looks like the Sun climbing up to meet you. It isn't going anywhere. Your patch of Earth is rolling toward it, and all night long the stars play the very same trick.

cards.headline: One spin, one day
cards.body: Earth spins on its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, about once every 24 hours. At any moment, the half facing the Sun has day and the half facing away has night. Nobody switches the Sun off at bedtime. Earth's spin simply carries your side of the planet from the sunny half into the dark one, and back again by breakfast.
cards.callout: One rotation ≈ one day

cards.headline: Why everything rises in the east
cards.body: Earth spins from west to east, so your eastern horizon turns toward the Sun first. From where you stand, the Sun seems to climb up in the east and sink in the west. The Moon, the planets and the stars do exactly the same, for exactly the same reason. They aren't parading around us. Earth's spin sweeps them all across the sky the same way, like scenery sliding past a train window.

cards.fact: At the equator, Earth's surface moves at about 1,670 km/h.
cards.context: So why don't you feel it? Because you, the ground and the air all move together at a steady speed. Nothing rushes past you, so there's no wind in your hair and no coffee in your lap. The whole planet is one very smooth ride.

cards.headline: Daily spin: understood

levels.title: A Year Around the Sun
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a year is, why leap years exist, and why the night sky changes with the seasons.
levels.summary: A year is one orbit of about 365.25 days. The quarter-days add up to leap days, and the night sky shifts as we orbit.

cards.headline: A year is just one lap.
cards.body: Every birthday, you've ridden once around the Sun since the last one. The candles on your cake are really a lap counter.

cards.headline: One lap, one year
cards.body: Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once, and that lap is what we call a year. It's no gentle stroll, either. Earth races along its orbit at about 30 km every second. Count to ten and you've traveled about 300 km through space, without ever leaving your chair.
cards.callout: Orbit = year · Spin = day

cards.headline: Where the quarter-days go
cards.body: Calendars count 365 days, but each orbit takes about 365.25. That spare quarter of a day looks harmless, yet it piles up: after four years, the calendar is a whole day behind Earth. So about every four years we add February 29 to catch up and keep the calendar in step with the seasons. Leap day is the calendar settling its debts.

cards.headline: A different night sky each season
cards.body: At night, your side of Earth faces away from the Sun, out into space. As Earth moves along its orbit, that night-time view swings toward different parts of space, so each season gets its own constellations. That's why Orion is a winter evening sight in the Northern Hemisphere. The view out of the back window changes as you go around the track.

cards.headline: Orbit: understood

questions.explanation: Earth’s axis stays tilted the same way as it orbits, so over one year each hemisphere leans toward the Sun (summer) and then away from it (winter).

levels.title: Connect the Dots: Constellations
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a constellation is and why its stars usually aren’t near each other.
levels.summary: There are 88 official constellations covering the sky. Their stars only line up from our viewpoint.

cards.headline: Orion isn't really a hunter, and his stars aren't even neighbors.
cards.body: A constellation is a picture we see from one spot in space: Earth. So what's actually up there?

cards.headline: From pictures to borders
cards.body: People have long joined up the stars into patterns and named them after figures, animals and objects. Today astronomers go further: the sky is divided into 88 official constellations, each one a region with set boundaries, like countries on a map. Together they cover the whole sky, so every star lands in some constellation, even the ones that aren't part of any picture.
cards.callout: Official count: 88

cards.headline: A trick of perspective
cards.body: Stars that look side by side can be very different distances from Earth. Remember light-years from Level 8? One star in a pattern could be a few dozen light-years away, its neighbor hundreds. They only look close together from where we stand, the way a faraway streetlight can seem to sit right next to your neighbor's porch light.

cards.fact: The Big Dipper is not a constellation.
cards.context: It's an asterism: a familiar star pattern that isn't one of the official constellations. The Dipper is part of the constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear. So if you've ever spotted the saucepan, congratulations: you've also seen part of a bear.

levels.title: The North Star
levels.objective: After this level you can find north with Polaris and explain why some stars never set.
levels.summary: Polaris sits above the North Pole, so it stays put while the sky wheels around it. Its height gives your latitude.

cards.headline: One star barely moves all night. Find it, and you've found north.
cards.body: Watch the sky for a few hours and the stars wheel slowly around. All but one, which sits almost still, as if the whole sky were pinned to it.

cards.headline: The star above the pole
cards.body: That star is Polaris, the North Star, and it lies almost directly above Earth's North Pole. As Earth spins, every other star circles around it while Polaris stays nearly fixed, like the hub of a turning wheel. Face it and you're facing north. One surprise: it isn't the brightest star in the sky. That's Sirius. Polaris is famous for where it sits, not how it shines.
cards.callout: Polaris = north

cards.headline: Stars that never set
cards.body: From mid-northern latitudes, stars close to Polaris trace small circles around it that never dip below the horizon. They're called circumpolar stars. While the rest of the sky rises and sets, these never leave: their circles around the pole stay above the horizon all night. And Polaris doubles as a free GPS. Its height above your horizon, in degrees, roughly equals your latitude.

cards.fact: Polaris won't be the North Star forever.
cards.context: Earth's axis slowly wobbles like a spinning top, tracing a circle about every 26,000 years, so over the ages the pole points at different stars. The Southern Hemisphere already knows the feeling: it has no bright pole star at all, so navigators there have used the Southern Cross to find south.

levels.title: The Ecliptic: The Planets’ Highway
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Sun, Moon and planets all travel along the same narrow band of sky.
levels.summary: The ecliptic is the Sun’s yearly path. The Moon and planets stay near it because the solar system is flat.

cards.headline: The planets don't roam the whole sky. They stick to one narrow road.
cards.body: The Sun, the Moon and every planet keep to the same slim strip of sky. It's no coincidence. It's a clue to the shape of the solar system.

cards.headline: The Sun's yearly path
cards.body: As Earth orbits, the Sun seems to drift slowly against the background stars, and after a year it's back where it started. The path the Sun appears to follow across the sky over a year is called the ecliptic. The zodiac constellations lie along it, plus a 13th that tradition leaves out: Ophiuchus. Sorry, Ophiuchus.
cards.callout: Ecliptic = the Sun's path over a year

cards.headline: A flat solar system
cards.body: Why does everything use the same road? The planets all orbit the Sun in nearly the same flat plane, and the Moon's orbit lies close to it too. Hold a dinner plate edge-on at eye level and everything on it lines up in a thin line. We're looking at the solar system edge-on from inside, and that line is the ecliptic. So a bright "star" near where the Sun set may well be a planet.

cards.fact: Eclipses can only happen when the Moon is on the ecliptic.
cards.context: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to the ecliptic, so most months the new Moon passes just above or below the Sun's path. Near miss. Only when a new or full Moon lands close to where the two paths cross do we get an eclipse.

levels.title: Wanderers: How Planets Move Across the Sky
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why planets drift against the stars and sometimes appear to loop backwards.
levels.summary: Planets drift against the stars as they orbit. When Earth overtakes an outer planet, it seems to go backwards: retrograde motion.

cards.headline: Every few years, Mars seems to stop, reverse and loop back across the sky.
cards.body: It never actually turns around. You're watching from a moving planet, and that changes what you see.

cards.headline: The wanderers
cards.body: Night after night, the stars hold their patterns. Planets don't: they slowly shift position against the background stars as they orbit the Sun, always keeping to the ecliptic road from Level 15. The ancient Greeks noticed these drifting lights, and the word "planet" comes from their word for "wanderer." The stars stay put; the planets go for a stroll.

cards.headline: Overtaking on the inside lane
cards.body: Earth orbits closer to the Sun than Mars does, and it moves faster. Every so often Earth, on its faster inner orbit, catches up with Mars and overtakes it. For a while, Mars appears to slide backwards against the stars, then it carries on forward. You've seen this on the highway: pass a slower car and it seems to drift backwards, though you're both going forward.
cards.callout: Retrograde = an overtaking illusion

cards.fact: Retrograde motion is only apparent.
cards.context: No planet ever reverses direction in its orbit. The backwards loop is a change in our viewpoint, not in the planet's path. Mars has no idea it's doing anything strange.

levels.title: Tides: The Moon’s Pull on the Ocean
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why most coasts get two high tides a day and what spring and neap tides are.
levels.summary: The Moon’s gravity makes two bulges of ocean water. Earth spins through both each day; the Sun makes tides bigger or smaller.

cards.headline: The Moon moves oceans. Twice a day.
cards.body: Every beach you've ever visited is being tugged by the Moon. The odd part is that most coasts get two high tides a day, not one.

cards.headline: Two bulges, not one
cards.body: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans and stretches them into two bulges: one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side of Earth. Earth spins through both bulges, so most coastlines get two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours and 50 minutes. High tide isn't the sea coming to visit. It's your beach passing under a bulge.
cards.callout: Two bulges → two high tides

cards.headline: The Sun joins in
cards.body: The Sun pulls on the oceans too, just more weakly than the Moon. Around new and full Moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up and their pulls combine: extra-high highs and extra-low lows, called spring tides. Around the quarter Moons, the Sun and Moon pull at right angles and the tides are gentler: neap tides. Teamwork makes big tides.

cards.fact: Spring tides have nothing to do with spring.
cards.context: They happen twice a month, all year round, including the middle of winter. They follow the Moon's phases, not the calendar. Blame the name, not the season.
